Which statement best compares the standard deviations of scores for these teams?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: D

whyCorrect: Standard deviation measures how far the values sit from their own mean, so you compare spread, not centre or total. Team A's scores all fall between 25 and 40 and pile up in the middle of that band, while team B's scores run from 20 to 50 with the biggest groups at the two ends and a dip in the middle. Values clustered near the centre give a small standard deviation; values pushed out to both extremes give a large one, so team A's is the smaller.

whyWrong.B: This reverses the comparison. Team A looks taller only because its scores are packed into fewer intervals, and bar height is frequency, not spread.
whyWrong.C: The two distributions have visibly different shapes — one tightly clustered, one spread to both ends — so their standard deviations cannot be equal.
whyWrong.D: The full distribution of both teams is given, which is everything the standard deviation depends on, so it can be compared.

The mean weight of the objects in group A is equal to 2.1, and the mean weight of the objects in group B is equal to 11.1. Which of the following statements about the standard deviations of weight for the objects in these two groups is true?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The standard deviation of weight for the objects in group A is less than the standard deviation of weight for the objects in group B.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The standard deviation of weight for the objects in group A is equal to the standard deviation of weight for the objects in group B.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The standard deviation of weight for the objects in group A is greater than the standard deviation of weight for the objects in group B.

choices.label: D
choices.content: There is not enough information to compare the standard deviations of weight for the objects in these two groups.

whyCorrect: The two groups cover the same 5-gram width, so what separates them is where the objects sit inside that width relative to their own mean. In group A the two tallest columns are at the far ends, so most objects are about 2 grams away from the mean of 2.1. In group B half the objects are in the single middle interval, right at the mean of 11.1, and only 4 of the 20 are at the ends. Larger typical distance from the mean means a larger standard deviation, so group A's is greater.

whyWrong.A: This reverses the comparison. Group B has the taller single bar, but bar height is how many objects share a weight, not how far apart the weights are.
whyWrong.B: The shapes are different — A is heaviest at both ends, B is heaviest in the middle — so the spreads cannot be equal.
whyWrong.D: The whole distribution of each group is given, and standard deviation depends only on that, so the comparison can be made. The very different means do not block it, because standard deviation measures distance from each group's own mean.

note: Source prints two histograms (Number of objects against Weight, width-1 bins). Converted to equivalent frequency tables; the means quoted in the stem are the book's.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. Which of the following equations is the most appropriate linear model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: Two features of the plot decide this without any calculation. The points fall as x increases, so the slope must be negative, which rules out any equation with a positive x coefficient. And near x = 0 the points sit around y = 25, so the constant term has to be close to 25, not 6. Only y = 28 - 6x has both a negative slope and a constant near 25.

whyWrong.A: The coefficient of x is +28, so this model rises steeply; the data falls.
whyWrong.B: The slope is negative, but the constant term 6 puts the line near y = 6 at x = 0, while the data starts around y = 25 there. This is the answer you get by pairing the right sign with the wrong two numbers.
whyWrong.C: Both numbers are the right size but the slope is positive, so the line rises when the data falls.

note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to 4 and y from 5 to 30. Points approximately (0, 25), (0.3, 26), (0.6, 24), (1.3, 17), (2, 13), (2.5, 14), (3, 7), (3.5, 8). | figure: Page shows the points at x = 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5; the recorded note gave 0, 0.3, 0.6, 1.3, ... Drawn from the page.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. A line of best fit is also shown. Which of the following best represents the line of best fit shown?
whyCorrect: All four choices share the same intercept, so only the slope can tell them apart — find how much y climbs per unit of x. The line starts near y = 77 at x = 0 and reaches roughly y = 865 at x = 10, a rise of about 790 over a run of 10, so the slope is about 79.

whyWrong.A: A slope of 0.01 would make the line essentially flat, rising by 0.1 across the whole graph, while the line climbs by hundreds.
whyWrong.B: A slope of 0.79 would take the line from 77 to only about 85 by x = 10 — still visually flat.
whyWrong.C: A slope of 68.9 puts the line at about 766 when x = 10, which is below the 800 gridline; the drawn line is above it there. This is the trap for reading the run as slightly too long or the rise as slightly too short.

note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to 10 and y from 0 to about 900, with a line of best fit from about (0, 77) to (10, 865). Points approximately (1, 90), (3, 280), (4, 490), (6, 620), (8, 710), (9, 690).

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. A line of best fit is also shown. Which of the following equations best represents the line of best fit shown?
whyCorrect: Read the two ends of the drawn line. It meets the y-axis at about 3.5, which kills any equation with a negative constant, and it reaches about y = 16 when x = 8. That is a rise of about 12.4 over a run of 8, so the slope is roughly 1.55, not 1.8.

whyWrong.A: The intercept is right but a slope of 1.8 would put the line at 3.5 + 14.4 = 17.9 when x = 8, above the top of the graph. Check the far end of the line, not just where it starts.
whyWrong.B: A constant of -2.4 puts the line below the x-axis at x = 0, but the drawn line crosses the y-axis above 3.
whyWrong.D: The slope is negative, so this line falls; the data and the drawn line both rise.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. Which of the equations is the most appropriate model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: The points fall to a lowest value and then rise again, so the model is a parabola, and the only things to match are where the bottom sits. The lowest points are near x = 0 with y just under 10, so the vertex is at about (0, 8). Writing the vertex form, a parabola with vertex on the y-axis at height 8 is \( y = x^{2} + 8 \).

whyWrong.A: \( y = x^{2} - 8 \) has its vertex at (0, -8), so it would predict negative y-values near x = 0; every plotted point has y above 8.
whyWrong.C: \( y = (x-8)^{2} \) has its vertex at x = 8, off to the right of every point shown, so it would be decreasing across the whole graph instead of turning around near x = 0.
whyWrong.D: \( y = (x+8)^{2} \) has its vertex at x = -8, so it would be increasing across the whole graph. The sign inside the parentheses shifts the curve left or right, not up or down.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. Which of the following equations is the most appropriate linear model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: The data falls as x increases, so the coefficient of x is negative — that rules out the two choices with a plus sign. Between the remaining two, the constant is the predicted value at x = 0. Extending the pattern back from (1, 7) gives about 8 or 9 there, so the constant is 8.7. The drop of about 6 units across 9 units of x also matches a slope of -0.8, not -8.7.

whyWrong.A: Positive slope; the line rises while the data falls.
whyWrong.B: Right sign, but the numbers are swapped. A slope of -8.7 would send the line from 0.8 down past -70 by x = 9.
whyWrong.C: Right constant, wrong sign on the slope.

stem: The scatterplot shows the recorded temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, against time, in days since June 1. During which of the following time periods did the greatest increase in recorded temperature take place?
whyCorrect: An increase means the later point is higher than the earlier one, so first discard any interval where the graph goes down. Only two intervals rise: 2 to 3 and 6 to 7. From x = 2 to x = 3 the temperature climbs from about 60°F to about 75°F, a jump of roughly 15 degrees, while from x = 6 to x = 7 it rises only about 2 degrees.

whyWrong.A: This interval does rise, but only from about 62°F to about 64°F — a much smaller increase.
whyWrong.B: From x = 5 to x = 6 the temperature falls, from about 67°F to about 62°F. A large change is not the same as a large increase.
whyWrong.D: From x = 1 to x = 2 the temperature falls from about 69°F to about 60°F. This is the biggest change of all, which is why it is the trap, but it is a decrease.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, for the data set P. A line of best fit for the data is also shown. Data set Q is created by adding 540 units to the value of x for each data point from the data set P. Which of the following could be an equation of a line of best fit for the data set Q?
whyCorrect: Sliding every point 540 units to the right shifts the line right by 540 but does not tilt it, so the slope is unchanged and only the constant moves. First get the slope from the graph: the drawn line climbs from about 14.2 at x = 100 to about 14.95 at x = 130, a rise of 0.75 over a run of 30, or about 0.027 — that is \( \frac{35}{1301} \), not \( \frac{1}{131} \approx 0.0076 \). Then apply the shift: replacing x by x - 540 lowers the constant by \( 540 \times \frac{35}{1301} \approx 14.5 \), and the original constant is about 14.2 - 100(0.027) ≈ 11.5, leaving about -3.

whyWrong.B: The slope \( \frac{1}{131} \) is about a third of the slope drawn on the graph, so this line is far too flat whatever its constant is.
whyWrong.C: Same wrong slope as choice B.
whyWrong.D: This has the right slope but the constant has been moved the wrong way. Shifting the data to larger x must decrease the value at x = 0, not raise it by about 14.5.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. Which of the following equations is the most appropriate model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: The points climb at a steady rate — equal steps right produce roughly equal steps up — so the model is linear, not exponential, and it is increasing. That leaves only y = -582 + 1.2x, whose slope of 1.2 matches the roughly one-to-one climb across the graph.

whyWrong.B: The coefficient of x is negative, so this model falls as x grows, while the data rises.
whyWrong.C: An exponential with a negative coefficient in front gives negative y-values for every x; all the plotted points are positive.
whyWrong.D: This grows by a factor of 1.2 for each increase of 1 in x. Over the plotted range, which runs to x = 4,000, that is an unimaginably large number, not 4,000. Exponential growth would also show as a curve that steepens, and these points lie on a straight path.

stem: In the given scatterplot, a line of best fit for the data is shown. Which of the following is closest to the slope of this line of best fit?
whyCorrect: The line falls from left to right, so the slope is negative — that removes both positive choices immediately. For the size, take two points on the line: it starts near (0, 7.5) and reaches about (10, 1), a drop of roughly 6.5 across 10 units of x, so the slope is about -0.65, closest to -0.7.

whyWrong.A: A slope of -7 would drop 7 units for every single unit of x; this line takes the whole width of the graph to drop that far.
whyWrong.C: Right size, wrong sign. A positive slope rises.
whyWrong.D: Wrong sign and about ten times too steep.

stem: The scatterplot shows the body length, in centimeters (cm), of a New Zealand fur seal from an age of 1 to 6 years old. A line of best fit is also shown. For a New Zealand fur seal at an age of 3 years old, what is the body length in centimeters predicted by the line of best fit, to the nearest 10 cm?
whyCorrect: The question asks what the line predicts, not where a data point sits, so go up from x = 3 to the line rather than to any dot. The line runs from about 88 cm at age 1 to about 135 cm at age 6, climbing roughly 9.4 cm per year, which puts it near 107 cm at age 3. Rounded to the nearest 10 cm that is 110.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, together with a line of best fit. Which of the following best represents the line of best fit shown?
whyCorrect: All four choices start at 148.13, so only the slope separates them — work out how much y gains per unit of x. The line climbs from about 148 at x = 0 to about 735 at x = 10, a rise of roughly 590 over 10, so the slope is close to 59. The two small slopes can be dismissed on sight, since a slope under 1 would leave the line essentially flat while this line climbs by hundreds.

whyWrong.A: A slope of 0.02 raises y by only 0.2 across the whole graph — a flat line.
whyWrong.B: A slope of 0.59 raises y by about 6 across the whole graph, still flat at this scale.
whyWrong.C: 48.61 is the right order of magnitude but too shallow: it puts the line at about 634 when x = 10, well below where the drawn line ends.

stem: The graph models the number of active projects a company was working on x months after the end of November 2011, where 0 ≤ x ≤ 6. According to the model, what is the predicted number of active projects the company was working on at the end of November 2011?
whyCorrect: "At the end of November 2011" is zero months after the end of November 2011, so set x = 0 and read the height of the curve where it meets the y-axis. That value is 8.

whyWrong.A: 0 is the x-value you substitute, not the y-value you read off. The curve does not touch the x-axis anywhere.
whyWrong.C: 11 is the value at x = 2 and again at x = 6, not at x = 0.
whyWrong.D: 12 is the highest point of the curve, reached at x = 4 — the maximum over the whole period, not the starting value.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, together with a line of best fit. Which of the following equations best represents the line of best fit shown?

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, for data set A. A line of best fit for the data is also shown. Data set B is created by subtracting 9 units from the value of y for each data point from data set A. Which of the following is closest to the y-coordinate of the y-intercept of the line of best fit for data set B?
whyCorrect: Lowering every y-value by 9 slides the whole line down 9 units without tilting it, so the new intercept is the old intercept minus 9. Get the old one by extending the drawn line back to the y-axis: it passes through roughly (12, 45) and (37, 20), a slope of about -1, so at x = 0 it is near 57 — and the only choice 9 below a value in that region is 45.57. The trap is that the line starts well to the right of the y-axis, so the intercept has to be extrapolated, not read.

whyWrong.B: 53 would require the original line to cross at 62, which is above the top of the plotted y-axis and far above where the drawn line is heading.
whyWrong.C: 59.62 is roughly the original intercept region, so this is the answer you get by forgetting to subtract the 9.
whyWrong.D: 62.75 is higher still, and would need a much steeper line than the one drawn.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. Which of the following equations is the most appropriate linear model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: The points rise as x increases, so the slope is positive and the two negative choices are out. For the size, compare a point's two coordinates: near x = 9 the value of y is about 10, and near x = 4 it is about 4.5. The y-value stays close to the x-value, so the slope is about 1, not 2.

whyWrong.A: Negative slope, and twice too steep; this line falls below the x-axis for every positive x.
whyWrong.B: Negative slope — the model would fall while the data rises.
whyWrong.D: A slope of 2 predicts y = 18 when x = 9, but the plotted value there is about 10. Doubling is the trap if you only check that the data rises.

stem:
In the figure, parallel lines a and b are intersected by lines c, d, and e. If x = 49, y = 136, and v < z, which statement about x and w must be true?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Look for the two triangles that x and w each sit in. Line c cuts both parallel lines, so the angle it makes with b and the angle it makes with a are equal — and each of those triangles has that same angle, 180 - 136 = 44 degrees, as a second angle. In the triangle containing x, the third angle is v, so x = 180 - 44 - v = 136 - v. In the triangle containing w, the third angle is z, so w = 136 - z by exactly the same count. Since v < z, subtracting the smaller number leaves the larger result, so x > w. (As a check, x = 49 forces v = 87, and z must then exceed 87.)

whyWrong.A: This is the comparison you get by carrying v < z straight through to x and w, but both appear subtracted from 136, which flips the inequality.
whyWrong.C: x = w would require v = z, and the problem states v < z.
whyWrong.D: x + w = 136 - v + 136 - z = 272 - (v + z), which is only 90 if v + z = 182 — nothing in the problem forces that.

note: Figure: two parallel vertical lines, a on the left and b on the right, crossed by three slanted lines. Line d runs down to the right across both, meeting a at the point where v is marked (right of a, below d). Line c runs up to the right across both, meeting b at the point where y is marked (right of b, below c). Lines c and d meet to the right of b at the point where x is marked (the wedge opening rightward). Line e runs down to the right across both, meeting b where z is marked (right of b, below e); c and e meet to the left of a, at the point where w is marked (the wedge opening leftward).
imageAlt: Geometry diagram: two parallel vertical lines labelled a and b crossed by three slanted lines labelled c, d and e; five of the angles formed are labelled with letters. Figure not drawn to scale.

stem: For two acute angles, ∠A and ∠B, \( \cos A = \sin B \). The measures, in degrees, of ∠A and ∠B are x + 8 and 4x + 2, respectively. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: For acute angles, the cosine of one equals the sine of another exactly when the two angles are complementary — that is the meaning of "co-sine". So set the measures to add to 90: (x + 8) + (4x + 2) = 90, giving 5x + 10 = 90 and x = 16. Check: the angles are 24° and 66°, which add to 90°.

whyWrong.A: 37 makes the angles 45° and 150°. Those sum to 195°, and 150° is not acute, so both stated conditions fail.
whyWrong.B: 34 makes the angles 42° and 138°, which sum to 180°, not 90°. Supplementary is the wrong relationship — that is what equal sines would give.
whyWrong.D: 2 makes the angles 10° and 10°. Equal angles would mean sin A = sin B, not cos A = sin B.

stem: For two acute angles ∠Q and ∠R, \( \cos Q = \sin R \). The measures, in degrees, of ∠Q and ∠R are x + 21 and 4x + 9, respectively. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: For acute angles, cosine and sine are equal exactly when the angles are complementary, so the two measures must add to 90. Solve (x + 21) + (4x + 9) = 90: that is 5x + 30 = 90, so x = 12. The angles are then 33° and 57°, which add to 90°.

whyWrong.A: 4 makes the angles 25° and 25°. Equal angles would give sin Q = sin R, not cos Q = sin R.
whyWrong.C: 30 makes the angles 51° and 129°, a sum of 180°. Supplementary is the wrong relationship, and 129° is not acute.
whyWrong.D: 69 makes the angles 90° and 285°, neither of which is acute, so it cannot satisfy the setup at all.

stem: The measure of angle R is \( \frac{2\pi}{3} \) radians. The measure of angle T is \( \frac{13\pi}{18} \) radians greater than the measure of angle R. What is the measure of angle T, in degrees?
whyCorrect: Add the two radian measures first, using a common denominator of 18: \( \frac{2\pi}{3} = \frac{12\pi}{18} \), so angle T is \( \frac{12\pi}{18} + \frac{13\pi}{18} = \frac{25\pi}{18} \) radians. Then multiply by \( \frac{180}{\pi} \) to convert: \( \frac{25\pi}{18} \times \frac{180}{\pi} = 25 \times 10 = 250 \) degrees.

whyWrong.A: 120 is angle R alone in degrees; the 13π/18 was never added.
whyWrong.B: 130 is the 13π/18 part alone in degrees; angle R was never added.
whyWrong.D: 500 comes from converting with a factor of 360/π instead of 180/π, or from doubling the correct answer.

stem:
In the figure, two lines intersect at a point. If w = 150, what is the value of z?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The angle marked w is above the crossing point and the angle marked z is below it, so they are vertical angles — opposite each other across the intersection, not side by side. Vertical angles are always equal, so z = 150. The figure not being drawn to scale does not matter; the relationship holds either way.

whyWrong.A: 30 is 180 - 150, which is the size of the two angles at the sides of the crossing. Those are supplementary to w, not equal to it, and z is not one of them.
whyWrong.B: 50 has no basis here; it looks like dividing 150 by 3.
whyWrong.C: 75 is half of 150; nothing in the figure halves the angle.

note: Figure: two straight lines crossing at one point, forming an X. The angle above the crossing is labelled w and the angle below it is labelled z. | figure: The book prints "Note: Figure not drawn to scale." beneath the figure; it is already carried in the question stem, so it is not repeated in the image.
imageAlt: Two straight lines crossing at a single point, forming an X. One angle above the crossing point is labelled w degrees and one angle below it is labelled z degrees.

stem:
In the figure shown, line r is parallel to line s, and both lines are intersected by line t. If x = 2w + 24, y = 5w + 29, and 7w = a, where a is a constant, what is the value of a?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The marked angles sit on the same side of the transversal, one below it and one above it, at the two parallel lines — so they are co-interior and add to 180, not equal. Write (2w + 24) + (5w + 29) = 180, which gives 7w + 53 = 180 and 7w = 127. The question asks for a = 7w, so you never need w itself: the answer is 127.
note: Figure: two parallel vertical lines, r on the left and s on the right, crossed by a line t that rises to the right. x is marked in the wedge to the left of r and below t; y is marked in the wedge to the left of s and above t.
imageAlt: Two parallel vertical lines r and s cut by a transversal t that rises to the right; one angle is marked at each intersection, labelled x degrees and y degrees.

stem: In the figure, line n intersects lines r and s. Line r is parallel to line s. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: Both marked angles sit in the same position relative to their intersection — above the horizontal line and to the right of n — so they are corresponding angles. When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal, so x = 164. No subtraction from 180 is needed, because the two angles are matching, not adjacent.
note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, r above and s below, crossed by a line n running from upper left to lower right. The 164-degree angle is marked above r and to the right of n; x is marked above s and to the right of n.
imageAlt: Two parallel horizontal lines r and s cut by a transversal n; one angle at the upper intersection carries a degree measure and an angle at the lower intersection is labelled x degrees.

stem: The difference between the measure of angle A and the measure of angle B is \( -\frac{3}{4}\pi \) radians. Which expression shows the difference between the measure of angle A and the measure of angle B, in degrees?
whyCorrect: To turn radians into degrees you multiply the whole radian measure by \( \frac{180^{\circ}}{\pi} \), because π radians and 180° are the same angle. The radian measure here is \( -\frac{3}{4}\pi \), all of it, so the expression is \( -\frac{3}{4}\pi \cdot \frac{180^{\circ}}{\pi} \). (It works out to -135°, which is a useful check.)

whyWrong.A: The π from the radian measure has been dropped, so this is \( -\frac{3}{4} \) of \( \frac{180}{\pi} \), about -43°, not -135°.
whyWrong.B: This uses the reverse conversion factor, \( \frac{\pi}{180^{\circ}} \), which turns degrees into radians. It gives about -0.04, far too small.
whyWrong.D: 360° corresponds to 2π radians, not π, so this factor doubles the result to -270°.

stem: In the figure, parallel lines r and s are intersected by lines t, u, and w. If d = 42, g = 143, and h > d, which statement about j and p must be true?
whyCorrect: Work with the angle each slanted line makes with the horizontal parallel lines. Because r and s are parallel, the angle a line makes at r is the same angle it makes at s, so h describes the tilt of line u and d describes the tilt of line w, while g describes the tilt of line t. Where two slanted lines meet, the angle between them is the difference of their tilts: \(j = g - h = 143 - h\) and \(p = g - d = 143 - 42 = 101\). Since h > 42, subtracting h takes away more than subtracting 42 does, so \(j \lt 101 = p\).

whyWrong.A: This would require h = d. You are told h > d, which is exactly the condition that forces the two angles apart.
whyWrong.B: p is already 101 on its own, so \(j+p\) cannot be 90 for any positive j.
whyWrong.C: This reverses the inequality. A larger h means a steeper line u relative to t, which makes the angle between them smaller, not larger.

note: Figure needed: horizontal parallel lines r (upper) and s (lower). Line t descends steeply left-to-right, line u ascends steeply left-to-right, and they cross above r with angle j marked in the upward-opening region between them. g is marked at t's intersection with r, in the region above r and right of t. h is marked at u's intersection with s, above s and right of u. Line w ascends left-to-right on the right side; d is marked at its intersection with r, above r and right of w. Lines t and w cross below s, with p marked in the downward-opening region between them.
imageAlt: Two horizontal parallel lines r and s cut by three slanted lines t, u and w; five of the angles formed are labelled with variables.

stem:
In the figure, line p is parallel to line q, and t intersects both of them. What is the value of x + 142?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The two marked angles sit side by side on the same side of line q, split by the transversal, so together they make the straight angle along q. That means x + 142 = 180 directly — you never have to find x on its own, and the fact that p is parallel to q is not needed at all.

whyWrong.A: 52 is not the sum of anything here; it may come from 142 - 90.
whyWrong.B: 90 would mean the two angles are complementary, but they lie along a straight line, not in a right angle.
whyWrong.C: 142 is one of the two angles; the question asks for their sum, so x is being treated as 0. This is the answer if you read the question as asking only for the marked value.

note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, p above and q below, crossed by a line t that descends from upper left to lower right. At t's crossing of q, x is marked above q on the left of t and 142 degrees is marked above q on the right of t.
imageAlt: Two parallel horizontal lines p and q cut by a transversal t; at the lower intersection one angle is labelled x degrees and the angle beside it carries a degree measure.

stem: In the figure shown, line m is parallel to line n, and line k intersects both lines. Which of the following statements is true?
whyCorrect: Work from the 135-degree angle, which sits below n on the left of k. The angle marked s is directly opposite it across the crossing point — above n on the right of k — so they are vertical angles and s = 135. Every other marked angle is on the same side of k or the same side of the horizontal line as the 135, which makes it a linear pair instead, worth 45.

whyWrong.A: q is above m on the left of k, which corresponds to the angle above n on the left of k. That one pairs with s along line n, so q = 45.
whyWrong.B: r is vertical to q, so r = 45 as well.
whyWrong.D: t is below n on the right of k, sharing line n with the 135-degree angle. They form a straight angle, so t = 45.

note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, m above and n below, crossed by a line k descending from upper left to lower right. At k's crossing of m: q is marked above m to the left of k, r below m to the right of k. At k's crossing of n: s is marked above n to the right of k, t below n to the right of k, and 135 degrees below n to the left of k.
imageAlt: Two parallel horizontal lines m and n cut by a transversal k; four angles are labelled with letters and one with a degree measure.

stem:
In the figure, line q is parallel to line r, and both lines are intersected by line s. If y = 2x + 9, what is the value of x?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Find y first. The 61-degree angle is above q on the right of s, while y is above r on the left of s — opposite sides of the transversal — so they are co-interior rather than corresponding, and y = 180 - 61 = 119. Then solve 119 = 2x + 9, giving 2x = 110 and x = 55.

whyWrong.A: 26 comes from setting y = 61 (treating the two angles as equal) and solving 61 = 2x + 9.
whyWrong.B: 35 comes from 2x + 9 = 79 or a similar slip; no angle in the figure measures 79 degrees.
whyWrong.D: 65 comes from solving 2x + 9 = 139, or from using 180 - 61 = 119 but then dividing before subtracting the 9.

note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, q above and r below, crossed by a line s rising from lower left to upper right. The 61-degree angle is marked above q to the right of s; y is marked above r to the left of s.
imageAlt: Two parallel horizontal lines q and r cut by a transversal s that rises to the right; one angle at the upper intersection carries a degree measure and one at the lower intersection is labelled y.

stem: In triangle ABC, the measure of angle A is 47°, the measure of angle B is 90°, and the measure of angle C is \( \left(\frac{k}{2}\right)^{\circ} \). What is the value of k?
whyCorrect: The three angles of a triangle add to 180, so angle C measures 180 - 47 - 90 = 43 degrees. But 43 is \( \frac{k}{2} \), not k, so multiply by 2: k = 86. The last step is the whole question — stopping at the angle instead of solving for the letter is the mistake it is built around.

whyWrong.A: 43 is the measure of angle C in degrees, which equals k/2, not k.
whyWrong.B: 45 comes from assuming the two non-right angles are equal, which would need angle A to be 45 as well.
whyWrong.D: 94 is twice 47, using angle A instead of angle C.

stem:
In the figure, two lines intersect at a point. If w = 128, what is the value of z?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The angle marked w sits above the crossing point and the angle marked z sits below it, directly opposite. Angles opposite each other at an intersection are vertical angles and are always equal, so z = 128.

whyWrong.A: 28 is 128 - 100, or a misread of 180 - 128.
whyWrong.B: 52 is 180 - 128, the size of the angles at the left and right of the crossing. Those are supplementary to w, but z is not one of them.
whyWrong.C: 64 is half of 128; nothing here bisects the angle.

note: Figure: two straight lines crossing at one point, forming an X. The angle above the crossing is labelled w and the angle below it is labelled z. Same structure as Lines&Angles question 11 in this book.
imageAlt: Two straight lines crossing at one point; the angle above the crossing is labelled w degrees and the angle below it is labelled z degrees.

stem:
In the figure shown, line l intersects lines j and k. Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that lines j and k are parallel?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: A fact only proves the lines parallel if it links the two intersections; a fact that is already forced within one intersection tells you nothing. The angle w sits above k on the right of l, exactly the position the 35-degree angle occupies above j, so w and 35 are corresponding angles. Corresponding angles are equal precisely when the lines are parallel, so w = 35° settles it.

whyWrong.B: x is vertical to w, so x = 145° would force w = 145°, which is not 35° — that would prove the lines are not parallel.
whyWrong.C: y is vertical to the 35-degree angle at the same intersection, so y = 35° is true no matter what line k does. It adds nothing.
whyWrong.D: z forms a straight angle with the 35-degree angle along line j, so z = 145° is automatically true and says nothing about k.

note: Figure: two roughly horizontal lines, k above and j below, both crossed by a line l rising from lower left to upper right. At l's crossing of k: w is marked above k to the right of l, x below k to the left of l. At l's crossing of j: 35 degrees is marked above j to the right of l, y below j to the left of l, z below j to the right of l.
imageAlt: Geometry diagram: two horizontal lines labelled k and j crossed by a slanted line labelled l; one angle is given a degree measure and four others are labelled with letters. Figure not drawn to scale.

stem: In the figure shown, the lines l and k are parallel and line t intersects both lines. If x > 154, which of the following must be true?
whyCorrect: x is above l on the right of t and y is above k on the left of t — opposite sides of the transversal — so with the lines parallel they are co-interior and x + y = 180 exactly. Then y = 180 - x, and x > 154 gives y < 180 - 154 = 26. Subtracting flips the inequality, which is the step the question is testing.

whyWrong.B: This carries the direction of x > 154 straight over to y, but y is 180 minus x, so a bigger x makes a smaller y.
whyWrong.C: x + y is exactly 180, never less.
whyWrong.D: x + y is exactly 180, never more. Both C and D fail for the same reason: the sum is fixed, so no strict inequality holds.

note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, l above and k below, crossed by a line t descending from upper left to lower right. x is marked above l to the right of t; y is marked above k to the left of t.
imageAlt: Two parallel horizontal lines l and k cut by a transversal t; one angle at each intersection is labelled, x degrees at the upper line and y degrees at the lower line.

stem: In the figure shown, line k intersects lines r and s. If w = 146°, which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that lines r and s are parallel?
whyCorrect: Only a fact that ties the two intersections together can prove parallelism. The angle y occupies the same corner at line s that w occupies at line r — above k and to the right of the vertical line — so w and y are corresponding angles. They are equal exactly when the lines are parallel, so y = 146 does it.

whyWrong.A: x and w lie on the same side of line r, split by k, so x = 180 - 146 = 34 is already forced. It says nothing about s.
whyWrong.C: w + y = 180 would make y = 34, not 146, which would prove the lines are not parallel.
whyWrong.D: y and z lie on the same side of line s, split by k, so their sum is 180 whatever r does.

note: Figure: two vertical lines, r on the left and s on the right, crossed by a line k descending from upper left to lower right. At k's crossing of r: w is marked to the right of r and above k, x to the right of r and below k. At k's crossing of s: y is marked to the right of s and above k, z to the right of s and below k.
imageAlt: Geometry diagram: two vertical lines labelled r and s crossed by a slanted line labelled k; the four angles at the two crossings are labelled with letters.

stem: The difference between the measure of angle A and the measure of angle B is \( -\frac{5}{12}\pi \) radians. Which expression shows the difference between the measure of angle A and the measure of angle B, in degrees?
whyCorrect: Radians become degrees when you multiply by \( \frac{180^{\circ}}{\pi} \), since π radians is 180°. Apply it to the whole radian measure: \( -\frac{5}{12}\pi \cdot \frac{180^{\circ}}{\pi} \), which simplifies to -75°.

whyWrong.B: \( \frac{\pi}{180^{\circ}} \) is the factor that converts degrees into radians, so this runs the conversion backwards.
whyWrong.C: This has both errors at once: the reciprocal factor and 360 in place of 180.
whyWrong.D: 360° corresponds to 2π radians, not π, so this factor is twice too large and gives -150°.

note: Same template as Lines&Angles question 17 in this book, with -5/12 pi in place of -3/4 pi.

stem: In the figure shown, line t intersects lines j and k. Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that lines j and k are parallel?
whyCorrect: Three of these facts are already true no matter how the lines are drawn, so they cannot prove anything. The angle w sits above j on the right of t, the same corner the 54-degree angle occupies above k, so w and 54 are corresponding angles — equal exactly when j and k are parallel.

whyWrong.B: x is vertical to w, so x = 126 would force w = 126, contradicting the 54 needed for parallel lines.
whyWrong.C: y is vertical to the 54-degree angle at the same intersection, so y = 54 holds regardless and says nothing about j.
whyWrong.D: z and the 54-degree angle form a straight angle along k, so z = 126 is automatic.

note: Figure: two roughly horizontal lines, j above and k below, crossed by a line t rising from lower left to upper right. At t's crossing of j: w is marked above j to the right of t, x below j to the left of t. At t's crossing of k: 54 degrees is marked above k to the right of t, y below k to the left of t, z below k to the right of t. Same template as Lines&Angles question 28 in this book. | figure: The printed figure leaves the transversal unlabelled although the stem calls it line t; the label t has been added so the stem's wording matches the picture. Nothing else was added.
imageAlt: Geometry diagram: two horizontal lines labelled j and k crossed by a slanted line labelled t; one angle is given a degree measure and four others are labelled with letters.

stem: In triangle ABC, the measure of angle A is 34° and the measure of angle B is 90°. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle C?
whyCorrect: The angles of any triangle add to 180°, so angle C = 180 - 34 - 90 = 56 degrees. Equivalently, in a right triangle the two non-right angles are complementary, so C = 90 - 34 = 56.

whyWrong.A: 34 is angle A; the two acute angles are only equal if both are 45°.
whyWrong.C: 90 is angle B; a triangle cannot have two right angles.
whyWrong.D: 180 is the total of all three angles, not one of them.

stem: In triangle DEF, the measure of ∠D is 114°. Which of the following could be the measure, in degrees, of ∠E?
whyCorrect: The three angles total 180°, so once D takes 114°, angles E and F must share the remaining 66°. Angle F has to be greater than 0, so E must be less than 66. Of the choices only 65 is under 66.

whyWrong.A: 115 alone would already push the total past 180 when added to 114.
whyWrong.C: 67 is the trap: 114 + 67 = 181, just one degree too much, leaving no room for angle F. Check the sum rather than eyeballing which values look small enough.

stem:
In the figure, line l is parallel to line m. What is the value of x?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Move the 111-degree angle across its own intersection first: it sits below m on the left of k, so the angle directly opposite it — above m on the right of k — is also 111° because vertical angles are equal. That angle is in the same corner at m that x is in at l, so the two are corresponding angles and x = 111. Both angles are obtuse in the figure, which is a quick sanity check.

whyWrong.A: 31 does not arise from any angle relationship here.
whyWrong.B: 69 is 180 - 111, the size of the acute angles at each crossing. It is what you get by treating x and the 111-degree angle as a linear pair, but they are at different intersections.
whyWrong.D: 131 has no basis; it appears to be 111 with a digit changed.

note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, l above and m below, crossed by a line k descending from upper left to lower right. x is marked above l to the right of k; 111 degrees is marked below m to the left of k.
imageAlt: Two parallel horizontal lines l and m cut by a transversal k; an angle above the upper line is labelled x degrees and an angle below the lower line carries a degree measure.

stem: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF, where angle A corresponds to angle D and angles C and F are right angles. The length \( \overline{AB} \) is 2.4 times the length of \( \overline{DE} \). If \( \tan A = \frac{21}{20} \), what is the value of \( \sin D \)?
whyCorrect: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles, so angle D equals angle A and sin D = sin A. The scale factor 2.4 changes the side lengths but not the angles, so it plays no part. From tan A = 21/20, build a right triangle with legs 21 (opposite A) and 20 (adjacent), giving a hypotenuse of \( \sqrt{21^{2} + 20^{2}} = \sqrt{841} = 29 \). Then sin D = sin A = opposite over hypotenuse = 21/29.
note: The 2.4 scale factor is a distractor; it does not affect any trigonometric ratio. Decimal equivalent 0.7241.

stem: The area of a triangle is equal to \( x^{2} \) square inches. The base of the triangle is 5 + 2x inches, and the height of the triangle is x - 2 inches. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: Write the area formula with the given expressions: \( \frac{1}{2}(5 + 2x)(x - 2) = x^{2} \). Clear the fraction to get (5 + 2x)(x - 2) = 2x^2, and expand the left side to \( 2x^{2} + x - 10 \). The \( 2x^{2} \) cancels from both sides, so what looked like a quadratic collapses to x - 10 = 0 and x = 10. Check it: base 25, height 8, area 100, and \( 10^{2} = 100 \).

whyWrong.A: 2.5 makes the base 10 and the height 0.5, so the formula gives an area of 2.5 square inches, but x squared is 6.25. It is the value that makes the height smallest, not the value that balances the equation.
whyWrong.B: 2.7 is what a calculator returns if you forget the factor of one half and solve \( (5+2x)(x-2) = x^{2} \) numerically.
whyWrong.C: 5 makes the base 15 and the height 3, an area of 22.5, but \( x^{2} = 25 \).

note: Book prints "The base of triangle is"; read as "of the triangle".

stem: The area of a triangle is equal to \(x^2\) square centimeters. The length of the base of the triangle is 2x + 6 centimeters, and the height of the triangle is x − 2 centimeters. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: Write the area two ways and set them equal: \(x^2 = \frac{1}{2}(2x + 6)(x - 2)\). Halving the base first makes the algebra easy: \(\frac{1}{2}(2x+6) = x + 3\), so the right side is \((x + 3)(x - 2) = x^2 + x - 6\). The \(x^2\) terms cancel, leaving x - 6 = 0, so x = 6 (base 18, height 4, area 36).

stem: The area of triangle ABC is 30 square centimeters. What is the height h, in centimeters, of this triangle?
whyCorrect: Use area = one half times base times height with the base of 10 cm shown in the figure: \( 30 = \frac{1}{2}(10)h \), so 30 = 5h and h = 6.

whyWrong.A: 3 comes from dividing 30 by 10 and then halving again — the one half is applied twice.
whyWrong.C: 10 is the base length given in the figure, not the height.
whyWrong.D: 12 is twice the correct height. It comes from doubling the area to 60 but then dividing by 5 instead of by the full base of 10.

note: Figure: triangle ABC with horizontal base AC marked 10 cm, apex B above, and a dashed vertical segment from B to AC labelled h with a right-angle mark where it meets AC.
imageAlt: Triangle ABC with a horizontal base AC carrying a dimension arrow and its measurement, and a dashed altitude from vertex B down to the base labelled h, with a right-angle mark at its foot.

stem: In right triangle RST, the sum of the measures of angle R and angle S is 90 degrees. The value of \( \sin(R) \) is \( \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{9} \). What is the value of \( \cos(S) \)?
whyCorrect: Angles R and S add to 90 degrees, so they are complementary, and the sine of an angle always equals the cosine of its complement. That means cos(S) = sin(R) with no computation at all, so \( \cos(S) = \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{9} \). In the triangle itself, the side opposite R is the side adjacent to S, and both ratios use the same hypotenuse.

whyWrong.B: Changing the denominator from 9 to 7 would require a different hypotenuse; nothing here changes it.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{7\sqrt{2}}{8} \approx 1.24 \), and no sine or cosine can exceed 1. It borrows the 7 from cos(R) = 7/9 but attaches the wrong radical and denominator.
whyWrong.D: A sine or cosine can never exceed 1, and \( \frac{9\sqrt{2}}{8} \approx 1.59 \), so this can be ruled out on sight.

stem: In triangle ABC, ∠B is a right angle and the length of \( \overline{BC} \) is 248 millimeters. If \( \cos A = \frac{3}{5} \), what is the length, in millimeters, of \( \overline{AB} \)?
whyCorrect: With the right angle at B, the hypotenuse is AC; relative to angle A, side AB is adjacent and BC is opposite. Since cos A = 3/5, the triangle is a 3-4-5 family triangle, so the opposite side is 4 parts and the adjacent side 3 parts, and tan A = 4/3. The known side BC is the opposite one, so \( AB = 248 \times \frac{3}{4} = 186 \).

whyWrong.A: 62 is 248 divided by 4 — one part of the ratio, not three.
whyWrong.C: 248 is the given side BC; the legs are not equal unless the acute angles are both 45 degrees.
whyWrong.D: 310 is the hypotenuse AC, found from \( 248 \times \frac{5}{4} \). It is what you get by mistaking AB for the hypotenuse; AB is a leg because the right angle is at B.

stem: In isosceles triangle ABC, sides AB and AC are congruent. Point D divides BC such that the length of \( \overline{BD} \) is \( \frac{5}{7} \) of the length of \( \overline{BC} \). Point E lies on side AB and point F lies on side AC such that when segments DE and DF are drawn, angle BED is congruent to angle CFD. If the length of \( \overline{BE} \) is 10, what is the length of \( \overline{CF} \)?
whyCorrect: Because AB and AC are congruent, the base angles B and C are equal, and you are told angles BED and CFD are equal too — two pairs of equal angles, so triangle BED is similar to triangle CFD with B matching C, E matching F and D matching D. That fixes the ratio: BE/CF = BD/CD. Since BD is \( \frac{5}{7} \) of BC, CD is the remaining \( \frac{2}{7} \), so BD/CD = 5/2. Then 10/CF = 5/2 and CF = 4.

whyWrong.B: 14 comes from using \( \frac{7}{5} \) as the ratio, i.e. comparing BD to the whole of BC instead of to CD.
whyWrong.C: 50 is 10 times 5, using the numerator of the fraction as a scale factor.
whyWrong.D: 70 is 10 times 7, scaling by the denominator. Both C and D come from multiplying when the similarity ratio calls for CF to be smaller than BE, since CD is shorter than BD.

stem: In a triangle ABC, the measure of angle A is 48°, the measure of angle B is 90°, and the measure of angle C is \( \left(\frac{k}{2}\right)^{\circ} \). What is the value of k?
whyCorrect: The angles sum to 180°, so angle C measures 180 - 48 - 90 = 42 degrees. That 42 is \( \frac{k}{2} \), not k, so double it: k = 84. Forgetting the last step is the whole point of the question.

whyWrong.A: 42 is the measure of angle C in degrees, which is k/2.
whyWrong.B: 45 assumes the two acute angles are equal, which would require angle A to be 45° as well.
whyWrong.D: 96 is twice 48, doubling angle A instead of angle C.

stem: The perimeter of an isosceles right triangle is \( 38 + 38\sqrt{2} \) inches. What is the length, in inches, of the hypotenuse of this triangle?
whyCorrect: In an isosceles right triangle with legs of length L, the hypotenuse is \( L\sqrt{2} \), so the perimeter is \( 2L + L\sqrt{2} = L(2 + \sqrt{2}) \). Set that equal to \( 38(1 + \sqrt{2}) \) and solve: \( L = \frac{38(1+\sqrt{2})}{2+\sqrt{2}} \), which rationalizes to \( 19\sqrt{2} \). The hypotenuse is then \( 19\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{2} = 38 \). Do not try to match the two terms of the perimeter to the legs and the hypotenuse by eye — that is the trap, and it gives the wrong split.

whyWrong.A: 19 comes from reading "38" as the two legs together, so each leg is 19. Substituting back gives a perimeter of \( 38 + 19\sqrt{2} \), not the one stated.
whyWrong.B: \( 19\sqrt{2} \) is the length of each leg, not the hypotenuse.
whyWrong.D: \( 38\sqrt{2} \) comes from matching the \( 38\sqrt{2} \) term of the perimeter directly to the hypotenuse. That would leave only 38 for both legs, giving legs of 19, and \( 19\sqrt{2} \ne 38\sqrt{2} \).

note: Book prints "A perimeter of an isosceles right triangle"; read as "The perimeter".

stem: In right triangle ABC, angles A and B are acute, side AC has a length of 21.7, and \( \tan B = \frac{1}{8} \). What is the length of side BC, rounded to the nearest tenth?
whyCorrect: If A and B are the acute angles, the right angle is at C, so AC and BC are the two legs. Relative to angle B, side AC is opposite and BC is adjacent, so \( \tan B = \frac{AC}{BC} = \frac{1}{8} \). That makes BC eight times AC: \( BC = 8(21.7) = 173.6 \).

whyWrong.A: 470.9 is 21.7 times 21.7, multiplying the side by itself instead of by 8.
whyWrong.C: 4.7 comes from taking the square root of 21.7, which no relationship here calls for.
whyWrong.D: 2.7 is 21.7 divided by 8 — the ratio applied upside down. Since tan B is less than 1, the side opposite B is the shorter one, so BC must be larger than AC, not smaller.

stem: In right triangle ABC, angles A and B are acute. Side AC has a length of 21.2, and \( \tan B = \frac{1}{6} \). What is the length of side BC, rounded to the nearest tenth?
whyCorrect: Angles A and B are the acute ones, so the right angle is at C and the two legs are AC and BC. From angle B, side AC is opposite and BC is adjacent, so \( \tan B = \frac{AC}{BC} = \frac{1}{6} \), which makes BC = 6(21.2) = 127.2.

whyWrong.A: 3.5 is 21.2 divided by 6, applying the ratio upside down. Because tan B is less than 1, the side adjacent to B must be the longer one.
whyWrong.B: 4.6 is roughly the square root of 21.2, which nothing here calls for.
whyWrong.D: 449.4 is 21.2 squared, multiplying the side by itself rather than by 6.

note: Book prints "tan B = 1/6 What is", missing the period.

stem:
In the triangle shown, what is the value of x?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The side marked x is opposite the 30-degree angle and the side marked 66 is adjacent to it, so use the tangent: \( \tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{x}{66} \). Since \( \tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \), \( x = \frac{66}{\sqrt{3}} = 22\sqrt{3} \), about 38.1. Note that x is a leg, not the hypotenuse — the right angle mark is at the other end of the 66 side.

whyWrong.A: 22 is 66 divided by 3, dropping the radical from \( \frac{66}{\sqrt{3}} \).
whyWrong.C: \( 66\sqrt{3} \) multiplies by \( \sqrt{3} \) instead of dividing, which is what you get from using tan 60° — the angle at the top of the triangle, not the marked one.
whyWrong.D: 132 is twice 66, the hypotenuse-to-short-leg relationship in a 30-60-90 triangle applied to the wrong side. Here 66 is the long leg, not the short one.

note: Figure: right triangle with the right angle at the lower left. The bottom (horizontal) leg is labelled 66, the left (vertical) leg is labelled x, and the angle at the lower-right vertex is marked 30 degrees.
imageAlt: A right triangle with the right angle at the lower-left vertex; the vertical leg is labelled x, the horizontal leg carries a length, and the lower-right angle carries a degree measure.

stem:
For triangle \(PQR\) and triangle \(STU\), angles \(P\) and \(S\) each measure 30°, \( QR = 16 \) and \( TU = 12 \). Which additional piece(s) of information is (are) sufficient to prove that triangle \(PQR\) is similar to triangle \(STU\)?
I. The length of \(PQ\) is \( \frac{4}{3} \) the length of \(ST\)
II. The length of \(PR\) is \( \frac{4}{3} \) the length of \(SU\)

choices.label: A
choices.content: I is sufficient, but II is not.

choices.label: B
choices.content: II is sufficient, but I is not.

choices.label: C
choices.content: I is sufficient, and II is sufficient.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Neither I nor II is sufficient.

whyCorrect: The 30° angle sits between \(PQ\) and \(PR\), while the known side \(QR\) is opposite it. So either statement leaves you with two sides and a non-included angle — the ambiguous SSA case, which does not determine a triangle. Concretely, with \( \angle P = 30^\circ \), \( PQ = 20 \) and \( QR = 16 \), the law of cosines gives \( PR^2-34.64PR+144 = 0 \), whose two positive roots \( PR \approx 29.8 \) and \( PR \approx 4.8 \) are both legitimate triangles. Scaling by \( \frac{3}{4} \) does the same to \(STU\), so you can pick the large solution for one triangle and the small one for the other and they are not similar. SAS similarity would need both sides around the 30° angle in the same ratio.

whyWrong.A: I gives the ratio for \(PQ\) and for \(QR\), but \(QR\) is opposite the 30° angle, not between the two known sides — that is SSA, which is ambiguous.
whyWrong.B: II has exactly the same structure as I with \(PR\) in place of \(PQ\), so it fails for the same reason.
whyWrong.C: Neither is enough on its own; together they would be, because \( \frac{PQ}{ST} = \frac{PR}{SU} \) with the included angle equal is SAS similarity.

stem: Triangle QRS is similar to triangle FGH such that Q, R, and S correspond to F, G, and H, respectively. Each side of triangle FGH has \( \frac{1}{4} \) the length of its corresponding side in triangle QRS. In triangle FGH, the measure of angle F is 35°, the measure of angle G is 8°, and FG = a. In triangle QRS, the measure of angle Q is b° and QR = 20. What is the value of a + b?
whyCorrect: Handle the angle and the side separately. Angles are unchanged by scaling, and Q corresponds to F, so b = 35 — the 8-degree angle at G is not needed. Side FG corresponds to side QR, and every side of FGH is a quarter of its partner, so \( a = \frac{1}{4}(20) = 5 \). Then a + b = 5 + 35 = 40.
note: The 8-degree angle at G is a distractor.

stem: In triangle \(FGH\) and triangle \(KLM\), the measures of angles \(G\) and \(L\) are each 60°. The lengths of \(GH\) and \(LM\) are each 34 centimeters, and \[ \frac{GH}{GF} = \frac{LM}{LK} \]Which additional piece of information would be necessary to prove that triangle \(FGH\) is congruent to triangle \(KLM\):

choices.label: A
choices.content: The lengths of \(FG\) and \(KM\) are each 17 centimeters.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The measures of angles \(H\) and \(M\) are each 30°.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The measures of angles \(F\) and \(K\) are each 90°.

whyCorrect: The proportion already does the work. Since \( GH = LM = 34 \), the equation \( \frac{GH}{GF} = \frac{LM}{LK} \) forces \( GF = LK \). So the two triangles have \( GH = LM \), \( GF = LK \), and the angle between those two sides equal (\( G = L = 60^\circ \)) — that is SAS, which already proves congruence.

whyWrong.A: Pinning \(FG\) to 17 adds nothing that is not already implied, and it pairs \(FG\) with \(KM\), which is not the side corresponding to \(FG\) (that is \(KL\)).
whyWrong.B: An extra angle is unnecessary once SAS is satisfied, and there is no reason these angles must be 30°.
whyWrong.C: Same problem: the congruence is already established, and nothing forces \(F\) and \(K\) to be right angles.

stem: If the perimeter of an equilateral triangle with a height of 46 units is \( a\sqrt{3} \) units, what is the value of a?
whyCorrect: An equilateral triangle of side s has height \( \frac{s\sqrt{3}}{2} \), because the altitude splits it into two 30-60-90 triangles. Set \( \frac{s\sqrt{3}}{2} = 46 \), so \( s = \frac{92}{\sqrt{3}} \). The perimeter is \( 3s = \frac{276}{\sqrt{3}} \), and rationalizing gives \( 92\sqrt{3} \). Matching that to \( a\sqrt{3} \) gives a = 92.

whyWrong.A: 46 is the height itself, not the coefficient in the perimeter.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{2{,}116}{3} \) is \( \frac{46^{2}}{3} \), which comes from squaring the height — an area-style step in a perimeter question.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{4{,}232}{3} \) is twice that, from the same squaring error.

stem: The perimeter of an isosceles right triangle is \( 18 + 18\sqrt{2} \) inches. What is the length, in inches, of the hypotenuse of this triangle?
whyCorrect: With legs of length L, the hypotenuse is \( L\sqrt{2} \) and the perimeter is \( L(2 + \sqrt{2}) \). Setting \( L(2+\sqrt{2}) = 18(1+\sqrt{2}) \) and rationalizing gives \( L = 9\sqrt{2} \), so the hypotenuse is \( 9\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{2} = 18 \). Do not pair the two printed terms of the perimeter with the legs and the hypotenuse by eye — that split does not check out.

whyWrong.A: 9 assumes the plain 18 is the two legs together. Legs of 9 would give a hypotenuse of \( 9\sqrt{2} \) and a perimeter of \( 18 + 9\sqrt{2} \), not the one stated.
whyWrong.B: \( 9\sqrt{2} \) is the length of each leg, not the hypotenuse.
whyWrong.D: \( 18\sqrt{2} \) comes from reading the \( 18\sqrt{2} \) term as the hypotenuse, which would leave 18 for both legs and give legs of 9 — and \( 9\sqrt{2} \ne 18\sqrt{2} \).

note: Same template as Triangles question 20 in this book, with 18 in place of 38.

stem: In the right triangle shown, what is the value of x?
whyCorrect: Both legs are 37 and x is the hypotenuse, so \( x^{2} = 37^{2} + 37^{2} = 2(37^{2}) \) and \( x = 37\sqrt{2} \). Equivalently, a right triangle with equal legs is a 45-45-90 triangle, whose hypotenuse is always a leg times \( \sqrt{2} \). A quick check: the hypotenuse must be longer than 37, and \( 37\sqrt{2} \approx 52 \).

whyWrong.A: \( \sqrt{2} \) is the ratio between the hypotenuse and a leg, not a length; it is far shorter than either leg.
whyWrong.B: \( \sqrt{37} \approx 6.1 \), shorter than the legs, so it cannot be the hypotenuse. This comes from taking a square root of 37 that the work never asks for.
whyWrong.C: \( \sqrt{74} \approx 8.6 \) comes from adding the legs as 37 + 37 = 74 and then rooting, instead of squaring each leg first: the sum of the squares is 2,738, not 74.

note: Figure: right triangle with the right angle at the lower left, the vertical leg labelled 37, the horizontal leg labelled 37, and the hypotenuse labelled x.
imageAlt: A right triangle with the right angle at the lower-left vertex; both legs carry lengths and the hypotenuse is labelled x.

stem: For triangle ABC shown, the length of AB is 11 less than the length of AC. Point D (not shown) lies on AC such that BD (not shown) is perpendicular to AC. What is the value of \(\frac{BC}{BD}\)?
whyCorrect: The right angle is at B and the hypotenuse AC is 28, so AB = 28 − 11 = 17. BD is the altitude drawn from the right angle to the hypotenuse, and its length satisfies \(BD=\frac{AB\cdot BC}{AC}\) - the area of the triangle computed two ways. Substituting, \(\frac{BC}{BD}=\frac{BC\cdot AC}{AB\cdot BC}=\frac{AC}{AB}=\frac{28}{17}\). The BC cancels, so you never have to compute it (it is \(3\sqrt{55}\), which would only make the arithmetic messy).
note: Figure needed: right triangle ABC with the right angle at B, A at the top, B at the lower left and C at the lower right, with the hypotenuse AC labelled 28. The right angle and the length 28 appear only in the figure.
imageAlt: Right triangle A B C with the right angle at B; A is directly above B and C is to the right of B. The hypotenuse carries a length label.

stem:
The table gives the perimeters of similar triangles TUV and XYZ, where TU corresponds to XY. The length of TU is 16.
Perimeter
Triangle TUV44
Triangle XYZ352
What is the length of XY?
whyCorrect: In similar figures the perimeters are in the same ratio as any pair of corresponding sides, so the scale factor is 352 ÷ 44 = 8. XYZ is the larger triangle, so multiply: XY = 16 × 8 = 128.

whyWrong.A: 2 is 16 divided by 8, scaling the wrong way — XYZ has the larger perimeter, so its sides must be longer.
whyWrong.B: 16 is the length of TU; corresponding sides of similar triangles are equal only when the scale factor is 1.
whyWrong.C: 60 has no basis here; it may come from adding 44 and 16.

stem: The area of a triangle is 270 square centimeters. The length of the base of the triangle is 12 centimeters greater than the height of the triangle. What is the height, in centimeters, of the triangle?
whyCorrect: Let the height be h; the base is then h + 12. The area formula gives \( \frac{1}{2}h(h + 12) = 270 \), so \( h^{2} + 12h - 540 = 0 \), which factors as (h + 30)(h - 18) = 0. A length cannot be negative, so h = 18, and the base is 30. Check: \( \frac{1}{2}(30)(18) = 270 \).

whyWrong.A: 15 makes the base 27 and the area 202.5, not 270. It is half of 30, the base length, and does not satisfy the equation.
whyWrong.C: 30 is the base, not the height. This is the answer if you solve correctly and then report the wrong quantity.
whyWrong.D: 36 comes from the other root of a sign-flipped equation, or from 270 divided by 7.5; substituting gives an area of 864.

stem: For the triangles shown, triangle ABC is dilated by a factor of 5 to obtain triangle XYZ, where d = 19. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle X?
whyCorrect: A dilation changes every length by the scale factor but leaves every angle measure alone. Triangle XYZ is the image of triangle ABC, so angle X corresponds to angle A, and the figure marks angle A as 60°. The value d = 19 is there only to tempt you into computing something; no length is needed. Angle X = 60°.

whyWrong.A: This divides 60 by the scale factor 5. Scale factors act on lengths, not on angles.
whyWrong.B: This subtracts the scale factor from the angle, which no property of dilation supports.
whyWrong.D: This adds the scale factor to the angle, which again treats the dilation as if it changed angle measures.

note: Figure: two triangles side by side, 'Note: Figure not drawn to scale'. Left triangle ABC with A top-left, B top-right, C below between them; the angle at A is labeled 60° and side AC is labeled d. Right triangle XYZ, same orientation (X top-left, Y top-right, Z below), drawn larger, no labels on its sides or angles.
imageAlt: Two triangles side by side: a smaller triangle ABC with one angle marked in degrees and one side labelled d, and a larger triangle XYZ of the same shape with no labels on its sides or angles.

stem: The line segment shown in the xy-plane represents one of the legs of a right triangle. The area of this triangle is \(48\sqrt{13}\) square units. What is the length, in units, of the other leg of this triangle?
whyCorrect: First get the length of the drawn leg from its endpoints with the distance formula: the horizontal change is 9 and the vertical change is 6, so the length is \(\sqrt{9^{2}+6^{2}}=\sqrt{117}=3\sqrt{13}\). For a right triangle the two legs are the base and the height, so \(\frac{1}{2}(3\sqrt{13})(L)=48\sqrt{13}\). Multiply by 2 and divide by \(3\sqrt{13}\): \(L=\frac{96\sqrt{13}}{3\sqrt{13}}=32\). The \(\sqrt{13}\) cancels entirely, which is the sign you set it up correctly.

whyWrong.A: This is what you get if you write the area as (leg)(leg) instead of \(\frac{1}{2}\)(leg)(leg) — it is exactly half of the right answer.
whyWrong.C: This is the length of the leg already drawn, not the other one.
whyWrong.D: This doubles the drawn leg. Doubling is not what the area equation asks for; you have to divide the doubled area by the drawn leg, and the radical cancels when you do.

note: Figure needed: a line segment in the xy-plane from (-5, 3) to (4, 9), drawn on a grid with x from -8 to 8 and y from 0 to 16.
imageAlt: A line segment with both endpoints marked, drawn on a square grid in the xy-plane; the x-axis runs from -8 to 8 and the y-axis from 0 to 16.

stem: For triangle \(ABC\), the length of \( \overline{AB} \) is 11 less than the length of \( \overline{AC} \). Point \(D\) (not shown) lies on \( \overline{AC} \) such that \( \overline{BD} \) (not shown) is perpendicular to \( \overline{AC} \). What is the value of \( \frac{BC}{BD} \)?
whyCorrect: From the figure the right angle is at \(B\) and \( AC = 28 \), so \( AB = 28-11 = 17 \). Dropping the altitude \( \overline{BD} \) to the hypotenuse creates triangle \(BDC\), which is similar to triangle \(ABC\) (both are right triangles sharing angle \(C\)). Matching corresponding sides, \( \frac{BC}{BD} = \frac{AC}{AB} = \frac{28}{17} \) — you never need \(BC\) itself. (Checking directly: \( BC = \sqrt{495} \) and \( BD = \frac{17\sqrt{495}}{28} \), whose ratio is \( \frac{28}{17} \).)
note: Figure needed: right triangle ABC with the right angle at B, A above B, C to the right, and hypotenuse AC labelled 28.
imageAlt: A right triangle with its three vertices labelled, the right angle marked with a small square, and the hypotenuse labelled with its length.

stem: The area of triangle ABC is 220 square centimeters. What is the height h, in centimeters, of this triangle?
whyCorrect: The height h in the figure is drawn perpendicular to side AC, so AC is the matching base and it is labeled 10 cm. Put both into the area formula: \(\tfrac{1}{2}(10)h = 220\), so 5h = 220 and h = 44. The step people skip is doubling the area before dividing.

whyWrong.A: This is the base length copied out of the figure, not the height.
whyWrong.B: This is \(220 \div 10\) — it divides by the base without first doubling the area, so it is half the right answer.
whyWrong.D: This doubles the area a second time: \(4 \times 220 \div 10\). The formula has only one factor of 2.

note: Figure: triangle ABC with A at the bottom left, C at the bottom right and B at the top, roughly above the middle of AC. The base AC is labeled 10 cm. A dashed vertical segment from B down to AC is labeled h, with a right-angle mark where it meets AC. 'Note: Figure not drawn to scale'.
imageAlt: Triangle ABC with a horizontal base AC carrying its measurement and a dashed altitude from vertex B down to the base labelled h, with a right-angle mark at its foot.

stem: In the right triangle shown, what is the value of a?
whyCorrect: The three angles of any triangle add to 180°. Here one angle is the marked right angle, 90°, and another is 24°, so a = 180 - 90 - 24 = 66. A shortcut worth remembering: in a right triangle the two non-right angles are complementary, so a = 90 - 24 straight away.

whyWrong.A: This copies the angle already given instead of finding the third one. The two acute angles here are not equal, since the triangle is not isosceles.
whyWrong.C: This is the right angle marked in the figure, not the angle labeled a°.
whyWrong.D: This subtracts 24 from 100 rather than from 90. The two acute angles of a right triangle add to 90°, not 100°.

note: Figure: a right triangle with the right angle marked at the bottom-left vertex, the top vertex directly above it, and the third vertex at the bottom right. The angle at the top vertex is labeled 24° and the angle at the bottom-right vertex is labeled a°. 'Note: Figure not drawn to scale'.
imageAlt: A right triangle with the right angle marked at the lower-left vertex; the angle at the top vertex carries a degree measure and the angle at the lower-right vertex is labelled a degrees.

stem: In right triangle JKL, the tangent of angle L is \(\frac{3}{4}\). What is the length of JK?
whyCorrect: The right angle is at K, so JL is the hypotenuse and JL = 90. From angle L, the opposite leg is JK and the adjacent leg is KL, so \(\tan L = \frac{JK}{KL} = \frac{3}{4}\). Legs in the ratio 3 : 4 make a 3-4-5 triangle, so the hypotenuse corresponds to 5. Scaling 5 up to 90 multiplies everything by 18, which gives JK = 3(18) = 54.

whyWrong.A: This is not reachable from any correct step. Note that it is smaller than 3, while the hypotenuse of this triangle is 90 — every side must be far larger.
whyWrong.B: This scales the 3-4-5 triangle to a hypotenuse of 5 rather than to the given hypotenuse of 90, so it is the answer for a triangle 18 times too small.
whyWrong.D: This is KL, the leg adjacent to angle L: 4(18) = 72. The tangent's numerator, not its denominator, matches the side opposite angle L.

note: Figure: right triangle JKL with the right angle marked at K. L is at the bottom left, K at the bottom right, J directly above K. The hypotenuse LJ is labeled 90. 'Note: Figure not drawn to scale'. The book misprints the fourth choice's label as 'C' — it is transcribed here as D.
imageAlt: Right triangle JKL with the right angle marked at K; L is at the lower left, K at the lower right and J directly above K, and the hypotenuse carries a length.

stem: The triangle shown has one side with a length of x inches and two sides each with a length of y inches. The perimeter of the triangle is 47 inches. Which equation represents this situation?
whyCorrect: Perimeter is the sum of all three side lengths, so add each side once: one side of length x plus two sides of length y each gives x + y + y = x + 2y. Setting that equal to the given perimeter gives x + 2y = 47.

whyWrong.A: This adds only two of the three sides — it counts the side of length y once instead of twice.
whyWrong.C: This doubles the wrong side. There is one side of length x and two of length y, not the other way around.
whyWrong.D: This counts four sides in total. A triangle has three.

stem: In triangle ABC, point D is the midpoint of segment AB and point E is the midpoint of segment BC. If BD = 8 and DE = 14, what is the length of segment AC?
whyCorrect: DE joins the midpoints of two sides of the triangle, so it is a midsegment. A midsegment is parallel to the third side and exactly half its length, so AC = 2(DE) = 2(14) = 28. BD = 8 is not needed for anything — it only tells you AB = 16.

whyWrong.B: This is a near miss for 28 and comes from a slip in doubling 14. Nothing in the problem produces 26.
whyWrong.C: This adds the two given lengths, 14 + 8. The midsegment relationship is a doubling, not a sum, and BD is on a different side of the triangle entirely.
whyWrong.D: This doubles the wrong length: 2(8) = 16 is AB, since D is the midpoint of AB. The question asks for AC, which is twice DE.

stem: In the figure, \(\overline{AD}\) and \(\overline{BC}\) intersect at point D. The measure of angle ABD is \(w^{\circ}\), the measure of angle CAD is \(z^{\circ}\), and AD = 178. If \(\cos w^{\circ} = \frac{9}{41}\), what is the value of \(\tan z^{\circ}\)?
whyCorrect: The key is that the two angles are equal. In right triangle ABD the angles at D and B are 90° and \(w^{\circ}\), so angle BAD is \((90 - w)^{\circ}\); and because angle BAC is a right angle, angle CAD = 90 - (90 - w) = w. So \(z = w\) and you only need \(\tan w^{\circ}\). From \(\cos w^{\circ} = \frac{9}{41}\), the legs are 9 and 40 (since \(9^{2}+40^{2}=41^{2}\)), so \(\tan w^{\circ} = \frac{40}{9}\). AD = 178 is not needed at all.
note: Figure: right triangle with the right angle marked at A (bottom left); C is at the bottom right and B is above A. Segment AD runs from A to point D on the hypotenuse BC, with a right angle marked at D. 'Note: Figure not drawn to scale'. Answer 40/9 = 4.444..., so 4.444 or 4.44 would also grid in correctly.
imageAlt: Right triangle with the right angle at A, B directly above A and C to the right of A; a segment is drawn from A to a point D on side BC, meeting BC at a right angle.

stem: In isosceles triangle ABC, sides AB and AC are congruent. Point D divides side BC such that the length of BD is \(\frac{4}{7}\) of the length of BC. Point E lies on side AB and point F lies on side AC such that when segments DE and DF are drawn, angle BED is congruent to angle CFD. If the length of BE is 8, what is the length of CF?
whyCorrect: Because AB and AC are congruent, the base angles satisfy angle B = angle C. You are also told angle BED = angle CFD. Two pairs of congruent angles give triangle BED ~ triangle CFD, with B matching C, E matching F and D matching D. Since BD is \(\frac{4}{7}\) of BC, CD is \(\frac{3}{7}\) of BC, so the ratio of similarity is BD : CD = 4 : 3. Then BE : CF = 4 : 3, and CF = 8 × \(\frac{3}{4}\) = 6.

whyWrong.B: This comes from adding rather than scaling — 8 + 6, or treating the 4 : 3 split as something to add onto the given length. The similar triangles give a multiplicative relationship, not an additive one.
whyWrong.C: This is 8 × 4, using the numerator of \(\frac{4}{7}\) as the scale factor. The scale factor is BD : CD = 4 : 3, not 4 : 1, and it must shrink BE, not enlarge it.
whyWrong.D: This is 8 × 7, using the whole of BC against BD. The triangle containing CF sits on CD, which is \(\frac{3}{7}\) of BC, not on BC itself.

stem: The perimeter of an obtuse triangle is 27 meters. The lengths of two sides of this triangle are 5 meters and 9 meters. What is the length, in meters, of the third side of this triangle?
whyCorrect: The perimeter is the sum of all three sides, so the third side is 27 - 5 - 9 = 13. The word 'obtuse' is a consistency check rather than an extra condition: 5 + 9 = 14 > 13, so a triangle exists, and \(13^{2} = 169\) is larger than \(5^{2}+9^{2} = 106\), so the angle across from the 13 is indeed obtuse.

whyWrong.B: This is 5 + 9, the sum of the two given sides. That value would make the three sides 5, 9 and 14, which lie flat in a line rather than forming a triangle.
whyWrong.C: This subtracts only the 9 from the perimeter and forgets the side of length 5.
whyWrong.D: This subtracts only the 5 from the perimeter and forgets the side of length 9.

stem: In triangle DEF, point G (not shown) lies on \(\overline{DE}\). If the measure of angle DFG is \(x^{\circ}\), and the measure of angle GFE is \(y^{\circ}\), what is the value of \(\cos x^{\circ} - \sin y^{\circ}\)?
whyCorrect: G is on DE, so ray FG splits angle DFE into the two pieces measuring \(x^{\circ}\) and \(y^{\circ}\), which means x + y = 90 because angle DFE is the right angle in the figure. Complementary angles trade sine for cosine: \(\sin y^{\circ} = \sin(90 - x)^{\circ} = \cos x^{\circ}\). So the expression is \(\cos x^{\circ} - \cos x^{\circ} = 0\). The side lengths 3 and 4 are never needed, and neither x nor y can be pinned down individually.
note: Figure: right triangle DEF with the right angle at F. D is at the top, F directly below D at the bottom left, E at the bottom right. Leg DF is labeled 4 and leg FE is labeled 3. | figure: The book prints no right-angle mark at F, but the question is unanswerable unless angle F is known to be 90 degrees (the book leaves it to the drawing), so the right-angle square was added.
imageAlt: A right triangle DEF drawn with D directly above F and E to the right of F; both legs carry lengths.

stem: According to a US law, ramps for use by the general public must form an angle with level ground such that \(\tan\theta < \frac{1}{12}\). If the ramp in the figure conforms to this law and has a height of 22.3 inches, what is the least possible value of x, in inches?
whyCorrect: In the figure \(\theta\) sits at the ground, with the height opposite it and x adjacent, so \(\tan\theta = \frac{22.3}{x}\). The law then requires \(\frac{22.3}{x} < \frac{1}{12}\). Cross-multiplying (x is positive, so the inequality direction is safe) gives x > 12(22.3) = 267.6. A shallower ramp means a longer run, so the smallest allowed x is 267.6 inches.
note: Figure: a right triangle representing a ramp. The horizontal bottom side is labeled x, the vertical right side is labeled 'height of the ramp' with a right angle marked where they meet, and the hypotenuse is labeled 'length of the ramp'. The angle at the bottom-left vertex, between the ground and the ramp, is labeled θ. Note: the inequality is strict, so strictly speaking there is no least value; 267.6 is the intended answer and is the greatest lower bound.
imageAlt: A right triangle representing a ramp: the horizontal bottom side is labelled x, the vertical side on the right is labelled height of the ramp with a right-angle mark where the two meet, the hypotenuse is labelled length of the ramp, and the angle at the left-hand vertex is labelled theta.

stem: According to a US law, ramps for use by the general public must form an angle with ground such that \(\tan\theta \le \frac{1}{12}\). If the ramp in the figure above conforms to this law and height of the ramp is 28.2 inches, what is the least possible value of x in inches?
whyCorrect: The angle \(\theta\) is at the ground, so the height is the leg opposite it and x is the leg adjacent: \(\tan\theta = \frac{28.2}{x}\). The law gives \(\frac{28.2}{x} \le \frac{1}{12}\), and multiplying both sides by 12x (positive) gives \(x \ge 12(28.2) = 338.4\). The gentler the required slope, the longer the horizontal run has to be, so 338.4 inches is the shortest run allowed.
note: Figure: a right triangle representing a ramp. The horizontal bottom side is labeled x, the vertical right side is labeled 'height of the ramp' with a right angle marked where they meet, and the hypotenuse is labeled 'length of the ramp'. The angle at the bottom-left vertex, between the ground and the ramp, is labeled θ.
imageAlt: A right triangle representing a ramp: the horizontal bottom side is labelled x, the vertical side on the right is labelled height of the ramp with a right-angle mark where the two meet, the hypotenuse is labelled length of the ramp, and the angle at the left-hand vertex is labelled theta.

stem: What is the value of \(\cos A\) in the triangle shown?
whyCorrect: Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse. The right angle is at C, so the hypotenuse is the side across from it, AB = 54. The leg touching angle A other than the hypotenuse is AC = 53. So \(\cos A = \frac{53}{54}\).

whyWrong.A: This puts 1 in the numerator instead of the adjacent leg. Cosine compares two side lengths; a 1 never appears unless a side actually measures 1.
whyWrong.B: Same error as the previous choice, with the hypotenuse in the denominator instead.
whyWrong.D: This is the reciprocal, hypotenuse over adjacent. Any cosine must be at most 1, so a value greater than 1 can be ruled out on sight.

note: Figure: right triangle with the right angle marked at C. A is at the bottom left, C at the bottom right, B directly above C. Side AC (the horizontal bottom) is labeled 53 and the hypotenuse AB is labeled 54. 'Note: Figure not drawn to a scale.'
imageAlt: A right triangle with the right angle marked at C, A at the lower left and B directly above C; the horizontal side and the hypotenuse each carry a length.

stem: In triangle ABC, angle B is a right angle and the length of \(\overline{BC}\) is 204 millimeters. If \(\cos A = \frac{3}{5}\), what is the length, in millimeters, of \(\overline{AB}\)?
whyCorrect: With the right angle at B, AC is the hypotenuse, AB is the leg adjacent to angle A and BC is the leg opposite it. So \(\cos A = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{3}{5}\), which makes this a 3-4-5 triangle with AB : BC : AC = 3 : 4 : 5. The given side BC = 204 matches the 4, so the scale factor is 204 ÷ 4 = 51, and AB = 3(51) = 153.

whyWrong.A: This is AC, the hypotenuse: 5(51) = 255. The question asks for the leg AB.
whyWrong.B: This just repeats the given length BC. BC is opposite angle A, not adjacent to it, so it is not the side the cosine's numerator refers to.
whyWrong.D: This is the scale factor 51 itself, from 204 ÷ 4. You still have to multiply it by the 3 in the ratio.

stem: In right triangle RST, the sum of the measures of angle R and angle S is 90 degrees. The value of \(\sin(R)\) is \(\frac{3\sqrt{17}}{13}\). What is the value of \(\cos(S)\)?
