imageAlt: Two parallel horizontal lines labelled r and s crossed by a slanted transversal labelled t; the two angles above line r at the upper intersection are marked with their degree measures, and one angle below line s at the lower intersection is marked x degrees. A caption reads: Note: Figure not drawn to scale.

stem: A rectangle has a perimeter of 36 inches. If the sum of the lengths of three sides of the rectangle is 21 inches, what is the length, in inches, of the fourth side?
whyCorrect: The perimeter is the sum of all four sides, so the fourth side is whatever is left after the other three: 36 − 21 = 15. You never need the individual length and width, which is the trap — setting up 2L + 2W = 36 wastes time here.

whyWrong.A: 3 is the other dimension of the rectangle, which is 3 by 15. It is a side, but not the one left out of the 21.
whyWrong.B: 57 comes from adding 36 and 21 instead of subtracting. The three sides are part of the perimeter, so the result must be smaller than 36.
whyWrong.D: 36 is the whole perimeter, which is all four sides together.

stem:
In the figure shown, lines r and s are parallel, and line t intersects both lines. What is the value of a?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: a sits above line s on the right of t, which is the same position as the 77° angle above line r on the right of t. Parallel lines cut by a transversal make those corresponding angles equal, so a = 77. You can also get there along line s: the 77° below s on the left is vertical to a.

whyWrong.A: 180 is the straight angle along line s, the sum of a and the angle beside it, not a itself.
whyWrong.C: 167 is not the measure of any angle here; every angle in the figure is either 77° or 103°.
whyWrong.D: 90 would require t to be perpendicular to the parallel lines, but the marked angles are 77° and 103°.

note: figure: The stem text already carries the line 'Note: Figure not drawn to scale.', and the book prints it beneath the figure as well, so it is drawn into the image too; drop one of the two if it reads as a duplicate.
imageAlt: Two parallel horizontal lines labelled r and s crossed by a slanted transversal labelled t; two angles at the upper intersection and one at the lower intersection carry degree measures, and a fourth angle at the lower intersection is marked a degrees. A caption reads: Note: Figure not drawn to scale.

stem: The measure of angle K is \( \frac{\pi}{2(12)} \) radians. The measure of angle L is 12 times the measure of angle K. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle L?
whyCorrect: Convert K to degrees before multiplying. Since \( \pi \) radians is 180°, \( \frac{\pi}{2(12)} = \frac{\pi}{24} \) radians is \( \frac{180}{24} = 7.5 \) degrees. Twelve times that is 90°. A shortcut: multiplying \( \frac{\pi}{24} \) by 12 gives \( \frac{\pi}{2} \) , and a half-turn of \( \pi \) is 180°, so a quarter of a turn is 90°.

whyWrong.A: 102 is 90 + 12, adding the multiplier instead of applying it.
whyWrong.B: 12 is how many times bigger L is than K, not a measure in degrees.
whyWrong.C: 78 is 90 − 12, subtracting the multiplier.

note: An unrelated display line, a/(b + c) = 55, is printed above this question in the book; it belongs to a neighbouring item and is not part of the stem.

stem: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF, where angle A corresponds to angle D and angle C corresponds to angle F. Angles C and F are right angles. If \( \tan A = \frac{612}{35} \) , what is the value of \( \sin D \) ?
whyCorrect: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles, so \( \sin D = \sin A \) and you can work entirely inside triangle ABC. With the right angle at C, \( \tan A = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \frac{612}{35} \) , so take the legs as 612 and 35 and find the hypotenuse: \( \sqrt{612^{2} + 35^{2}} = \sqrt{375{,}769} = 613 \) . Then \( \sin A = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{612}{613} \) .

whyWrong.B: \( \frac{35}{613} \) is \( \cos A \) , the sine of the other acute angle. Sine uses the leg across from the angle, and 35 is the leg beside it.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{613}{612} \) is the reciprocal of the answer; the hypotenuse belongs in the denominator, since a sine can never exceed 1.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{613}{35} \) is the reciprocal of the cosine, and again greater than 1.

stem:
In the figure, lines r and s are parallel and line t intersects both lines. If \( a = 4k + 57 \) and \( b = \frac{k}{2} + 55 \) , what is the value of c?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Place the three angles first. a and b are both between the parallel lines and both on the same side of t, so they are same-side interior angles and a + b = 180. b and c share line s, so they are a linear pair and b + c = 180 — which makes c equal to a. Solving \( (4k + 57) + \left(\frac{k}{2} + 55\right) = 180 \) gives \( \frac{9k}{2} = 68 \) , so \( k = \frac{136}{9} \) and \( c = a = 4k + 57 = \frac{1057}{9} \approx 117.44 \) .
note: The numbers do not come out whole: k = 136/9 and c = 1057/9 = 117.444..., so the intended answer is probably a round number and one of the printed constants is likely mistyped. Answer recorded as the exact consequence of the stem as printed.
imageAlt: Two vertical parallel lines r and s crossed by a slanted line t running from upper left to lower right; one angle is labelled at the crossing with r and two are labelled at the crossing with s.

stem:
In the figure, line p is parallel to line r, and line t intersects both lines. What is the value of x?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Both marked angles sit at the same intersection, where t crosses p: x is above p on the left of t, and 72° is below p on the right of t. Angles in opposite corners of a crossing are vertical angles and are equal, so x = 72. Line r is not needed at all.

whyWrong.A: 36 is half of 72, from treating the transversal as bisecting the angle.
whyWrong.C: 180 is the straight angle along p, which is x plus the angle next to it.
whyWrong.D: 252 is 180 + 72, from adding the straight angle to the marked angle instead of matching vertical angles.

note: figure: The stem text already carries the line 'Note: Figure not drawn to scale.', and the book prints it beneath the figure as well, so it is drawn into the image too; drop one of the two if it reads as a duplicate.
imageAlt: Two parallel horizontal lines labelled p and r crossed by a transversal labelled t that slopes downward to the right; at the intersection with line p one angle is marked x degrees and the opposite angle carries a degree measure. A caption reads: Note: Figure not drawn to scale.

stem:
In the figure shown, line k intersects lines r and s. If w = 147, which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that lines r and s are parallel?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: To prove two lines are parallel you need a fact that is not already true regardless. w and y sit in the same position at their own intersections — both to the right of their line and above k — so they are corresponding angles, and corresponding angles are equal exactly when the lines are parallel. y = 147 = w is therefore the fact that does it.

whyWrong.A: x = 33 follows automatically from w = 147, because w and x form a straight line along r. A statement that is already true tells you nothing about s.
whyWrong.C: If w + y = 180 with w = 147, then y = 33, so the corresponding angles would differ and the lines would not be parallel.
whyWrong.D: y and z form a straight line along s, so y + z = 180 is true whatever the lines do. It never mentions r.

imageAlt: A transversal line k crossing two vertical lines r and s. Four angles are labelled with variables: w and x at the intersection with r, y and z at the intersection with s.

stem: In triangle ABC, the measure of angle A is 56° and AC = 35. In triangle PQR, the measure of angle P is 56° and PR = 105. Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle ABC is similar to triangle PQR?

choices.label: B
choices.content: The measures of angle B and angle R are 32° and 92°, respectively.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The measures of angle B and angle Q are 56° and 32°, respectively.

whyCorrect: Two triangles are similar as soon as two pairs of angles match, so look for a choice that pins down a second pair. If angle B is 32°, then angle C is 180 − 56 − 32 = 92°; and angle R is given as 92°, so angle C matches angle R while angle A already matches angle P. That is AA similarity. The side lengths 35 and 105 are a ratio of 1 to 3 and are not needed.

whyWrong.A: AB and PQ are corresponding sides, so for similarity they would have to be in the same 1 to 3 ratio as AC and PR. Equal lengths of 50 and 50 would make the triangles impossible to be similar, not similar.
whyWrong.C: This gives triangle ABC angles of 56°, 56°, 68° and triangle PQR angles of 56°, 32°, 92°. Only one pair matches, so the triangles are not similar.
whyWrong.D: AB corresponds to PQ, and QR corresponds to BC, so these two lengths are not a corresponding pair. Knowing them gives no ratio to compare with 35 to 105.

stem: In triangle RST, angle T is a right angle, point L lies on RS, point K lies on ST, and LK is parallel to RT. If the length of RT is 63 units, the length of LK is 21 units, and the area of triangle RST is 630 square units, what is the length of KT, in units?
whyCorrect: Use the area to get ST first: \( \frac{1}{2}(63)(ST) = 630 \) , so ST = 20. Since LK is parallel to RT, triangle SLK is similar to triangle SRT with ratio \( \frac{21}{63} = \frac{1}{3} \) , which makes \( SK = \frac{20}{3} \) . KT is the rest of ST: \( 20 - \frac{20}{3} = \frac{40}{3} \) , about 13.33. Stopping at SK is the common slip — the similarity gives the piece next to S, not the piece next to T.
note: The book prints "If the length RT of is 63 units"; the words are transposed and are transcribed here as "the length of RT".

stem:
Which equation gives the relationship between the side lengths of the triangle shown?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: In the Pythagorean theorem the hypotenuse is always alone on one side of the equation, and the hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle. Here the right-angle mark is between a and 12, so those are the legs and 14 is the hypotenuse: \( a^{2} + 12^{2} = 14^{2} \) .

whyWrong.A: This treats a as the hypotenuse. a is a leg — it touches the right angle, so it cannot be the longest side.
whyWrong.C: Side lengths in a right triangle do not add like this; the relationship is between the squares, and 12 + a is greater than 14 for the true value of a.
whyWrong.D: Adding two sides gives the third only in a degenerate flat triangle, and again a is a leg, not the sum of the others.

note: The book prints "the side length"; the figure labels three sides, so it is read as "side lengths".
imageAlt: A right triangle with the right angle at the lower left. The vertical leg is labelled a and the horizontal leg and hypotenuse each carry a number.

stem:
In triangle XYZ, the measure of angle Y is 90 degrees. Triangle RST (not shown) is similar to triangle XYZ such that R, S, and T correspond to X, Y, and Z, respectively. Each side of triangle RST is 19 times the length of the corresponding side of triangle XYZ. What is the measure, in degrees, of one of the angles in triangle RST?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Similar triangles have identical angles no matter how the sides are scaled, so the factor of 19 changes nothing here — it is there to pull you toward multiplying. Triangle XYZ has angles 90° at Y, 35° at Z, and 180 − 90 − 35 = 55° at X, so triangle RST has those same three angles. Any one of 35, 55 or 90 answers the question.
note: Free response with three correct answers: 35, 55 and 90 are all angles of triangle RST. Recorded 35; a key listing only one of the three is still not wrong.
imageAlt: A right triangle with vertices X at the top left, Y at the lower left where the right angle is marked, and Z at the lower right; the angle at Z is labelled with its degree measure.

stem: In the right triangle shown, what is the value of \( \cos A \) ?
whyCorrect: Cosine is the side next to the angle over the hypotenuse. The right angle is at B, so the hypotenuse is AC = 43, and the leg touching angle A is AB = 23. That gives \( \cos A = \frac{23}{43} \) .

whyWrong.A: \( \frac{1}{43} \) has the right denominator but a numerator of 1 instead of the adjacent leg 23.
whyWrong.B: \( \frac{1}{23} \) puts the leg in the denominator and invents a 1 on top; the hypotenuse must be the denominator for a cosine.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{43}{23} \) is upside down. Any cosine is at most 1, so a value bigger than 1 cannot be right.

imageAlt: A right triangle with vertex A at the top left, B at the lower left where the right angle is marked, and C at the lower right. The vertical leg and the hypotenuse each carry a length label.

stem:
In triangle JKL, \( \cos y^{\circ} = \frac{54}{55} \) . What is the length of KL?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: y° is the angle at L and the right angle is at K, so KL is the leg beside y and JL is the hypotenuse: \( \cos y^{\circ} = \frac{KL}{JL} \) . The hypotenuse JL is 55, so \( \frac{KL}{55} = \frac{54}{55} \) and KL = 54. No Pythagorean work is needed — the given ratio already has 55 as its denominator.
note: In the book the length 55 is printed on top of the right-angle mark at K rather than beside a side. It must be the hypotenuse JL: reading it as the leg JK gives KL \u2248 284.5, which is not a plausible intended answer, and the parallel question on the facing page (59 with cos y = 58/59) has the same layout. | figure: On the page the length 55 is printed on top of the right-angle mark at K, overlapping it, rather than beside a side. Redrawn with 55 beside the hypotenuse JL, which is the only reading the arithmetic supports.
imageAlt: A right triangle with vertex J at the top left, K at the lower left where the right angle is marked, and L at the lower right. The hypotenuse carries a length label and the angle at L is labelled y degrees.

stem:
In triangle QRS, what is the value of \( \tan y^{\circ} \) ?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Tangent uses the two legs only, never the hypotenuse: opposite over adjacent. y° is at S, so the leg opposite it is QR = 4 and the leg beside it is RS = 10, giving \( \tan y^{\circ} = \frac{4}{10} \) .

whyWrong.A: c is the hypotenuse, which no tangent ever uses.
whyWrong.B: Same problem: bringing the hypotenuse in makes this a secant, not a tangent.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{10}{4} \) is opposite and adjacent swapped — it is the tangent of the angle at Q, not at S.

note: figure: On the page the hypotenuse label c is printed on top of the right-angle mark at R rather than beside the hypotenuse; redrawn beside QS, the only side it can belong to since both legs already carry numbers.
imageAlt: A right triangle with vertex Q at the top left, R at the lower left where the right angle is marked, and S at the lower right. The two legs carry numbers, the hypotenuse is labelled c, and the angle at S is labelled y degrees.

stem: In triangle QRS, what is the value of \( \tan y \) ?
whyCorrect: The right angle is at R, so QR = 4 and RS = 9 are the legs and c is the hypotenuse. y is the angle at S, so the opposite leg is QR = 4 and the adjacent leg is RS = 9: \( \tan y = \frac{4}{9} \) .

whyWrong.A: The hypotenuse c never appears in a tangent; this is a secant-type ratio.
whyWrong.C: Same error as A, with the other leg underneath.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{9}{4} \) reverses opposite and adjacent, giving the tangent of the angle at Q instead.

note: figure: The printed labels are misplaced: 4 and 9 are both crowded at vertex R and c sits on top of the right-angle mark. Redrawn with 4 on leg QR, 9 on leg RS and c on the hypotenuse, which is the only assignment the answer choices allow.
imageAlt: A right triangle with vertex Q at the top left, R at the lower left where the right angle is marked, and S at the lower right. The two legs carry numbers, the hypotenuse is labelled c, and the angle at S is labelled y.

stem: In triangle JKL, \( \cos y = \frac{58}{59} \) . What is the length of KL?
whyCorrect: The right angle is at K and y is the angle at L, so the side beside y is KL and the hypotenuse is JL: \( \cos y = \frac{KL}{JL} \) . The hypotenuse is 59, so \( \frac{KL}{59} = \frac{58}{59} \) and KL = 58. The ratio is already written with the hypotenuse as its denominator, so no further computation is needed.
note: As in the companion question earlier in the chapter, the book prints the length 59 on top of the right-angle mark at K instead of beside a side; it has to be the hypotenuse JL for the numbers to work. | figure: On the page the length 59 is printed on top of the right-angle mark at K rather than beside a side. Redrawn with 59 beside the hypotenuse JL, the only reading the arithmetic supports. The figure is deliberately not drawn to scale, since a to-scale drawing would give away KL.

stem: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF, where angle A corresponds to angle D and angle C corresponds to angle F. Angles B and E are right angles. If \( \cos A = \frac{14}{\sqrt{421}} \) , what is the value of \( \frac{1}{\sin F} \) ?
whyCorrect: F corresponds to C, so \( \sin F = \sin C \) and you can work inside triangle ABC. The right angle is at B, so AC is the hypotenuse: \( \cos A = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{14}{\sqrt{421}} \) gives AB = 14 and \( AC = \sqrt{421} \) . For angle C the opposite leg is that same AB, so \( \sin C = \frac{14}{\sqrt{421}} \) — the two acute angles swap sine and cosine. The question asks for the reciprocal, \( \frac{\sqrt{421}}{14} \) .

whyWrong.A: \( \frac{15}{\sqrt{421}} \) uses the third side, \( BC = \sqrt{421 - 196} = 15 \) ; that is \( \cos C \) , and it is not reciprocated either.
whyWrong.B: \( \frac{14}{\sqrt{421}} \) is \( \sin F \) itself. The question asks for one divided by it.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{\sqrt{421}}{15} \) is the reciprocal of the cosine of F, built from the leg beside C rather than across from it.

stem: Circles A and B are graphed in the xy-plane. Circle A is represented by the equation \( (x + 8)^{2} + (y - 8)^{2} = 64 \) and intersects the x-axis at the point (r, s). Circle B has its center at (r, s) and has a radius of the same length as circle A. Which equation represents circle B?
whyCorrect: Circle A has centre (−8, 8) and radius 8, so it just touches the x-axis. Setting y = 0 in its equation gives \( (x + 8)^{2} = 0 \) , so the only point on the x-axis is (−8, 0) — that is (r, s). Circle B therefore has centre (−8, 0) and the same radius 8: \( (x + 8)^{2} + y^{2} = 64 \) . Remember the sign flip: a centre of −8 appears as (x + 8) in the equation.

whyWrong.A: Centre (0, −8), which is on the y-axis. This swaps which coordinate the tangent point zeroed out.
whyWrong.B: Centre (0, 8) — the x- and y-coordinates of circle A's centre have been exchanged.
whyWrong.D: Centre (8, 0) has the correct y but the wrong sign on x. Circle A sits to the left of the y-axis, so r is negative.

stem: A circle in the xy-plane has its center at (−4, −7). Line k is tangent to this circle at the point (−7, −8). What is the slope of line k?
whyCorrect: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact, so find the radius's slope first and then flip it. The radius runs from (−4, −7) to (−7, −8), a slope of \( \frac{-8 - (-7)}{-7 - (-4)} = \frac{-1}{-3} = \frac{1}{3} \) . The negative reciprocal of \( \frac{1}{3} \) is −3.

whyWrong.B: \( -\frac{1}{3} \) only negates the radius's slope; a perpendicular slope must also be flipped upside down.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{1}{3} \) is the slope of the radius itself, not of the tangent.
whyWrong.D: 3 flips the fraction but keeps the sign. Perpendicular slopes must have opposite signs, since their product is −1.

stem: A circle in the xy-plane has its center at (−4, 1) and the point (−8, 4) lies on the circle. Which equation represents this circle?
whyCorrect: Two things must be right: the signs and the squaring. A centre of (−4, 1) appears in the equation as \( (x + 4)^{2} + (y - 1)^{2} \) , because the form subtracts the centre's coordinates. The radius is the distance from (−4, 1) to (−8, 4), which is \( \sqrt{(-4)^{2} + 3^{2}} = 5 \) , and the right-hand side is the radius squared, 25.

whyWrong.A: Both signs are flipped, so this is centred at (4, −1), and the right-hand side is the radius rather than its square.
whyWrong.C: The signs give a centre of (4, −1) instead of (−4, 1), though the 25 is right.
whyWrong.D: The centre is right, but 5 is the radius; the equation needs \( r^{2} \) .

stem: The points (0, 15), (10, 8), and (10, 3) are shown in the xy-plane, where the x-axis and y-axis are measured in units. These points define one of the bases of a triangular prism. The distance between the two bases of the prism is 20 units. What is the volume, in cubic units, of the prism?
whyCorrect: A prism's volume is the area of one base times the distance between the bases, so the only real work is the triangle's area. Two of the points share x = 10, so take that vertical segment as the base: its length is 8 − 3 = 5. The height is then the horizontal distance from the line x = 10 out to (0, 15), which is 10. The area is \( \frac{1}{2}(5)(10) = 25 \) , and the volume is 25 × 20 = 500.

stem: The width of a rectangle is 3 centimeters. The length of the rectangle is 20 centimeters longer than the width. What is the area, in square centimeters, of this rectangle?
whyCorrect: "20 longer than the width" means add, not multiply: the length is 3 + 20 = 23 centimeters. Area is length times width, so 23 × 3 = 69 square centimeters.

whyWrong.A: 6 is 3 + 3, or twice the width; the length was never found.
whyWrong.B: 26 is 3 + 23, the sum of the two sides rather than their product. That is half the perimeter.
whyWrong.D: 3 is the width, copied straight from the stem.

stem:
\[ h(x) = \frac{1}{2}(x)(77) \]

The given function h represents the area, in square inches, of a triangle with a base of x inches and a fixed height. What is the height, in inches, of the triangle?
whyCorrect: Match the given function against the area formula \( A = \frac{1}{2}(\text{base})(\text{height}) \) . The \( \frac{1}{2} \) is already written out and x is named as the base, so the remaining factor, 77, is the height.

whyWrong.A: \( \frac{1}{77} \) is the reciprocal of the height and does not appear in the formula at all.
whyWrong.B: \( \frac{77}{2} \) folds the \( \frac{1}{2} \) into the height, but the \( \frac{1}{2} \) is a separate factor of the area formula.
whyWrong.D: 154 is 77 × 2, undoing the \( \frac{1}{2} \) as if it had already been absorbed into the 77.

stem: Cube B has a volume of 216 cubic inches. The length of each edge of cube A is k times the length of each edge of cube B. If cube A has a volume of 5,832 cubic inches, what is the value of k?
whyCorrect: k compares edges, but the volumes are cubes of the edges, so take cube roots: \( \sqrt[3]{216} = 6 \) and \( \sqrt[3]{5{,}832} = 18 \) . Then \( k = \frac{18}{6} = 3 \) . Equivalently, the volume ratio is 27 and k is its cube root.

whyWrong.A: 27 is the ratio of the volumes, \( \frac{5{,}832}{216} \) . Edges scale by the cube root of that.
whyWrong.C: 6 is the edge length of cube B, not a ratio.
whyWrong.D: 36 is \( 6^{2} \) , the ratio of the surface areas rather than of the edges.

stem: A right square pyramid has a height of 6 units and a volume of 128 cubic units. What is the length, in units, of one side of the base of the pyramid?
whyCorrect: A pyramid's volume is \( \frac{1}{3}(\text{base area})(\text{height}) \) , and the base is a square of side s, so \( \frac{1}{3}s^{2}(6) = 128 \) . That simplifies to \( 2s^{2} = 128 \) , so \( s^{2} = 64 \) and s = 8. The last step is the one people skip: the equation gives the base area, and the side is its square root.

whyWrong.A: 256 is \( 2 \times 128 \) , from solving as though the volume were \( \frac{1}{2}s \cdot h \) ; it is also far too large for a solid of volume 128.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{64}{3} \) comes from dividing by the height without clearing the \( \frac{1}{3} \) , and it never takes the square root.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{8\sqrt{3}}{3} \) is \( \frac{8}{\sqrt{3}} \) , which appears if the \( \frac{1}{3} \) is mistakenly put inside the square root.

stem: A rectangle has an area of 66 square meters and a length of 11 meters. What is the width, in meters, of the rectangle?
whyCorrect: Width is area divided by length: \( \frac{66}{11} = 6 \) meters. Multiply back to check: 11 × 6 = 66.

whyWrong.B: 55 is 66 − 11; area and length do not subtract.
whyWrong.C: 726 is 66 × 11, multiplying instead of dividing.
whyWrong.D: 121 is \( 11^{2} \) , which ignores the given area entirely.

stem: The length of the diagonal of a square is \( \frac{186\sqrt{2}}{2} \) units. What is the area, in square units, of the square?
whyCorrect: Simplify the diagonal first: \( \frac{186\sqrt{2}}{2} = 93\sqrt{2} \) . For a square of side s the diagonal is \( s\sqrt{2} \) , so s = 93 and the area is \( 93^{2} = 8{,}649 \) .

whyWrong.B: 17,298 is the diagonal squared, which is twice the area of the square.
whyWrong.C: 93 is the side length, not the area.
whyWrong.D: 372 is 4 × 93, the perimeter.

stem: Cube B has a volume of 125 cubic inches. The length of each edge of cube A is k times the length of each edge of cube B. If cube A has a volume of 3,375 cubic inches, what is the value of k?
whyCorrect: Edges scale by k, so volumes scale by \( k^{3} \) . Here \( \frac{3{,}375}{125} = 27 \) , and \( k = \sqrt[3]{27} = 3 \) . Checking directly: the edges are \( \sqrt[3]{125} = 5 \) and \( \sqrt[3]{3{,}375} = 15 \) , a ratio of 3.

whyWrong.A: 27 is the volume ratio itself; the edge ratio is its cube root.
whyWrong.C: 25 is \( 5^{2} \) , cube B's face area, which is not a ratio of anything here.
whyWrong.D: 5 is cube B's edge length, not the factor connecting the two cubes.

stem: A triangle has a base length of 48 centimeters and a height of 96 centimeters. What is the area, in square centimeters, of the triangle?
whyCorrect: Area of a triangle is \( \frac{1}{2}(\text{base})(\text{height}) = \frac{1}{2}(48)(96) \) . Halve 48 first to keep it simple: 24 × 96 = 2,304 square centimeters.

whyWrong.B: 1152 halves twice — it is \( \frac{1}{2} \) of the correct area.
whyWrong.C: 4608 is 48 × 96, the rectangle's area, with the \( \frac{1}{2} \) forgotten.
whyWrong.D: 144 is 48 + 96, adding the dimensions instead of multiplying.

stem: A right circular cylinder has a height of 16 inches and a volume of \( 3136\pi \) cubic inches. What is the radius, in inches, of this cylinder?
whyCorrect: Use \( V = \pi r^{2} h \) . The \( \pi \) cancels on both sides, leaving \( 16r^{2} = 3136 \) , so \( r^{2} = 196 \) and r = 14. Remember the final square root: \( r^{2} \) is 196, which is not the answer.

stem: The length of a side of square X is 9 centimeters. The area of rectangle Y is 32 square centimeters. What is the total area, in square centimeters, of square X and rectangle Y?
whyCorrect: The 9 is a side, not an area, so square it first: square X has area \( 9^{2} = 81 \) square centimeters. Adding rectangle Y's 32 gives 81 + 32 = 113.

whyWrong.A: 145 comes from using 4 × 9 = 36 (the perimeter) plus... more simply, it is 113 + 32, adding Y's area twice.
whyWrong.C: 82 adds the side length 9 to 32 and then adds 41 again; more directly, it treats the square's area as 50. The square's area is 81.
whyWrong.D: 81 is square X's area alone, with rectangle Y left out.

stem:
Kyle invented a new temperature scale he called the Tutorllini scale. The function T(x) gives the temperature, in degrees Torte, that corresponds to a temperature of x degrees Celsius.

\[ T(x) = \frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{26x}{7} - 800\right) + 15.50 \]

If a temperature increased by 3.3 degrees Torte, by how much did the temperature increase, in degrees Celsius?
whyCorrect: Only the rate of change matters, so ignore every constant. Expanding, the coefficient of x is \( \frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{26}{7} = \frac{39}{14} \) , meaning each Celsius degree is worth \( \frac{39}{14} \) Torte degrees. To find the Celsius change that produces 3.3 Torte, divide rather than multiply: \( 3.3 \div \frac{39}{14} = \frac{33}{10} \cdot \frac{14}{39} = \frac{77}{65} \approx 1.185 \) . The −800 and the +15.50 shift the scale but never change how fast it moves.
note: The answer is not a round number: 77/65 = 1.1846..., so a grid entry would be 77/65 or 1.18/1.19.

stem:
In the given system of equations, p is a constant. If the system has no solution, what is the value of p?

\[ \frac{3}{2}y - \frac{1}{4}x = \frac{2}{3} - \frac{3}{2}y \]
\[ \frac{1}{6}x + \frac{3}{6} = py + \frac{9}{5} \]
whyCorrect: No solution means the two lines are parallel: the x and y coefficients are in the same ratio while the constants are not. Put both equations in the form \( ax + by = c \) first. The first becomes \( -\frac{1}{4}x + 3y = \frac{2}{3} \) once the \( \frac{3}{2}y \) is brought across; the second becomes \( \frac{1}{6}x - py = \frac{13}{10} \) . Matching x-coefficients, \( \frac{1}{6} \div \left(-\frac{1}{4}\right) = -\frac{2}{3} \) , so the y-coefficients must satisfy \( -p = 3\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) = -2 \) , giving p = 2. The constants do not follow the same ratio, so the lines really are parallel and not identical.

stem:
\[ f(x) = 3 + \left| -2x - x^{2} \right| \]
\[ g(w) = \left| -\frac{w}{w - 1} \right| - w + 5 \]

The functions f and g are defined by the given equations. If \( f(-4) = c \) , where c is a constant, what is the value of \( g(c) \) ?
whyCorrect: Work strictly inside out, and keep the absolute value bars until the very last moment. \( f(-4) = 3 + \left| -2(-4) - (-4)^{2} \right| = 3 + |8 - 16| = 3 + 8 = 11 \) — note \( (-4)^{2} \) is +16, so the inside is −8 and the bars make it 8. So c = 11. Then \( g(11) = \left| -\frac{11}{10} \right| - 11 + 5 = 1.1 - 6 = -4.9 \) . Only the fraction sits inside the bars; the −w + 5 is outside and stays negative.

stem:
The equation \( 9x + 5 = a(x + b) \) , where a and b are constants, has no solutions. Which of the following must be true?

I. a = 9
II. b = 5
III. \( b \ne \frac{5}{9} \)
whyCorrect:
Expand the right side to \( ax + ab \) . A linear equation has no solution only when the x-terms match but the constants do not, so you need a = 9 and \( ab 
e 5 \) . With a = 9 the second condition becomes \( 9b 
e 5 \) , that is \( b 
e  rac{5}{9} \) . So statements I and III must hold. Statement II is one allowed value of b among infinitely many, not a requirement.

whyWrong.A: a = 9 alone is not enough: if a = 9 and \( b = \frac{5}{9} \) the two sides are identical and every x is a solution, which is not "no solutions".
whyWrong.B: Without a = 9 the x-coefficients differ, and then the equation has exactly one solution rather than none.
whyWrong.D: Both I and III are forced, so "none of the above" cannot be right.

stem:
In the given pair of equations, a and b are constants. The graph of this pair of equations in the xy-plane is a pair of perpendicular lines.

\[ 5x + 7y = 1 \]
\[ ax + by = 1 \]

Which of the following pairs of equations also represents a pair of perpendicular lines?
whyCorrect: From the original pair, \( 5x + 7y = 1 \) has slope \( -\frac{5}{7} \) , so the other line's slope must be \( \frac{7}{5} \) : \( -\frac{a}{b} = \frac{7}{5} \) , which fixes \( \frac{a}{b} = -\frac{7}{5} \) . Now test each pair with that ratio. In choice B the slopes are \( -\frac{10}{7} \) and \( -\frac{a}{2b} = \frac{7}{10} \) , and their product is −1.

whyWrong.A: The slopes come out as \( -\frac{10}{7} \) and \( -\frac{7}{10} \) . Their product is +1, so the lines are reflections of each other, not perpendicular.
whyWrong.C: Doubling a instead of b gives slopes \( -\frac{10}{7} \) and \( \frac{14}{5} \) , whose product is −4.
whyWrong.D: Flipping the sign on 7y changes the first slope to \( \frac{5}{7} \) while the second line is untouched at \( \frac{7}{5} \) ; the product is +1.

stem:
In the system of equations below, a and c are constants.

\[ ax + y = c \]
\[ \frac{1}{2}x + \frac{1}{3}y = \frac{1}{6} \]

If the system of equations has an infinite number of solutions (x, y), what is the value of a?
whyCorrect: Infinitely many solutions means the two equations describe the same line, so scale one until it looks like the other. The first equation has a coefficient of 1 on y, so multiply the second by 3 to match: \( \frac{3}{2}x + y = \frac{1}{2} \) . Comparing term by term, \( a = \frac{3}{2} \) (and c would be \( \frac{1}{2} \) ). Scaling to match the y-terms first is what makes this quick.

stem: 3 consecutive even integers are ordered from smallest to largest. 5 times the first integer is at least 9 more than the sum of the second and third integers. What is the minimum possible value for the second integer?
whyCorrect: Call the integers n, n + 2 and n + 4. "At least 9 more than" gives \( 5n \ge (n + 2) + (n + 4) + 9 \) , which simplifies to \( 5n \ge 2n + 15 \) , so \( n \ge 5 \) . The catch is the word even: n = 5 is not allowed, so the smallest permitted first integer is 6. The question asks for the second integer, which is then 6 + 2 = 8.

stem:
\[ -32x + 18y + 150 = 15y + 4x \]
\[ 52 + \frac{w}{3}x + 18y = -32 \]

In the given system of equations, w is a constant. The system has only one solution. Find the value that w is not equal to.
whyCorrect: A linear system fails to have exactly one solution only when the two lines are parallel, so find the w that makes the slopes equal — that is the forbidden value. Tidy the first equation: \( -36x + 3y = -150 \) , or \( y = 12x - 50 \) , slope 12. The second is \( \frac{w}{3}x + 18y = -84 \) , slope \( -\frac{w}{54} \) . Setting \( -\frac{w}{54} = 12 \) gives w = −648, so w can be anything except −648.

stem: Line s is defined by \( x - 4y = 24 \) . Line t is perpendicular to line s in the xy-plane and passes through the points (k, 0) and (60, −k). What is the value of k?
whyCorrect: Rewrite line s as \( y = \frac{1}{4}x - 6 \) , so its slope is \( \frac{1}{4} \) and line t has slope −4. Now use the two points on t: \( \frac{-k - 0}{60 - k} = -4 \) . Multiplying out, \( -k = -240 + 4k \) , so \( 5k = 240 \) and k = 48. Check: (48, 0) and (60, −48) give a slope of \( \frac{-48}{12} = -4 \) .

stem:
\[ t = \frac{1}{2}v \]

For the equation above, which of the following is the graph of v as a function of t?
whyCorrect: "v as a function of t" means t goes on the horizontal axis, so solve for v first: \( v = 2t \) . That is a line through the origin with slope 2, rising 2 units for each 1 unit right and reaching v = 10 at t = 5. Graph A is the only one that does this. Reading the equation as it stands, with slope \( \frac{1}{2} \) , is the trap.

whyWrong.B: This line is far too shallow — it climbs only about 2 units across the whole width, a slope near \( \frac{1}{2} \) of \( \frac{1}{2} \) .
whyWrong.C: This has slope 1, the average of the two numbers rather than either of them.
whyWrong.D: This is steeper than slope 2, reaching 10 by t = 3.

note: The four choices are graphs; they must be supplied as images. Choice text here is a placeholder. | figure: The four answer choices ARE these graphs, so all four are supplied as a single labelled image on the question; the choice texts stay A/B/C/D. Neither axis is labelled in the book.

stem:
There is a linear relationship between x and y. The table shows three values of x and their corresponding values of y in terms of a constant n.

xy
0n
4n + 21
8n + 42

What is the slope of the line in the xy-plane that represents this relationship?
whyCorrect: Slope is the change in y divided by the change in x, and the unknown n cancels because it appears in every y-value. From the first row to the second, y goes from n to n + 21, a rise of 21, while x goes from 0 to 4, a run of 4. The slope is \( \frac{21}{4} \) , and the third row confirms it: another 21 up for another 4 across.

whyWrong.A: 21 is the rise alone, taken as though x increased by 1 each row.
whyWrong.B: 2 is close to the number of steps between rows and has no bearing on the ratio; it may come from dividing 8 by 4.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{4}{21} \) is run over rise, the slope upside down.

note: The slice records this as free response, but the book prints four answer choices; treated as multiple choice.

stem: In the xy-plane, line r passes through the points (3, 12) and (7, 13). Line s passes through the point (1, 2) and is perpendicular to line r. An equation of line s is \( ax + 7y = c \) , where a and c are constants. What is the value of c?
whyCorrect: Line r has slope \( \frac{13 - 12}{7 - 3} = \frac{1}{4} \) , so line s has slope −4. Through (1, 2) that is \( y = -4x + 6 \) . Now match the requested form: the printed equation has 7y, so multiply the whole equation by 7 — \( 28x + 7y = 42 \) — which gives c = 42 (and a = 28). Rescaling to match the 7 is the step that is easy to forget.

stem:
\[ 7x + 8y = 3 \]

The given equation is one equation in a system of two linear equations. If the system of equations has at least one solution, which of the following equations could be the other equation in the system?

I. \( 14x + 16y = 12 \)
II. \( 14x + 16y = 6 \)
whyCorrect: Both candidates have left sides that are exactly twice \( 7x + 8y \) , so the only question is what the right side should be. Doubling the given equation gives \( 14x + 16y = 6 \) , which is statement II — the same line written twice, so every point on it solves the system. Statement I demands \( 14x + 16y = 12 \) , i.e. \( 7x + 8y = 6 \) , which cannot hold at the same time as \( 7x + 8y = 3 \) .

whyWrong.A: I gives two parallel lines: same slope, different intercepts, so there is no solution at all.
whyWrong.C: I fails, so the pair cannot both work.
whyWrong.D: II does work — it is the original equation multiplied by 2, so the system has infinitely many solutions, which counts as at least one.

stem:
\[ a(4 - x) = 28 - 7x \]

In the given equation, a is a constant. The equation has exactly one solution. Which of the following CANNOT be the value of a?
whyCorrect: Expand and collect the x-terms: \( 4a - ax = 28 - 7x \) becomes \( (7 - a)x = 28 - 4a \) . A linear equation has exactly one solution as long as the coefficient of x is not zero, so the forbidden value is a = 7. Putting a = 7 back in gives \( 7(4 - x) = 28 - 7x \) , which is true for every x — infinitely many solutions, not one.

whyWrong.A: With a = 1 the coefficient of x is 6, so x is determined uniquely.
whyWrong.B: With a = 4 the coefficient is 3 and the equation solves to a single value of x.
whyWrong.D: With a = 28 the coefficient is −21, again giving exactly one solution.

stem:
\[ \frac{x}{7} + \frac{y}{5} = \frac{41}{35} \]

An engineer connects resistors in series, where the resistors in the series have a total resistance of \( \frac{41}{35} \) ohms. In this series, there are x resistors of type A, which each have a resistance of a ohms, and y resistors of type B, which each have a resistance of b ohms. The given equation represents this situation. According to this equation, what is the positive difference between the value of a and the value of b?
whyCorrect: In series the resistances add, so the total is \( ax + by \) . Matching that against \( \frac{x}{7} + \frac{y}{5} \) term by term, the coefficient of x is \( a = \frac{1}{7} \) and the coefficient of y is \( b = \frac{1}{5} \) . The difference is \( \frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{7} = \frac{7 - 5}{35} = \frac{2}{35} \) . The 7 and 5 are denominators, so a and b are their reciprocals, not the numbers themselves.

whyWrong.A: \( \frac{1}{35} \) is \( \frac{1}{7} \times \frac{1}{5} \) , the product of the two resistances rather than their difference.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{3}{35} \) does not come from these values; check the subtraction, \( \frac{7 - 5}{35} \) .
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{12}{35} \) is \( \frac{1}{7} + \frac{1}{5} \) , the sum instead of the difference.

stem:
\[ j(x - k) = \frac{3}{4}x + 15 \]

In the equation above, j and k are constants. If the equation has infinitely many solutions for x, what is the value of k?
whyCorrect: Infinitely many solutions means the two sides are the same expression, so expand and match coefficients. The left becomes \( jx - jk \) . Matching the x-terms gives \( j = \frac{3}{4} \) ; matching the constants gives \( -jk = 15 \) . Substituting, \( -\frac{3}{4}k = 15 \) , so \( k = -20 \) . Watch the minus sign that comes out of the parentheses — dropping it gives +20.

stem: Line segment GH and point R are shown in the xy-plane. If line \( \ell \) (not shown) contains point R and is perpendicular to line segment GH, which of the following is an equation of line \( \ell \) ?
whyCorrect: Read the two endpoints off the grid: G is at (0, 3) and H at (4, 0), so segment GH has slope \( \frac{0 - 3}{4 - 0} = -\frac{3}{4} \) and the perpendicular slope is \( \frac{4}{3} \) . Line \( \ell \) passes through R at (0, 2), so \( y = \frac{4}{3}x + 2 \) . Clearing the fraction gives \( 3y = 4x + 6 \) , that is \( -4x + 3y = 6 \) . Checking a choice quickly: put x = 0 and see whether y = 2.

whyWrong.B: Its slope is \( \frac{3}{4} \) , the negative of GH's slope rather than the negative reciprocal, and at x = 0 it gives y = 2 by coincidence.
whyWrong.C: Its slope is \( -\frac{3}{4} \) , which is parallel to GH, not perpendicular.
whyWrong.D: Its slope is \( -\frac{4}{3} \) : the fraction is flipped but the sign is wrong, so it is perpendicular to the wrong line.

stem: The graph shows the total amount of rainfall y, in centimeters, from the start of a 10-hour period, where x is the number of hours after the start of the period. Which of the following statements about the rainfall during this time period is true?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The rate of rainfall was 2 centimeters per hour between x = 2 and x = 4.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The rate of rainfall was the greatest between x = 4 and x = 10.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The rate of rainfall increased between x = 0 and x = 2.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The rate of rainfall was 0 centimeters per hour between x = 2 and x = 4.

whyCorrect: The graph plots the total rainfall so far, so the rate of rainfall is the graph's steepness, not its height. Between x = 2 and x = 4 the graph is flat at 2 centimeters: the total is not growing, so no rain fell and the rate was 0 centimeters per hour.

whyWrong.A: 2 is the height of the graph over that stretch, the total accumulated, not the slope. The slope there is zero.
whyWrong.B: From x = 4 to x = 10 the graph rises only about 0.6 centimeters in 6 hours, a rate of about 0.1. The steepest stretch is the first two hours, at about 1 centimeter per hour.
whyWrong.C: From x = 0 to x = 2 the graph is a straight line, so the rate is constant. The total rises, but a constant slope means an unchanging rate.

stem:
In the xy-plane, the quadrants are labeled in the usual way, with quadrant I in the upper right and the numbering continuing counterclockwise. The graph of the equation

\[ y = 3(x + a)^{2} + b \]

where a and b are positive constants, has a vertex in which quadrant?
whyCorrect: In vertex form \( y = A(x - h)^{2} + k \) the vertex is (h, k), and the sign inside the parentheses flips: \( (x + a)^{2} \) means h = −a. Since a is positive, the vertex's x-coordinate is negative, and since b is positive its y-coordinate is positive. Left of the y-axis and above the x-axis is quadrant II.

whyWrong.A: Quadrant I would need a positive x-coordinate, which requires \( (x - a)^{2} \) .
whyWrong.C: Quadrant III would need b negative as well; b is given as positive.
whyWrong.D: Quadrant IV reverses both signs, treating the vertex as (a, −b).

note: The book shows the quadrant numbering as a small figure; it is the standard labelling and is stated in words here. The slice records this as free response; the book prints four choices.

stem: The solutions to \( x^{2} + 12x + 35 = 0 \) are r and s, where \( r < s \) . The solutions to \( x^{2} + 12x + 27 = 0 \) are t and u, where \( t < u \) . The solutions to \( x^{2} + 24x + c = 0 \) , where c is a constant, are \( r + u \) and \( s + t \) . What is the value of c?
whyCorrect: Factor both quadratics. \( x^{2} + 12x + 35 = (x + 7)(x + 5) \) gives r = −7 and s = −5, and \( x^{2} + 12x + 27 = (x + 9)(x + 3) \) gives t = −9 and u = −3 — keeping the ordering \( r < s \) and \( t < u \) straight is what makes the rest work. The new roots are \( r + u = -10 \) and \( s + t = -14 \) . For a monic quadratic the constant term is the product of the roots, so \( c = (-10)(-14) = 140 \) . (Their sum, −24, matches the given 24x, a useful check.)

stem: If \( x = \sqrt[2n]{2x^{n} + 35} \) , where n is a positive integer constant, what is the value of \( x^{n} \) ?
whyCorrect: Raise both sides to the power 2n to clear the radical: \( x^{2n} = 2x^{n} + 35 \) . Now notice that \( x^{2n} = (x^{n})^{2} \) , so with \( u = x^{n} \) this is \( u^{2} - 2u - 35 = 0 \) , which factors as (u - 7)(u + 5) = 0. An even root is never negative, so x and therefore \( x^{n} \) cannot be -5; the value is 7.
note: This question is printed twice on the same page of the book, as Advanced Math #3 and #6, word for word. Do not place both in one test.

stem:
The graph of \( y = g(x) \) is shown, where the function g is defined by

\[ g(x) = f(x + a) + b \]

and a and b are constants. If the function f is defined by \( f(x) = x^{3} \) , what is the value of \( a + b \) ?
whyCorrect: With \( f(x) = x^{3} \) , \( g(x) = (x + a)^{3} + b \) . The graph of \( y = x^{3} \) has its flat centre at the origin, so on the shifted graph that centre sits at \( (-a, b) \) . The picture shows the flattening at (4, −1), so \( -a = 4 \) and \( b = -1 \) , giving a = −4 and \( a + b = -5 \) . The sign flip on a is the whole question: \( x + a \) inside the function moves the graph in the opposite direction.

whyWrong.B: −1 is b by itself, with the horizontal shift left out.
whyWrong.C: 1 comes from reading the shift as (4, −1) but then taking a = −4 with b = +... check the vertical shift: the centre is below the x-axis, so b is negative.
whyWrong.D: 5 reads the centre as (−4, 1), reversing both shifts; \( (x + a)^{3} \) with positive a moves the graph left, not right.

stem:
\[ (3x + p)(5x^{2} - 45)(2x^{2} - 16x + 6p) = 0 \]

In the given equation, p is a positive constant. The sum of the solutions to the equation is \( \frac{20}{3} \) . What is the value of p?
whyCorrect: Handle each factor separately and add the sums; you never need the individual roots of the last one. From \( 3x + p = 0 \) the solution is \( -\frac{p}{3} \) . From \( 5x^{2} - 45 = 0 \) the solutions are 3 and −3, which contribute 0. For \( 2x^{2} - 16x + 6p = 0 \) , the sum of the roots is \( \frac{16}{2} = 8 \) . So \( -\frac{p}{3} + 0 + 8 = \frac{20}{3} \) , which gives \( \frac{p}{3} = \frac{4}{3} \) and p = 4. Check that the last factor still has real roots: with p = 4 it is \( 2(x - 2)(x - 6) \) .

stem:
\[ f(x) = ax^{2} + 6x + c \]

In the given quadratic function, a and c are constants. The graph of \( y = f(x) \) in the xy-plane is a parabola that opens upward and has a vertex at the point (h, k), where h and k are constants. If \( k > 0 \) and \( f(-7) = f(5) \) , which of the following must be true?

I. \( c > 3 \)
II. \( a > 3 \)
whyCorrect: Equal outputs at −7 and 5 mean those points are mirror images, so the axis of symmetry is halfway between them: \( h = \frac{-7 + 5}{2} = -1 \) . Since \( h = -\frac{6}{2a} = -\frac{3}{a} \) , this forces a = 3 exactly. Then \( k = f(-1) = 3 - 6 + c = c - 3 \) , and \( k > 0 \) gives \( c > 3 \) . So I must be true and II cannot be, because a equals 3 rather than exceeding it.

whyWrong.B: a is pinned to exactly 3 by the symmetry condition, so "a > 3" is false, not merely unproven.
whyWrong.C: I holds but II does not, so they cannot both be true.
whyWrong.D: I does follow: the vertex height is c − 3, and it is given to be positive.

stem: Function f is a quadratic function. The graph of \( y = f(x) \) in the xy-plane has a vertex at (9, −7), contains the point (8, −9), and has a y-intercept at (0, a). The graph of \( y = 6 \cdot f(x) \) has a y-intercept at (0, b). What is the positive difference between a and b?
whyCorrect: Start in vertex form: \( f(x) = A(x - 9)^{2} - 7 \) . The point (8, −9) gives \( A(1) - 7 = -9 \) , so A = −2. Then \( a = f(0) = -2(81) - 7 = -169 \) . Multiplying the whole function by 6 multiplies every output by 6, so \( b = 6(-169) = -1014 \) . The positive difference is \( |-169 - (-1014)| = 845 \) . Equivalently, b − a is 5 times a, so the gap is \( 5 \times 169 \) .

stem:
The graph of \( y = f(x) \) is shown in the xy-plane. If the function g is defined by

\[ g(x) = (x + 3)(x - 1) \]

for which of the following values of x is \( f(x) > g(x) \) ?
whyCorrect: You do not need a formula for f — just compare heights at each candidate x. g is an upward parabola with zeros at −3 and 1, so it is negative in between and positive outside. At x = −2, g(−2) = (1)(−3) = −3, while the graph puts f near its maximum, well above the x-axis. So f(−2) is comfortably greater than g(−2).

whyWrong.A: At x = −3, g is exactly 0 and f is at or barely above the axis; this is the boundary, not a clear win.
whyWrong.C: At x = 1, g is again 0 and f is close to the axis, so the inequality is not securely satisfied here.
whyWrong.D: At x = 2, g(2) = (5)(1) = 5 while f has already dropped below the x-axis, so f is smaller.

note: As drawn, f's zeros are slightly outside −3 and 1 (about −3.4 and 1.4), which would make choices A and C true as well; the question only has a single answer if f's zeros are exactly −3 and 1, in which case f = −g. B is correct on either reading. The slice records this as free response; the book prints four choices.
imageAlt: Coordinate grid in the xy-plane with the x-axis marked from −4 to 4 and the y-axis from −4 to 4, showing a single downward-opening parabola labelled y = f(x).

stem: Which of the following could be the equation of the graph shown?
whyCorrect: Two features decide it. The curve touches the x-axis without crossing at x = −2 and x = 3, so the factors are \( (x + 2)^{2} \) and \( (x - 3)^{2} \) — note the sign flip, a zero at −2 comes from \( (x + 2) \) . That leaves A and C, separated by their height: at x = 0, A gives \( 4 \cdot 9 = 36 \) but the graph is up near 70, and C gives \( 2 \cdot 4 \cdot 9 = 72 \) . C also matches the local maximum of about 78.

whyWrong.A: The zeros are right, but every value is half what the graph shows: it would peak near 39, not near 78.
whyWrong.B: Its zeros are at 2 and −3, the mirror image of the graph's.
whyWrong.D: Same wrong zeros as B, with the correct vertical stretch applied to the wrong shape.

imageAlt: Coordinate grid in the xy-plane, x-axis marked from −4 to 4 and y-axis marked in twenties up to 100, showing a single W-shaped quartic curve.

stem:
An equation for the graph shown is

\[ y = a(x + 3)(x + b) \]

where a and b are constants. What is the value of ab?
whyCorrect: The graph crosses the x-axis at −3 and 4. The factor \( (x + 3) \) already accounts for the zero at −3, so \( (x + b) \) must vanish at x = 4, which means b = −4 — the sign flips. For a, use the y-intercept: the curve passes through (0, −4), and \( a(3)(-4) = -12a = -4 \) gives \( a = \frac{1}{3} \) . So \( ab = \frac{1}{3}(-4) = -\frac{4}{3} \) .

whyWrong.A: −2 comes from misreading the y-intercept as −6, which would make \( a = \frac{1}{2} \) .
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{1}{2} \) is a value of a from that same misreading, not the product ab.
whyWrong.D: 8 keeps b = 4 instead of −4 (forgetting that a zero at 4 needs the factor x − 4) and pairs it with a = 2.

stem:
The graph of \( f(x) \) is the result of shifting the graph of \( g(x) \) 3 units to the right and 3 units up. If the equation of \( f(x) \) is

\[ f(x) = x^{2} + 4x \]

what is the equation of \( g(x) \) ?
whyCorrect: f is the shifted one, so to recover g you undo the shift: move 3 left and 3 down, that is \( g(x) = f(x + 3) - 3 \) . Put f in vertex form first: \( f(x) = (x + 2)^{2} - 4 \) , with vertex (−2, −4). Undoing the shift moves the vertex to (−5, −7), so \( g(x) = (x + 5)^{2} - 7 \) .

whyWrong.A: This shifts f the same way again instead of undoing it, and it adds 3 rather than subtracting.
whyWrong.B: The vertical part is right, but the horizontal shift went the wrong way, to +5 instead of −5.
whyWrong.D: The horizontal shift is right but the vertical one was never applied: −4 is f's vertex height, not g's.

stem: The xy-plane above shows two points of intersection of the graphs of a linear function and a quadratic function. The vertex of the graph of the quadratic function is at (3, −4) and (r, s) is one of the points of intersection of the graphs. What is the value of r?
whyCorrect: Build both functions from the figure. The line passes through (0, −6) and the vertex (3, −4), so its slope is \( \frac{2}{3} \) and \( y = \frac{2}{3}x - 6 \) . The parabola has vertex (3, −4) and x-intercepts at 0 and 6, so \( y = A(x - 3)^{2} - 4 \) with \( 9A = 4 \) , that is \( A = \frac{4}{9} \) . Setting them equal, \( \frac{4}{9}(x - 3)^{2} = \frac{2}{3}(x - 3) \) , and factoring out \( (x - 3) \) leaves \( \frac{4}{9}(x - 3) = \frac{2}{3} \) , so \( x - 3 = \frac{3}{2} \) and r = 4.5. Factoring rather than expanding keeps the known root x = 3 out of the way.
note: The stem alone does not fix the parabola's leading coefficient; it has to be read off the figure, where the curve meets the x-axis at 0 and 6, giving A = 4/9.
imageAlt: The xy-plane showing an upward-opening parabola and a straight line that cross each other; two intersection points and the line's y-intercept are marked with dots.

stem: \[ f(x) = m\sqrt{-x-n} \]where \(m\) and \(n\) are constants. If \( f(8)=0 \) and \( f(4) < -16 \), which of the following must be true?
whyCorrect: Pin down \(n\) first. \( f(8) = m\sqrt{-8-n} = 0 \) forces either \(m=0\) or the radical to be 0, and \(m=0\) would make \(f(4)=0\), which contradicts \( f(4) < -16 \). So \( -8-n = 0 \), giving \( n = -8 \) and \( f(x) = m\sqrt{8-x} \). Then \( f(4) = m\sqrt{4} = 2m < -16 \), so \( m < -8 \). With \(n=-8\), \( n-m = -8-m \), and \( m < -8 \) makes \( -8-m > 0 \).

whyWrong.A: This reverses the inequality. Dividing \( 2m < -16 \) by 2 gives \( m < -8 \), not \( m > -8 \).
whyWrong.B: \( n+m=0 \) with \(n=-8\) would mean \(m=8\), a positive \(m\); then \(f(4)=16\), not less than \(-16\).
whyWrong.C: \( n+m > 0 \) means \( m > 8 \), the opposite sign for \(m\). It comes from treating \(m\) as positive after dropping the minus sign in \( f(4) < -16 \).

stem: \[ 8rx^2 - 80sx + 8r = 0 \]For the given equation, \(r\) and \(s\) are constants such that \( r > 0 \), \( s < 0 \) and \( \frac{r}{s} > k \). What is the least value of \(k\) that ensures that the equation has two distinct real solutions?
whyCorrect: Two distinct real solutions means the discriminant is positive: \( (-80s)^2 - 4(8r)(8r) > 0 \), i.e. \( 6400s^2 - 256r^2 > 0 \), so \( r^2 < 25s^2 \). Divide by \( s^2 \) to get \( \left(\frac{r}{s}\right)^2 < 25 \), so \( -5 < \frac{r}{s} < 5 \). Because \( r > 0 \) and \( s < 0 \), the ratio \( \frac{r}{s} \) is already negative, so the only part of that range that can bind is \( \frac{r}{s} > -5 \). The smallest \(k\) for which \( \frac{r}{s} > k \) still guarantees a positive discriminant is therefore \( k = -5 \).

stem:
The functions \(f\) and \(g\) are defined by the given equations, where \( x \ge 0 \). Which of the following equations displays, as a constant or coefficient, the maximum value of the function it defines, where \( x \ge 0 \)?
I. \( f(x) = 16(1.24)^x + 43 \)
II. \( g(x) = 8(0.72)^x \)
whyCorrect: Check whether each function even has a maximum on \( x \ge 0 \). In I the base is 1.24, greater than 1, so \(f\) grows without bound as \(x\) increases — there is no maximum value at all, so no number in the equation can display one. In II the base is 0.72, less than 1, so \(g\) decreases; its largest value on \( x \ge 0 \) is at \( x=0 \), where \( g(0) = 8(0.72)^0 = 8 \). That 8 is the coefficient sitting in the equation, so only II displays its maximum.

whyWrong.A: For I, the 43 is the minimum the graph approaches from above as \(x\) decreases, and on \( x \ge 0 \) the smallest value is \( 16+43 = 59 \). Either way it is a floor, not a maximum — an increasing exponential has no maximum.
whyWrong.C: This requires I to have a maximum, which it does not; a base greater than 1 makes the function unbounded above.
whyWrong.D: This misses that a decaying exponential does have a maximum on \( x \ge 0 \), reached at \( x = 0 \), and that its value there is exactly the coefficient 8.

stem: The expression \( 6x^4 + 17x^2 + 7 \) can be rewritten as \( (3x^2+a)(2x^2+b) \), where \(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers, or as \( (3x^2+c)(2x^2+d) \), where \(c\) and \(d\) are positive nonintegers. What is the value of \( a+c \)?
whyCorrect: Expanding \( (3x^2+a)(2x^2+b) \) gives \( 6x^4 + (3b+2a)x^2 + ab \), so you need \( ab = 7 \) and \( 3b+2a = 17 \). The integer pair is \( a=7 \), \( b=1 \) (the other order gives 23, not 17). The same two conditions with nonintegers: substitute \( d = \frac{7}{c} \) into \( 3d+2c = 17 \) to get \( 2c^2 - 17c + 21 = 0 \), whose roots are \( c = 7 \) and \( c = 1.5 \); the noninteger one is \( c = 1.5 \) (with \( d = \frac{14}{3} \)). So \( a + c = 7 + 1.5 = 8.5 \).

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \( f(x) = \frac{x^2+ax+b}{2x+c} \), where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are constants. The graph of the function \(f\) in the xy-plane, where \( y = f(x) \), does not intersect the line \( x = 4 \). If \( f(5) = f(6) = 0 \), what is the value of \( a+b+c \)?
whyCorrect: The zeros of a rational function are the zeros of its numerator, so \( x^2+ax+b = (x-5)(x-6) = x^2-11x+30 \), giving \( a=-11 \) and \( b=30 \). The graph misses the vertical line \( x=4 \) only if \(f\) is undefined there, so \( 2(4)+c = 0 \) and \( c = -8 \) (the numerator is 2 at \( x=4 \), so this is a genuine asymptote, not a hole). Then \( a+b+c = -11+30-8 = 11 \).
note: Exact duplicate of question 28 in the same chapter.

stem: The function \(h\) is defined by \[ h(x) = -\sqrt{x^2+bx+c} \]The graph of \( y = h(x) \) passes through \( (2,0) \) and \( \left(0, -\sqrt{358}\right) \). If \( h(m) = 0 \), what is the greatest possible value of \(m\)?
whyCorrect: Use the second point first, because \( x = 0 \) kills two terms: \( h(0) = -\sqrt{c} = -\sqrt{358} \), so \( c = 358 \). The point \( (2,0) \) gives \( -\sqrt{4+2b+358} = 0 \), so \( 2b + 362 = 0 \) and \( b = -181 \). Now \( h(m)=0 \) means \( m^2 - 181m + 358 = 0 \); the discriminant is \( 32761 - 1432 = 31329 = 177^2 \), so \( m = \frac{181 \pm 177}{2} \), i.e. \( m = 2 \) or \( m = 179 \). The greatest is 179.

stem: \[ \sqrt[7]{p^4} = t^{\frac{5}{7}} \]In the given equation, \( p > 1 \) and \( t > 1 \). If \( t = p^{2n-1} \), where \(n\) is a constant, what is the value of \(n\)?
whyCorrect: Rewrite the radical as a power: \( \sqrt[7]{p^4} = p^{\frac{4}{7}} \), so \( p^{\frac{4}{7}} = t^{\frac{5}{7}} \). Raise both sides to the 7th power to clear the sevenths: \( p^4 = t^5 \), so \( t = p^{\frac{4}{5}} \). Since \( p > 1 \), the base is not 0, 1 or \(-1\), so equal powers of \(p\) force equal exponents: \( 2n-1 = \frac{4}{5} \). That gives \( 2n = \frac{9}{5} \) and \( n = \frac{9}{10} = 0.9 \).
note: Book prints the last sentence as two fragments ("If t = p^{2n-1}, where n is a constant. What is the value of n?"); joined into one sentence.

stem: In the xy-plane, a parabola has vertex \( (9,-14) \) and intersects the x-axis at two points. If the equation of the parabola is written in the form \( y = ax^2+bx+c \) where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are constants, which of the following could be the value of \( a+b+c \)?
whyCorrect: Notice that \( a+b+c \) is just \( y \) when \( x = 1 \). Write the parabola in vertex form, \( y = a(x-9)^2 - 14 \); since the vertex is below the x-axis and the curve still crosses it twice, the parabola opens upward, so \( a > 0 \). At \( x = 1 \), \( y = 64a - 14 \), and with \( a > 0 \) that is strictly greater than \(-14\). Only \(-12\) clears that bound (it needs \( a = \frac{1}{32} \)).

whyWrong.A: \(-23\) is below \(-14\), which would require \( 64a-14 = -23 \), i.e. a negative \(a\) — then the parabola opens downward from a vertex already below the x-axis and never crosses it.
whyWrong.B: Same problem: \(-19 < -14\) forces \( a < 0 \), contradicting a parabola with two x-intercepts and vertex \( (9,-14) \).
whyWrong.C: \(-14\) is the vertex's y-value, reached only at \( x=9 \); getting it at \( x=1 \) needs \( a=0 \), which is not a parabola at all.

stem: \[ y = ax^2+bx+c \]The function \(f\) is defined above, where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are constants. The graph of \( y = f(x) \) in the xy-plane passes through the points \( (-16,0) \) and \( (9,0) \). If \(a\) is an integer greater than 3, what is the smallest possible value of \( 3b-2a \)?
whyCorrect: The two given points are the x-intercepts, so factored form gives \( y = a(x+16)(x-9) = a(x^2+7x-144) \). Matching coefficients, \( b = 7a \), so \( 3b-2a = 21a-2a = 19a \) — it depends only on \(a\). Since \(a\) is an integer greater than 3, the smallest allowed value is \( a = 4 \), and \( 19(4) = 76 \).
note: Book labels the displayed equation with y but calls the function f in the prose; transcribed as printed.

stem: \[ f(x) = ax^2+bx+c \]The function \(f\) is defined above, where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are constants and \( 4 < b < 7 \). The graph of \( y = f(x) \) is such that \( f(1) = f(5) \). If \(b\) is an integer, what could be the value of \( ab \)?
whyCorrect: Equal outputs at \( x=1 \) and \( x=5 \) put the axis of symmetry halfway between them, at \( x = 3 \). So \( -\frac{b}{2a} = 3 \), which rearranges to \( b = -6a \), i.e. \( a = -\frac{b}{6} \). The integers strictly between 4 and 7 are 5 and 6, and \( ab = -\frac{b^2}{6} \); taking \( b = 6 \) gives \( a = -1 \) and \( ab = -6 \).
note: Nothing in the stem forces a to be an integer, so b = 5 (a = -5/6, ab = -25/6) also satisfies every stated condition. -6 is the intended value; a grader should accept -25/6 as well.

stem: \[ f(x) = \sqrt[3]{x^3+ax^2+bx+c} \]The function \(f\) is defined by the given equation, where \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) are integers. The graph of \( y = f(x) \) passes through the point \( (9,0) \), and \( f(0) = 27 \). What is the value of \( 9a+b \)?
whyCorrect: A cube root is 0 only when its radicand is 0, so \( f(9)=0 \) gives \( 729 + 81a + 9b + c = 0 \). The other condition is easier: \( f(0) = \sqrt[3]{c} = 27 \), so \( c = 27^3 = 19{,}683 \). Substituting, \( 81a + 9b = -729 - 19{,}683 = -20{,}412 \). The question asks for \( 9a+b \), which is that expression divided by 9: \( -20{,}412 \div 9 = -2{,}268 \).

stem: \[ y = ax^2+bx+c \]The equation of a parabola is given, where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are constants. In the xy-plane, the parabola has vertex \( (3,11) \) and \( c < 0 \). Which of the following could be the value of \(b\)?
whyCorrect: The vertex's x-coordinate gives \( -\frac{b}{2a} = 3 \), so \( b = -6a \). The constant \(c\) is the y-intercept, and from vertex form \( y = a(x-3)^2+11 \) that is \( c = 9a+11 \). Requiring \( c < 0 \) gives \( a < -\frac{11}{9} \), and multiplying by \(-6\) flips the inequality: \( b = -6a > \frac{66}{9} = 7\frac{1}{3} \). Only 8 exceeds that.

whyWrong.A: \( b=5 \) gives \( a = -\frac{5}{6} \) and \( c = 9\left(-\frac{5}{6}\right)+11 = 3.5 \), which is positive, so \( c < 0 \) fails.
whyWrong.B: \( b=6 \) gives \( a = -1 \) and \( c = 2 \) — still positive.
whyWrong.C: \( b=7 \) gives \( a = -\frac{7}{6} \) and \( c = 11 - 10.5 = 0.5 \), positive by a hair. This is the trap: \(b\) must exceed \( \frac{22}{3} \approx 7.33 \), not just 7.

stem: If \( p(x) = x^2+kx+4 \) has no real zeros, what is the range of possible values for \(k\)?

choices.label: D
choices.content: No range, \(k\) can be any real number.

whyCorrect: No real zeros means the discriminant is negative: \( k^2 - 4(1)(4) < 0 \), so \( k^2 < 16 \). Taking the square root of both sides of \( k^2 < 16 \) gives \( |k| < 4 \), which is the two-sided range \( -4 < k < 4 \), not a one-sided one. Large \(|k|\) in either direction is what forces the parabola to cross the x-axis.

whyWrong.A: This keeps only the negative half and, worse, has the inequality backwards — \( k < -4 \) makes \( k^2 > 16 \), so there are two real zeros.
whyWrong.C: Same error on the positive side: \( k > 4 \) gives \( k^2 > 16 \), a positive discriminant and two real zeros.
whyWrong.D: The discriminant does depend on \(k\); at \( k = 5 \), for instance, \( p(x) = x^2+5x+4 = (x+1)(x+4) \) has real zeros, so not every \(k\) works.

stem:
\[ f(x) = -3x^2+bx+c \]In the given quadratic function \(b\) and \(c\) are constants. The graph of \( y = f(x) \) in the xy-plane is a parabola that has a vertex at the point \( (h,k) \), where \(h\) and \(k\) are constants. If \( f(-4) = f(8) \), and the quadratic function has x-intercepts at \( (r,0) \) and \( (s,0) \), which of the following must be true?
I. \( r+s = 4 \)
II. \( b < 0 \)
III. \( c < k \)
whyCorrect: Equal outputs at \( x=-4 \) and \( x=8 \) put the axis of symmetry at their midpoint, \( h = 2 \). The x-intercepts are symmetric about that axis, so \( \frac{r+s}{2} = 2 \) and \( r+s = 4 \) — statement I holds. From \( -\frac{b}{2(-3)} = 2 \) you get \( b = 12 \), which is positive, so II fails. For III, \( k = f(2) = -12 + 24 + c = c + 12 \), so \( c \) is always 12 less than \(k\) and \( c < k \) always holds.

whyWrong.A: II is false: solving \( -\frac{b}{-6} = 2 \) gives \( b = 12 \). The sign trap is forgetting that the leading coefficient is \(-3\), which flips the sign of \(b\) you need for a positive axis of symmetry.
whyWrong.B: II is false for the reason above, and this choice also drops the true statement I.
whyWrong.D: Everything except II is right; a parabola opening downward does not force \( b < 0 \) — the sign of \(b\) follows from where the vertex sits, and here the vertex is at \( x = 2 > 0 \).

stem:
The functions \(f\) and \(g\) are defined by the given equations, where \( 2 \le x \le 8 \). Which of the following equations displays, as a constant or coefficient, the minimum value of the function it defines, where \( 2 \le x \le 8 \)?
I. \( f(x) = 0.0625(0.5)(2)^{x+2} \)
II. \( g(x) = 1500(0.2)^{x-3} \)
whyCorrect: Find where each function bottoms out on the interval, then see whether that number is actually written in the equation. \(f\) has base 2, so it increases and its least value is at \( x = 2 \): \( 0.0625(0.5)(2)^4 = 0.0625(0.5)(16) = 0.5 \) — and 0.5 is sitting there as a coefficient. \(g\) has base 0.2, so it decreases and its least value is at \( x = 8 \): \( 1500(0.2)^5 = 0.48 \), a number that appears nowhere in the equation. So only I displays its minimum.

whyWrong.B: \(g\) does attain its minimum at \( x=8 \), but that value is \( 1500(0.2)^5 = 0.48 \); the visible constants are 1500 (the value at \( x=3 \)) and 0.2 (the decay factor), neither of which is the minimum on \( 2 \le x \le 8 \).
whyWrong.C: Requires II, which fails; 0.48 is not displayed.
whyWrong.D: Misses that \( 0.0625(0.5)(2)^{2+2} \) collapses to exactly 0.5, so the 0.5 in the equation is the minimum value on the interval.

stem: The given expression is \[ -16(5x-3)^2 + 4(5x-2)^2 \]The given expression can be rewritten as \( \frac{ax^2}{4} + \frac{bx}{4} + \frac{c}{4} \), where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are constants. What is the value of \( a+b+c \)?
whyCorrect: Expand both squares and combine: \( -16(25x^2-30x+9) = -400x^2+480x-144 \) and \( 4(25x^2-20x+4) = 100x^2-80x+16 \), which add to \( -300x^2+400x-128 \). Now match that against \( \frac{a}{4}x^2 + \frac{b}{4}x + \frac{c}{4} \): every coefficient in the target form is divided by 4, so you must multiply by 4, not divide. That gives \( a = -1200 \), \( b = 1600 \), \( c = -512 \), and \( a+b+c = -112 \).

stem: Given the expression \[ \sqrt[4]{40n} \times \left(\sqrt[5]{40n}\right)^3 \]find the value of \(y\) for which the expression is equivalent to \( (40n)^{30y} \), where \( n > 1 \).
whyCorrect: Treat \( 40n \) as a single base and convert both radicals to fractional exponents: \( \sqrt[4]{40n} = (40n)^{\frac{1}{4}} \) and \( \left(\sqrt[5]{40n}\right)^3 = (40n)^{\frac{3}{5}} \). Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents: \( \frac{1}{4}+\frac{3}{5} = \frac{5+12}{20} = \frac{17}{20} \). Setting \( 30y = \frac{17}{20} \) gives \( y = \frac{17}{600} \).

whyWrong.B: \( \frac{10}{600} \) comes from \( 30y = \frac{1}{2} \), i.e. adding the exponents as \( \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4} \) and ignoring the cube on the fifth root.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{7}{600} \) comes from \( \frac{1}{4}+\frac{3}{5} \) computed as \( \frac{1+3}{4+5} \)-style guesswork, or from subtracting instead of adding somewhere; the correct sum over the common denominator 20 is \( \frac{17}{20} \).
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{14}{600} \) corresponds to \( 30y = \frac{7}{10} \), which is \( \frac{1}{10}+\frac{3}{5} \) — the fourth root treated as a tenth root.

stem: \[ f(x) = 5(0.92)^{3x} \]The function \(f\) is defined by the given equation. The equation can be rewritten as \( f(x) = 5\left(1-\frac{p}{100}\right)^{x} \), where \(p\) is a constant. Which of the following is closest to the value of \(p\)?
whyCorrect: The two forms have the same coefficient, so the bases must match once the exponents are made the same. Use \( (0.92)^{3x} = \left((0.92)^3\right)^x \), and \( (0.92)^3 = 0.778688 \). So \( 1-\frac{p}{100} = 0.778688 \), giving \( \frac{p}{100} = 0.221312 \) and \( p \approx 22.1 \) — closest to 22.

whyWrong.A: 8 is the per-unit decay percentage before the exponent 3 is folded in: \( 1-0.92 = 0.08 \). That is the rate for one increase in \( 3x \), not for one increase in \(x\).
whyWrong.B: 12 does not follow from anything in the equation; it is roughly \( 3 \times 8 \) halved, and multiplying the rate by 3 is not how repeated decay works anyway.
whyWrong.D: 24 is \( 3 \times 8 \), the result of tripling the 8% rate. Compounding three times shrinks the total decay to 22.1%, because each 8% is taken off a smaller amount.

stem: Which of the following expressions has \( 6x-5b \) as a factor, where \(b\) is a positive integer constant?
whyCorrect: Every choice has first term \( 24x^2 \) and last term \( -15b^2 \), so if \( 6x-5b \) is a factor the other factor must be \( 4x+3b \) (because \( 6 \times 4 = 24 \) and \( -5b \times 3b = -15b^2 \)). Multiply it out: \( (6x-5b)(4x+3b) = 24x^2+18xb-20xb-15b^2 = 24x^2-2xb-15b^2 \). Only the middle coefficient distinguishes the choices, and \(-2\) is the one that results.

whyWrong.B: \( 24x^2+18xb-15b^2 = 3(4x+5b)(2x-b) \) — the 18 comes from keeping only the \( 6x \cdot 3b \) product and forgetting the \( -5b \cdot 4x \) one.
whyWrong.C: \( 24x^2+36xb-15b^2 \) does not factor with \( 6x-5b \); its factorisation \( 3(8x^2+12xb-5b^2) \) has irrational roots in \( \frac{x}{b} \).
whyWrong.D: \(-484\) does not arise from any pairing of the required factors; the middle term is forced to be \( 18-20 = -2 \) times \( xb \).

note: Closely related to question 46 in the same chapter (24x^2 - 22x - 15b), which is the same setup with b appearing only in the constant term.

stem: The expression \[ bx^2-13x+22 \]can be rewritten as \( (hx-k)(x+j) \) where \(b\) is a constant and \(h\), \(j\), and \(k\) are integer constants. Which of the following must be an integer?
whyCorrect: Multiply out the factored form: \( (hx-k)(x+j) = hx^2 + (hj-k)x - kj \). Matching the middle term gives \( hj-k = -13 \), so \( k-13 = hj \) and therefore \( \frac{k-13}{h} = j \), which the stem already says is an integer. Nothing forces \(h\) itself to be \( \pm 1 \): for example \( h=-9 \), \( j=-1 \), \( k=22 \) gives \( -9x^2-13x+22 \), a valid case that kills the other three choices.

whyWrong.B: \( b = h \), and \(h\) need not divide 13. In the case \( h=-9 \), \( \frac{13}{b} = -\frac{13}{9} \).
whyWrong.C: From \( -kj = 22 \) you know \(j\) divides 22, not that 22 divides \(j\). With \( j=-1 \), \( -\frac{j}{22} = \frac{1}{22} \).
whyWrong.D: This is an integer only when \( h = \pm 1 \), which is not required; with \( h = -9 \) it is \( -\frac{1}{9} \).

stem: In the given equation, \(k\) is a constant. The equation \[ \sqrt{k-x} = 43-x \]has exactly one real solution. What is the minimum possible value of \( 4k \)?
whyCorrect: Square both sides: \( k-x = x^2-86x+1849 \), so \( x^2-85x+1849-k = 0 \), whose roots are \( x = \frac{85 \pm \sqrt{4k-171}}{2} \). Squaring can create extra roots, so keep only those with \( 43-x \ge 0 \). If \( 4k-171 < 0 \) there is no real solution at all; if \( 4k-171 = 0 \) there is a single double root \( x = 42.5 \), which satisfies \( x \le 43 \), so exactly one solution. Any larger \(k\) either gives two valid roots (when \( 171 < 4k \le 172 \)) or one valid root again (when \( 4k > 172 \)), so the smallest \(4k\) that works is 171.
note: 4k > 172 also yields exactly one solution (the larger root then exceeds 43 and is extraneous), but 171 is the minimum.

stem:
The functions \(f\) and \(g\) are defined by the given equations, where \( 2 \le x \le 5 \). Which of the following equations displays, as a constant or coefficient, the maximum value of the function it defines, where \( 2 \le x \le 5 \)?
I. \( f(x) = -(x-4)^2+7 \)
II. \( g(x) = -(x+4)^2+7 \)
whyCorrect: Both are downward parabolas in vertex form, so each has maximum value 7 — but only at its vertex, and the vertex has to lie inside the interval. \(f\) has vertex \( x = 4 \), which is between 2 and 5, so \( f \) really does reach 7 there and the 7 in the equation is the maximum. \(g\) has vertex \( x = -4 \), far outside the interval; on \( 2 \le x \le 5 \) it is decreasing, so its greatest value is \( g(2) = -36+7 = -29 \), which is nowhere in the equation.

whyWrong.B: \(g\)'s vertex is at \( x=-4 \), not in \( 2 \le x \le 5 \); the 7 is a value \(g\) never attains on that interval.
whyWrong.C: Requires II, which fails on the vertex-location check.
whyWrong.D: Misses that \(f\)'s vertex \( x=4 \) is inside the interval, so \(f\) does attain the displayed 7.

stem: In the given equations, \(a\) and \(b\) are constants, \( a > 1 \) and \( b > 1 \). What is the value of \(x\)? \[ \sqrt[7]{a^5} = \sqrt{b^5} \] \[ a^{3x-3} = b^3 \]
whyCorrect: Convert the radicals to exponents: the first equation is \( a^{\frac{5}{7}} = b^{\frac{5}{2}} \). Raise both sides to the power \( \frac{7}{5} \) to isolate \(a\): \( a = b^{\frac{7}{2}} \). Substituting into the second equation gives \( b^{\frac{7}{2}(3x-3)} = b^3 \), and since \( b > 1 \) the exponents must be equal: \( \frac{7}{2}(3x-3) = 3 \), so \( 3x-3 = \frac{6}{7} \) and \( x = \frac{9}{7} = \frac{27}{21} \).

whyWrong.B: \( \frac{21}{27} = \frac{7}{9} \) is the reciprocal of the answer — it comes from writing \( b = a^{\frac{7}{2}} \) instead of \( a = b^{\frac{7}{2}} \).
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{32}{21} \) comes from solving \( 3x-3 = \frac{6}{7} \) as \( 3x = \frac{6}{7}+3 \) but then adding rather than dividing at the last step.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{38}{21} \) follows from using \( a = b^{\frac{2}{7}} \) or otherwise inverting one of the fractional exponents; the exponent equation to solve is \( \frac{7}{2}(3x-3)=3 \).

stem:
Quadratic function \(h\) is defined by \[ h(x) = ax^2-2x+c \]where \(a\) and \(c\) are constants. The graph of \( y = h(x) \) in the xy-plane is a parabola that opens downward and has a vertex of \( (h,k) \), where \( k > 0 \). If \( h(1) = h(-13) \), which of the following must be true?
I. \( -1 < a < 0 \)
II. \( c > 0 \)
whyCorrect: Equal outputs at \( x=1 \) and \( x=-13 \) put the axis of symmetry at their midpoint, \( x = -6 \). With \( b = -2 \), the axis is \( -\frac{-2}{2a} = \frac{1}{a} \), so \( \frac{1}{a} = -6 \) and \( a = -\frac{1}{6} \) — a single value, and it does lie strictly between \(-1\) and 0, so I must be true. For II, \( k = h(-6) = 36a + 12 + c = c + 6 \), and \( k > 0 \) only forces \( c > -6 \); taking \( c = -1 \) gives a legal parabola with \( k = 5 > 0 \) and \( c < 0 \).

whyWrong.B: \( c > 0 \) is not forced: \( k = c+6 \), so any \( c > -6 \) keeps the vertex above the x-axis, and \( c \) may be negative or zero.
whyWrong.C: I is true but II is not, for the reason above.
whyWrong.D: I is forced: the symmetry condition pins \(a\) to exactly \( -\frac{1}{6} \), which satisfies \( -1 < a < 0 \).

note: The stem reuses h for both the function name and the vertex's x-coordinate, as printed in the book.

stem:
\[ f(x) = -2x^2+bx+c \]In the given quadratic function, \(b\) and \(c\) are constants. The graph of \( y = f(x) \) is a parabola that has a vertex at the point \( (h,k) \), where \(h\) and \(k\) are constants. If \( k < 0 \) and \( f(-5) = f(7) \), which of the following must be true?
I. \( c < -1 \)
II. \( b \ge 3 \)
whyCorrect: Equal outputs at \( x=-5 \) and \( x=7 \) put the axis of symmetry at their midpoint, \( x = 1 \). So \( -\frac{b}{2(-2)} = \frac{b}{4} = 1 \), fixing \( b = 4 \), which satisfies \( b \ge 3 \). The vertex value is \( k = f(1) = -2+4+c = c+2 \), and \( k < 0 \) gives \( c < -2 \); anything less than \(-2\) is certainly less than \(-1\), so I holds too.

whyWrong.A: II is also forced — the symmetry condition pins \( b = 4 \) exactly, and \( 4 \ge 3 \).
whyWrong.B: I is also forced: \( k = c+2 < 0 \) means \( c < -2 \), which implies \( c < -1 \).
whyWrong.D: Both statements follow; the axis of symmetry gives \(b\) and the vertex value gives the bound on \(c\).

note: Book prints "a and c are constants" though the equation uses b and c; corrected to b and c.

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \[ f(x) = 9x^2+kx-21 \]where \(k\) is a constant. In the xy-plane, the graph of \( y = f(x) \) passes through the points \( (r,23) \) and \( (2r,139) \), where \(r\) is a constant. Which of the following could be the value of \(k\)?
whyCorrect: Substitute both points: \( 9r^2+kr-21 = 23 \) gives \( 9r^2+kr = 44 \), and \( 36r^2+2kr-21 = 139 \) gives \( 36r^2+2kr = 160 \), i.e. \( 18r^2+kr = 80 \). Subtracting the first from the second eliminates \(k\): \( 9r^2 = 36 \), so \( r = \pm 2 \). Putting \( r = 2 \) back gives \( 36+2k = 44 \), so \( k = 4 \) (and \( r=-2 \) gives \( k=-4 \), which is not offered).

whyWrong.B: 12 does not satisfy either equation; with \( k=12 \) the two conditions give incompatible values of \(r\).
whyWrong.C: 116 is what you get by keeping \( 9r^2+kr = 44 \) and \( 18r^2+kr = 80 \) but solving for \(kr\) instead of \(k\) and forgetting to divide by \(r\).
whyWrong.D: 162 comes from adding the two equations rather than subtracting, which does not eliminate anything usable.

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \[ f(x) = a\sqrt{-x+b} \]where \(a\) and \(b\) are constants. In the xy-plane, the graph of \( y = f(x) \) passes through the point \( (5,0) \), and \( f(-12) > f(-7) \). Which of the following must be true?
whyCorrect: The point \( (5,0) \) forces \( a\sqrt{b-5} = 0 \); \( a = 0 \) would make \(f\) constant and contradict \( f(-12) > f(-7) \), so \( b = 5 \) and \( f(x) = a\sqrt{5-x} \). Since \( \sqrt{17} > \sqrt{12} \), the inequality \( a\sqrt{17} > a\sqrt{12} \) can only hold if \( a > 0 \) — that is all you learn about \(a\). With \( b=5 \), choice C compares \( f(3) = a\sqrt{2} \) with \( f(-10) = a\sqrt{15} \), and a positive \(a\) makes \( a\sqrt{2} < a\sqrt{15} \) always.

whyWrong.A: \( f(b) = f(5) = 0 \), so this says \( a < 0 \) — the opposite of what \( f(-12) > f(-7) \) forces.
