whyWrong.B: Nothing bounds the size of \(a\); \( a = 1 \) with \( b = 5 \) satisfies every condition and makes \( a < b \).
whyWrong.D: Equally unforced in the other direction: \( a = 100 \) also satisfies every condition, giving \( a > b \). Only the sign of \(a\) is determined.

stem: The function \[ v(x) = \frac{x^2+bx+c}{(x-7)(x-17)} \]where \(b\), \(c\) are constants goes through the points \( \left(0, \frac{99}{119}\right) \) and \( (11,0) \). There is another point where \( v(q) = 0 \). What is the value of \(q\)?
whyCorrect: Use \( x = 0 \) first, because it kills the \(b\) term: \( v(0) = \frac{c}{(-7)(-17)} = \frac{c}{119} = \frac{99}{119} \), so \( c = 99 \). A fraction is zero only when its numerator is, so \( v(11)=0 \) gives \( 121+11b+99 = 0 \) and \( b = -20 \). The numerator is then \( x^2-20x+99 = (x-9)(x-11) \), so the other zero is \( q = 9 \) — and 9 is not 7 or 17, so it is not cancelled by the denominator.

stem:
The function \[ f(x) = 6(x-a)(x-b)(x-c) \]is defined by the given equation, where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are distinct constants. When \( a < x < b \), the value of \( f(x) \) is positive. The graph of \( y = f(x) \) in the xy-plane contains the point \( (r,s) \), where \(r\) and \(s\) are constants. If \( s = 9 \), which of the following could be true?
I. \( r < a \)
II. \( b < r < c \)
III. \( r > c \)
whyCorrect: First order the zeros. A cubic with positive leading coefficient is negative below its smallest zero, then alternates: positive, negative, positive as \(x\) passes each zero. For \(f\) to be positive on the whole interval \( (a,b) \), that interval must be the first gap, so \( a < b < c \). Then \(f\) is positive exactly on \( (a,b) \) and on \( x > c \). Since \( s = 9 > 0 \), \(r\) has to sit in one of those two regions, and only \( r > c \) appears in the list.

whyWrong.A: For \( r < a \), \(r\) is below the smallest zero, where the cubic is negative — it cannot give \( s = 9 \).
whyWrong.C: III is possible but I is not, for the reason above.
whyWrong.D: On \( b < r < c \) the graph is between the second and third zeros, where a positive-leading cubic is negative, so II is impossible.

stem:
\[ g(x) = 12(x-a)(x-b)(x-c) \]where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are distinct constants. When \( a < x < b \), \( g(x) \) will be positive. If \( (p,q) \) is on the graph of \( g(x) \), where \(p\) and \(q\) are constants, and \( q = 45 \), which of the following could be true?
I. \( p < a \)
II. \( b < p < c \)
III. \( p > c \)
whyCorrect: The leading coefficient 12 is positive, so the cubic is negative to the left of its smallest zero and then alternates sign at each zero. The only way \(g\) is positive across all of \( (a,b) \) is for that to be the first gap between zeros, so \( a < b < c \), and \(g\) is positive exactly on \( (a,b) \) and on \( x > c \). Since \( q = 45 \) is positive, \(p\) must lie in one of those regions, and of the three statements only \( p > c \) does.

whyWrong.A: Below the smallest zero a positive-leading cubic is negative, so \( p < a \) cannot produce \( q = 45 \).
whyWrong.C: III works, I does not.
whyWrong.D: Between the second and third zeros the cubic is negative, so II is impossible.

note: Nearly identical to question 65 in the same chapter (same setup, coefficient 6 vs 12 and s = 9 vs q = 45) — a template repeat inside the book.

stem: The polynomial \[ 8x^4+50x^2+63 \]can be factored, and one of the factors is of the form \( (ax^2+b) \). What is one possible value of the product \( a \cdot b \)?
whyCorrect: Treat it as a quadratic in \( x^2 \): with \( u = x^2 \) you are factoring \( 8u^2+50u+63 \). Look for two numbers multiplying to \( 8 \times 63 = 504 \) and adding to 50 — those are 14 and 36. Splitting gives \( 8u^2+14u+36u+63 = 2u(4u+7)+9(4u+7) = (4u+7)(2u+9) \), so the polynomial is \( (4x^2+7)(2x^2+9) \). Taking the first factor, \( a \cdot b = 4 \times 7 = 28 \).
note: The other factor gives a valid answer too: 2 x 9 = 18. Both 28 and 18 should be accepted.

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \[ f(x) = ax^2+bx+c \]where \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are constants. The graph of \( y = f(x) \) in the xy-plane passes through the points \( (13,0) \) and \( (-6,0) \). Which of the following is the value of \( a+b \) in terms of \(a\)?
whyCorrect: The two points are the zeros, so the sum of the roots is \( 13+(-6) = 7 \). For \( ax^2+bx+c \) the sum of the roots is \( -\frac{b}{a} \), so \( -\frac{b}{a} = 7 \) and \( b = -7a \). Then \( a+b = a-7a = -6a \).

whyWrong.A: \( 7a \) is what you get from \( b = 7a \) — forgetting the minus sign in \( -\frac{b}{a} \) — and then also dropping the \(a\) you started with.
whyWrong.B: \( 6a \) is \( a + 7a \) with a sign slip, or \( a - (-7a) \); the sum is \( a + (-7a) \).
whyWrong.D: \( -7a \) is \(b\) itself, not \( a+b \).

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \[ f(x) = 3x^2-5x+10 \]If the function \( f(x-2) \) is written in the form \( ax^2+bx+c \), what is the value of \( a+b+c \)?
whyCorrect: There is a shortcut: \( a+b+c \) is the value of the new quadratic at \( x = 1 \), and the new quadratic at \( x=1 \) is \( f(1-2) = f(-1) \). So \( a+b+c = 3(-1)^2-5(-1)+10 = 3+5+10 = 18 \). Expanding confirms it: \( f(x-2) = 3(x-2)^2-5(x-2)+10 = 3x^2-17x+32 \), and \( 3-17+32 = 18 \).

stem: In the given equation, \(p\) is a positive constant. The product of the solutions to the equation \[ (3x-7p)(5x^2+8x-4p)(x^3+3x^2-16x-48) = 0 \]is \( -\frac{560}{9} \). What is the value of \(p\)?
whyCorrect: Handle each factor separately. \( 3x-7p=0 \) gives the single root \( \frac{7p}{3} \). For \( 5x^2+8x-4p \), you do not need the roots themselves — their product is \( \frac{-4p}{5} \). The cubic factors by grouping: \( x^2(x+3)-16(x+3) = (x+3)(x-4)(x+4) \), whose roots multiply to \( (-3)(4)(-4) = 48 \). So the total product is \( \frac{7p}{3} \cdot \left(-\frac{4p}{5}\right) \cdot 48 = -\frac{448}{5}p^2 \). Setting that equal to \( -\frac{560}{9} \) gives \( p^2 = \frac{25}{36} \), so \( p = \frac{5}{6} \).

stem:
The functions \(f\), \(g\) and \(h\) are defined by the given equations, where \( x \ge 0 \). Which of the following equations displays, as a constant or coefficient, the maximum or minimum value of the function it defines, where \( x \ge 0 \)?
I. \( f(x) = (x-3)^2+6 \)
II. \( g(x) = (x+3)^2+6 \)
III. \( h(x) = (x-5)^2+8 \)
whyCorrect: All three open upward, so each has a minimum at its vertex — but only if the vertex is in the allowed region \( x \ge 0 \). \(f\) has vertex \( x=3 \) and \(h\) has vertex \( x=5 \), both allowed, so their displayed constants 6 and 8 really are the minimum values. \(g\) has vertex \( x=-3 \), which is excluded; on \( x \ge 0 \) it increases, so its smallest value is \( g(0) = 15 \), and 15 appears nowhere in the equation.

whyWrong.A: III passes the same test as I — its vertex \( x=5 \) is in \( x \ge 0 \), so the 8 is a genuine minimum.
whyWrong.C: II fails: the vertex at \( x=-3 \) is outside the domain, so \(g\) never takes the value 6 there.
whyWrong.D: Two of the three do display their minimum; the check is whether the vertex lies in \( x \ge 0 \).

stem:
\[ f(x) = -2(x-a)(x-b)(x-c) \]The function \(f\) is defined by the given equation, where \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are distinct constants. When \( b < x < c \), the value of \( f(x) \) is positive. The graph of \( y = f(x) \) in the xy-plane contains the point \( (m,n) \), where \(m\) and \(n\) are constants. If \(n\) is equal to -5, which of the following could be true?
I. \( m < a \)
II. \( a < m < b \)
III. \( m > c \)
whyCorrect: The leading coefficient is negative, so the cubic is positive to the left of its smallest zero and then alternates: negative, positive, negative. For the positive stretch to be the interval \( (b,c) \), that must be the second gap, so the order of the zeros is \( a < b < c \). Then \(f\) is negative exactly on \( (a,b) \) and on \( x > c \). Since \( n = -5 \) is negative, \(m\) must lie in one of those two regions — statements II and III.

whyWrong.A: Left of the smallest zero a negative-leading cubic is positive, so \( m < a \) cannot give \( n = -5 \).
whyWrong.B: II works, but so does III: past the largest zero the graph is negative again.
whyWrong.D: III works, but I does not, for the sign reason above.

stem:
Which of the following below has a factor of \( 4x+7b \), where \(b\) is a non-positive integer?
I. \( 16x^2-49 \)
II. \( 16x^2+56x+49 \)
III. \( 64x^3+343 \)
whyCorrect: The constraint that \(b\) is non-positive is the whole question — the factor has to be \( 4x+7b \) with \( 7b \le 0 \), i.e. \( 4x-7 \), \( 4x-14 \), \( 4x \), and so on. I is a difference of squares, \( 16x^2-49 = (4x-7)(4x+7) \), and \( 4x-7 \) is \( 4x+7b \) with \( b = -1 \). II is the perfect square \( (4x+7)^2 \) and III is the sum of cubes \( (4x+7)(16x^2-28x+49) \); both have only \( 4x+7 \), which needs \( b = 1 \), a positive integer.

whyWrong.B: Both II and III factor with \( 4x+7 \) only, requiring \( b=1 \); III's quadratic factor \( 16x^2-28x+49 \) has a negative discriminant, so it contributes no other linear factor.
whyWrong.C: I qualifies but III does not, since \( 64x^3+343 = (4x+7)(16x^2-28x+49) \) forces \( b=1 \).
whyWrong.D: Only I contains a factor of the form \( 4x+7b \) with \(b\) non-positive.

stem: The equation \( N(m) = 63(Q)^{\frac{m}{6}} \) gives the predicted population \( N(m) \), in thousands, of a certain bacteria colony \(m\) minutes after the initial measurement, where \(Q\) is a constant greater than 1. The predicted population increases by \(p\)% every 180 seconds. What is the value of \(p\) in terms of \(Q\)?
whyCorrect: Convert the units first: \(m\) is in minutes, and 180 seconds is 3 minutes. Over 3 minutes the population is multiplied by \( Q^{\frac{3}{6}} = Q^{\frac{1}{2}} \). A growth factor of \( Q^{\frac{1}{2}} \) is an increase of \( Q^{\frac{1}{2}}-1 \) as a decimal, so as a percent \( p = 100\left(Q^{\frac{1}{2}}-1\right) \).

whyWrong.A: \( Q^{30} \) treats 180 as a count of minutes and divides by 6; the 180 is in seconds, so it is 3 minutes, not 180.
whyWrong.C: Two errors: the wrong exponent, and adding 1 instead of subtracting. The percent increase is factor minus 1.
whyWrong.D: The exponent is right but the sign is not: \( Q^{\frac{1}{2}}+1 \) would be the percent increase only if the population had started from zero.

stem: For the polynomial function \(v\), \( v(2) = 3 \) and \( v(0) = -13 \). The graph of \( y = v(x) \) in the xy-plane passes through the points \( (-2,7) \) and \( (6,0) \). Which of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.content: When \( v(x) \) is divided by \( (x+13) \), the remainder is 0.

choices.label: B
choices.content: When \( v(x) \) is divided by \( (x+7) \), the remainder is -2.

choices.label: C
choices.content: When \( v(x) \) is divided by \( (x+2) \), the remainder is 7.

choices.label: D
choices.content: When \( v(x) \) is divided by \( (x-6) \), the remainder is -13.

whyCorrect: The remainder theorem says dividing by \( x-r \) leaves the remainder \( v(r) \) — so you need the sign flipped when the divisor is written as \( x+r \). Dividing by \( x+2 \) means \( r = -2 \), and the point \( (-2,7) \) tells you \( v(-2) = 7 \), so the remainder is 7.

whyWrong.A: This asks for \( v(-13) \). The \(-13\) you were given is an output, \( v(0) = -13 \), not an input, so nothing is known about \( v(-13) \).
whyWrong.B: This asks for \( v(-7) \), which is never given; the 7 in the data is the output at \( x=-2 \).
whyWrong.D: Dividing by \( x-6 \) leaves \( v(6) \), and the point \( (6,0) \) makes that 0, not \(-13\).

stem: When the polynomial \( P(x) = 2x^3-5x^2+ax+b \) is divided by \( x-2 \), the remainder is 10. When \( P(x) \) is divided by \( x+1 \), the remainder is 1. What is the value of \( a+b \)?
whyCorrect: By the remainder theorem the two facts are \( P(2) = 10 \) and \( P(-1) = 1 \). Substituting gives \( 16-20+2a+b = 10 \), i.e. \( 2a+b = 14 \), and \( -2-5-a+b = 1 \), i.e. \( b-a = 8 \). Adding \( b = a+8 \) into the first equation gives \( 3a+8 = 14 \), so \( a = 2 \) and \( b = 10 \), and \( a+b = 12 \).

stem: \[ \frac{x^2}{\sqrt{x^2-c^2}} = \frac{c^2}{\sqrt{x^2-c^2}} + 39 \]In the given equation, \(c\) is a positive constant. Which of the following is one of the solutions to the given equation?
whyCorrect: Both fractions have the same denominator, so move them together: \( \frac{x^2-c^2}{\sqrt{x^2-c^2}} = 39 \). A quantity divided by its own square root is that square root, so this is just \( \sqrt{x^2-c^2} = 39 \). Squaring gives \( x^2 = c^2+39^2 \), so \( x = \pm\sqrt{c^2+39^2} \), and the negative one is listed.

whyWrong.A: \( x = -c \) makes \( x^2-c^2 = 0 \), so both denominators are zero and the expression is undefined.
whyWrong.B: This is \( x^2 \) with a sign error, not \(x\); you still have to take a square root, and \( -c^2-39^2 \) is negative, so its square cannot equal \( c^2+39^2 \).
whyWrong.C: Subtracting instead of adding: squaring gives \( x^2 = 39^2-c^2 \), which makes \( x^2-c^2 = 39^2-2c^2 \), not \( 39^2 \).

note: DEFECT in the book's typesetting: the +39 is printed under the right-hand radical, as c^2/sqrt(x^2-c^2+39). Taken literally that equation has no real solutions for any positive c (checked with sympy for c = 1, 5, 13, 20, 50 — all four roots complex), and none of the choices satisfies it. Transcribed with the 39 as a separate term, which is the only reading under which a listed choice works and which the choices themselves (all built on 39^2) confirm.

stem: The expression \[ 12x^2+41x+35 \]can be rewritten as \( (4x+r)(3x+s) \), where \(r\) and \(s\) are integers, or as \( (4x+t)(3x+v) \), where \(t\) and \(v\) are not integers. What is the value of \( s+v \)?
whyCorrect: Expanding \( (4x+r)(3x+s) \) gives \( 12x^2+(4s+3r)x+rs \), so you need \( rs = 35 \) and \( 4s+3r = 41 \). The integer pair is \( r=7 \), \( s=5 \) (the other order gives 43). For the non-integer pair, substitute \( v = \frac{35}{t} \) into \( 4v+3t = 41 \) to get \( 3t^2-41t+140 = 0 \), whose roots are \( t = 7 \) and \( t = \frac{20}{3} \); the non-integer one gives \( v = \frac{21}{4} \). So \( s+v = 5+\frac{21}{4} = \frac{41}{4} \).

whyWrong.A: \( \frac{41}{3} \) is \( t+? \)-style bookkeeping on the wrong pair — it is what you get by adding the two t-values \( 7+\frac{20}{3} \) and dividing, not \( s+v \).
whyWrong.C: 12 is the leading coefficient, not a sum of the two second constants.
whyWrong.D: 35 is the product \( rs \), the constant term.

stem: \[ x(9x-2a) + b(9x-2a) - (x+b) = 0 \]In the given equation, \(a\) and \(b\) are positive constants. A solution to the equation is \( x = 42 \). What is the value of \(a\)?
whyCorrect: Do not expand — factor. The first two terms share \( 9x-2a \), giving \( (x+b)(9x-2a) \), and the third term is \( -(x+b) \), so the whole left side is \( (x+b)(9x-2a-1) \). The solutions are therefore \( x = -b \) and \( x = \frac{2a+1}{9} \). Since \(b\) is positive, \( -b \) cannot be 42, so \( \frac{2a+1}{9} = 42 \), giving \( 2a+1 = 378 \) and \( a = 188.5 \).

stem: For a polynomial function \(f\), the graph of \( y = f(x) \) in the xy-plane contains the points \( (-6,0) \), \( (7,0) \), \( (0,0) \), and \( (4,0) \). Which of the following must be a factor of \( f(x) \)?
whyCorrect: Each listed point has y-coordinate 0, so \(-6\), 7, 0 and 4 are all zeros of \(f\), and a quadratic can only be a factor if both of its own zeros are on that list. Factor each choice: \( x^2-7x = x(x-7) \) has zeros 0 and 7, both on the list, so it divides \( f(x) \).

whyWrong.A: \( x^2-2x-24 = (x-6)(x+4) \), with zeros 6 and \(-4\) — the signs of the given zeros \(-6\) and 4 are flipped.
whyWrong.B: \( x^2-x+42 \) has discriminant \( 1-168 < 0 \), so it has no real zeros at all and cannot be built from these x-intercepts. It looks plausible only because \( -6 \times 7 = -42 \), and even that sign is wrong.
whyWrong.C: \( x^2-11x-28 \) does not factor over the integers; its zeros are \( \frac{11\pm\sqrt{233}}{2} \), neither of which is a listed zero.

stem: In the xy-plane above, the function \(f\) is defined by \( f(x) = 2x^3+3x^2+ax+b \), where \(a\) and \(b\) are constants. If the graph of \(f\) intersects the x-axis at three points, what is the value of \(a\)?
whyCorrect: Read the two labelled zeros, \( x = -3 \) and \( x = 2 \), off the graph. For \( 2x^3+3x^2+ax+b \) the three zeros sum to \( -\frac{3}{2} \), so the third zero is \( -\frac{3}{2}-(-3)-2 = -\frac{1}{2} \). That makes \( f(x) = 2(x+3)(x-2)\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right) = (x+3)(x-2)(2x+1) \); expanding gives \( 2x^3+3x^2-11x-6 \), so \( a = -11 \) (and \( b = -6 \), matching the labelled y-intercept).
note: Depends on the graph: the cubic is drawn with x-intercepts labelled -3 and 2, a third unlabelled crossing between them, and y-intercept -6.
imageAlt: The xy-plane showing a single cubic curve labelled y = f(x); two of its x-axis crossings and its y-intercept are marked with values on the axes.

stem: The graph of \( y = a(x+1)(x-5) \) is shown in the xy-plane above, where \(a\) is a constant. If the graph with vertex \( (h,k) \) intersects the y-axis at point \( (0,5) \), which of the following is equal to \(k\)?
whyCorrect: Find \(a\) from the given point: substituting \( (0,5) \) gives \( a(1)(-5) = 5 \), so \( a = -1 \). The vertex sits halfway between the zeros \(-1\) and 5, at \( h = 2 \). Then \( k = -(2+1)(2-5) = -(3)(-3) = 9 \).

whyWrong.A: 7 does not come from any consistent value of \(a\); with \( a = -1 \) the vertex height is fixed at 9.
whyWrong.B: 8 would be the vertex value if the zeros were \(-1\) and 5 with \( a \approx -0.89 \); the point \( (0,5) \) pins \( a = -1 \) exactly.
whyWrong.D: 10 is the result of using \( h = 2 \) but computing \( k \) as \( 5+5 \), adding the y-intercept to itself instead of evaluating the function at the vertex.

note: The graph is shown in the book (downward parabola through (-1,0), (5,0) and (0,5) with vertex labelled (h,k)), but every number needed is stated in the text.
imageAlt: A downward-opening parabola drawn in the xy-plane, crossing the x-axis at two labelled points, meeting the y-axis at a marked point, and with its vertex labelled (h, k).

stem: In the xy-plane above, the graph of a quadratic function \( y = f(x) \) intersects the x-axis at points \(O\) and \(Q\), and has a vertex at point \(P\). If line \( \ell \) passes through points \(P\) and \(Q\), what is the y-intercept of line \( \ell \)?
whyCorrect: \(O\) is the origin, so one zero is \( x=0 \), and the vertex \( P(3,5) \) sits halfway between the zeros — that puts \(Q\) at \( (6,0) \). The line through \( (3,5) \) and \( (6,0) \) has slope \( \frac{0-5}{6-3} = -\frac{5}{3} \). Going from \( P \) back to \( x=0 \) is 3 more units left, raising \(y\) by another 5, so the y-intercept is \( 5+5 = 10 \).
note: Depends on the graph: the parabola through the origin and (6,0) with vertex labelled P(3,5), and line l drawn through P and Q.
imageAlt: An xy-plane showing a downward-opening parabola that meets the x-axis at the origin and at one labelled point, together with a straight line drawn through the parabola's labelled vertex and that x-intercept; the y-axis carries numbered tick marks.

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \( f(x) = x^3 \). The function \(g\) is defined by \( g(x) = a \cdot f(x+b)+c \), where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are constants. The graph of \( y = g(x) \) is shown in the xy-plane. Find the value of \( ab \).
whyCorrect: \( g(x) = a(x+b)^3+c \), so the point where the curve flattens out — its point of inflection — is \( (-b, c) \). The graph flattens at the marked point \( (4,6) \), giving \( b = -4 \) and \( c = 6 \). Then the other marked point \( (5,24) \) gives \( a(5-4)^3+6 = 24 \), so \( a = 18 \), and \( ab = 18(-4) = -72 \).
note: Depends on the graph: a cubic through the marked points (4,6) — its point of inflection — and (5,24).
imageAlt: An xy-plane with a light rectangular grid showing a steeply rising cubic curve; two points on the curve are marked with dots, labelled with their coordinates, and joined to the y-axis by dashed horizontal leader lines.

stem: The graphs of \( y = x^2 \) and \( y = mx-1 \) are shown in the xy-plane below, where \(m\) is the slope of the line. If the graph of \( y = mx-1 \) is tangent to the graph of \( y = x^2 \), what is the value of \(m\)?
whyCorrect: Tangent means the two graphs meet at exactly one point, so set them equal and force a single solution: \( x^2 = mx-1 \) becomes \( x^2-mx+1 = 0 \), and one solution means the discriminant is zero: \( m^2-4 = 0 \), so \( m = \pm 2 \). The line in the figure slopes upward, so \( m = 2 \) (touching the parabola at \( x = 1 \)).
note: The algebra alone gives m = 2 or m = -2; the figure, which shows an upward-sloping line, is what selects +2.
imageAlt: An xy-plane with numbered tick marks on both axes showing an upward-opening parabola labelled y = x squared and a straight line labelled y = mx minus 1 that touches the parabola at a single marked point.

stem: Which of the following could be the equation of the graph shown in the xy-plane?
whyCorrect: Read the zeros and how the curve meets them. The graph crosses the axis at \( x=-1 \), only touches it at \( x=4 \) and crosses again at \( x=6 \) — a touch means an even multiplicity, a crossing an odd one. That is exactly \( (x+1) \), \( (x-4)^2 \), \( (x-6) \), and the sign of the factored form matters too: with the leading coefficient negative and degree 4, both ends fall, which the graph does. Checking one value confirms it: at \( x=1 \), \( -\frac{1}{15}(-5)(9)(2) = 6 \), matching the local maximum near 7.

whyWrong.B: This has the double root at \( x=6 \) and \( x=-1 \) and a simple root at 4, which is the touching/crossing pattern reversed; it is also degree 5, so its ends go in opposite directions.
whyWrong.C: The signs inside the factors are flipped, putting the zeros at \(-6\), \(-4\) and \(-1\) — all on the left of the origin, where the graph shows no such behaviour.
whyWrong.D: Zeros at \(-6\), \(-4\) and 1 (the last a touch), none of which matches the graph, and it is again degree 5.

note: Depends on the graph: a quartic falling on both ends, crossing at x = -1, a local maximum near (1,7), touching the axis at x = 4, a small local maximum near x = 5, and crossing at x = 6.
imageAlt: An xy-plane with a light square grid and numbered tick marks, showing a smooth polynomial curve that rises to a maximum, falls, levels off near the x-axis and then falls again.

stem: For a certain circuit, its power \(P\), in watts; current \(C\), in amperes; voltage \(V\), in volts; and resistance \(R\), in ohms, are related as \[ \frac{CV^2}{P} = \sqrt{PR} \]where \(P\), \(C\), \(V\) and \(R\) are positive. When \( R = 18 \), which equation correctly expresses \(P\) in terms of \(C\) and \(V\)?
whyCorrect: Substitute \( R=18 \) and square both sides to kill the radical: \( \frac{C^2V^4}{P^2} = 18P \). Multiply by \( P^2 \) to get \( C^2V^4 = 18P^3 \), so \( P^3 = \frac{C^2V^4}{18} \) and \( P = \sqrt[3]{\frac{C^2V^4}{18}} \). The key step is that squaring turns the single \(P\) under the radical into a third power once the \( P^2 \) is cleared.

whyWrong.A: \(P\) still appears on the right, so this does not express \(P\) in terms of \(C\) and \(V\) at all.
whyWrong.B: This drops the \(P\) inside the radical, as if \( \sqrt{PR} \) were \( \sqrt{R} \); the \(P\) under the root is what makes the result a cube root.
whyWrong.D: The fraction is upside down: \( P^3 = \frac{C^2V^4}{18} \), not \( \frac{18}{C^2V^4} \).

stem: In the xy-plane above, the graphs of \( y = x^2-4 \) and \( y = mx+k \) intersect at \( x = -2 \) and \( x = 3 \). What is the value of \(k\)?
whyCorrect: Get the two intersection points from the parabola, since the line passes through the same points: at \( x=-2 \), \( y = 4-4 = 0 \); at \( x=3 \), \( y = 9-4 = 5 \). The line through \( (-2,0) \) and \( (3,5) \) has slope \( \frac{5-0}{3-(-2)} = 1 \), so \( y = x+k \) and \( 0 = -2+k \) gives \( k = 2 \).

whyWrong.A: 1 is the slope \(m\), not the intercept.
whyWrong.C: 3 is an x-coordinate of an intersection point, not the y-intercept of the line.
whyWrong.D: 4 is the constant in the parabola's equation; the line's intercept comes from the two shared points.

note: A figure is printed, but the equation and both intersection x-values are stated in the text, so it is not needed.

stem: \[ \frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{q} + \frac{1}{s} + \frac{1}{13} \]A parallel electric circuit contains four resistors with resistances of \(p\) ohms, \(q\) ohms, \(s\) ohms, and 13 ohms. The given equation relates the resistance \(R\), in ohms, of the circuit, to the resistances of the four individual resistors it contains. Which equation correctly expresses \(R\) in terms of \(p\), \(q\), and \(s\)?
whyCorrect: Add the four fractions over the common denominator \( 13pqs \): \( \frac{1}{R} = \frac{13qs+13ps+13pq+pqs}{13pqs} \). That gives \( \frac{1}{R} \), not \(R\) — take the reciprocal of the whole thing to finish, which flips the fraction to \( R = \frac{13pqs}{13qs+13ps+13pq+pqs} \).

whyWrong.A: This adds the denominators directly, as if \( \frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q} \) were \( \frac{1}{p+q} \), which it is not.
whyWrong.C: This is \( \frac{1}{R} \), the sum as computed — the reciprocal step was skipped.
whyWrong.D: This is the series formula, which just adds the resistances; the given equation adds reciprocals.

stem: The function \(v\) is defined by the equation \[ v(x) = \frac{x^2+bx+c}{(x+5)(x-15)} \]where \(b\) and \(c\) are constants. In the xy-plane, the graph of \( y = v(x) \) passes through the points \( \left(0,\frac{22}{25}\right) \) and \( (11,0) \). If \( v(q)=0 \), which of the following could be the value of \(q\)?
whyCorrect: Start at \( x=0 \), where the \(b\) term disappears: \( v(0) = \frac{c}{(5)(-15)} = \frac{c}{-75} = \frac{22}{25} \), so \( c = -66 \). A rational function is zero only where its numerator is, so \( v(11)=0 \) gives \( 121+11b-66 = 0 \) and \( b = -5 \). The numerator is then \( x^2-5x-66 = (x-11)(x+6) \), so the other zero is \( q = -6 \).

whyWrong.B: \(-5\) is a zero of the denominator, not the numerator — the function is undefined there, so \( v(-5) \) is not 0.
whyWrong.C: 5 is the value of \(-b\), not a zero; substituting \( x=5 \) gives numerator \( 25-25-66 = -66 \neq 0 \).
whyWrong.D: 6 has the sign wrong: the numerator factors as \( (x-11)(x+6) \), so the zero is \(-6\).

stem: \[ 2x^2-8x-21 = 0 \]One solution to the given equation can be written as \( x = h - \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{k} \), where \(h\) and \(k\) are integer constants. What is the value of \( h+k \)?
whyCorrect: The quadratic formula gives \( x = \frac{8 \pm \sqrt{64+168}}{4} = \frac{8 \pm \sqrt{232}}{4} \). Now match the required shape: \( \frac{8}{4} = 2 \), and \( \frac{\sqrt{232}}{4} \) has to become \( \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{k} \). Since \( \sqrt{232} = 2\sqrt{58} \), the radical term is \( \frac{2\sqrt{58}}{4} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{58} \), so \( h=2 \), \( k=58 \) and \( h+k = 60 \).

whyWrong.A: \(-24\) comes from reading off the equation's own coefficients rather than solving it.
whyWrong.B: 10 is what you get from \( h=2 \) with \( k=8 \) — using the discriminant's leading digits instead of \( \sqrt{232} = 2\sqrt{58} \).
whyWrong.C: 29 is \( \frac{58}{2} \); the halving belongs to the radical, \( \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{58} \), not to the number under it (and \(h\) is still 2).

stem: \[ r(x) = 9(x-3) \] \[ s(x) = x^3+nx^2+3nx+27 \]For the given functions \(r\) and \(s\), \(n\) is a constant. If \( r(x) \cdot s(x) = 9(x^4-81) \), what is the value of \(n\)?
whyCorrect: Cancel the 9 from both sides: \( (x-3)s(x) = x^4-81 \). Factor the right side as a difference of squares twice: \( x^4-81 = (x^2-9)(x^2+9) = (x-3)(x+3)(x^2+9) \). Dividing out \( x-3 \) leaves \( s(x) = (x+3)(x^2+9) = x^3+3x^2+9x+27 \). Comparing with \( x^3+nx^2+3nx+27 \) gives \( n = 3 \), and the \(x\) term checks out too: \( 3n = 9 \).

stem: The function \(j\) is defined by \( j(x) = \frac{10x+5}{3p} \), and the function \(k\) is defined by \( k(x) = \frac{j(x) \cdot p}{x+1} \), where \(p\) is a positive constant. What is the value of \( k(9) \)?
whyCorrect: The unknown \(p\) cancels, so you never need its value. \( j(9) = \frac{95}{3p} \), and \( k(9) = \frac{j(9) \cdot p}{10} = \frac{95}{3p} \cdot \frac{p}{10} = \frac{95}{30} = \frac{19}{6} \).

whyWrong.B: \( \frac{10}{3} \) is \( \frac{100}{30} \) — using \( 10(9)+10 \) instead of \( 10(9)+5 \) in the numerator.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{95}{13} \) divides by \( 3+10 \) instead of by \( 3 \times 10 \); the denominators multiply, they do not add.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{85}{3} \) forgets to divide by \( x+1 = 10 \) and mis-adds the numerator.

stem: \[ (x-k)^2 = (k-5a)(x-k) \]In the given equation, \(a\) and \(k\) are constants, where \( k > 5a \). The sum of the solutions to the equation is \( 3k+32 \). What is the value of \(a\)?
whyCorrect: Do not expand — both sides share the factor \( x-k \). Moving everything left gives \( (x-k)\left[(x-k)-(k-5a)\right] = 0 \), so the solutions are \( x = k \) and \( x = 2k-5a \) (distinct because \( k > 5a \)). Their sum is \( 3k-5a \), and setting \( 3k-5a = 3k+32 \) gives \( -5a = 32 \), so \( a = -\frac{32}{5} = -6.4 \).
note: Duplicate of question 26 in the same chapter (identical stem).

stem: If the perimeter of an equilateral triangle with a height of 21 is \( a\sqrt{3} \), what is the value of \(a\)?
whyCorrect: The height of an equilateral triangle with side \(s\) splits it into two 30-60-90 triangles, giving \( h = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s \). So \( 21 = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s \) and \( s = \frac{42}{\sqrt{3}} = 14\sqrt{3} \). The perimeter is \( 3s = 42\sqrt{3} \), so \( a = 42 \).

stem: The three points shown define a circle. The circumference of this circle is \(k\pi\), where k is a constant. What is the value of k?
whyCorrect: Two of the points share the x-coordinate 12, so the chord joining them is vertical and the center lies on its perpendicular bisector, the horizontal line y = 7. Write the center as (h, 7) and set the distances to two of the points equal: \((h-12)^{2}+3^{2}=(h-9)^{2}\). Expanding gives \(-24h+153=-18h+81\), so h = 12 and the center is (12, 7) with radius 3. The circumference is \(2\pi(3)=6\pi\), so k = 6.

whyWrong.A: 3 is the radius. Circumference is \(2\pi r\), so the coefficient of \(\pi\) is 6.
whyWrong.C: 9 is \(r^{2}\), the coefficient of \(\pi\) in the area, not the circumference.
whyWrong.D: This uses the diameter 6 in place of the radius in \(2\pi r\), doubling the circumference.

note: Figure needed: an xy-grid with both axes running from 0 to about 15, with three plotted points at (12, 10), (9, 7) and (12, 4). The coordinates appear only in the figure.
imageAlt: Three plotted points on a square grid in the xy-plane, with both axes running from 0 to 15.

stem: In the figure, parallel lines \(a\) and \(b\) are intersected by lines \(c\), \(d\), and \(e\). If \( z = 49 \), \( y = 136 \), and \( v < z \), which statement about \(x\) and \(w\) must be true?
whyCorrect: Each of \(x\) and \(w\) is an angle of a triangle-like crossing formed by two of the transversals, and the exterior-angle relationship (using the parallel lines to transfer angles from \(a\) to \(b\)) gives \( w = y - z \) and \( x = y - v \). With \( y = 136 \) and \( z = 49 \), \( w = 87 \). Since \( v < z \), subtracting the smaller \(v\) leaves more, so \( x = 136 - v > 136 - 49 = 87 = w \).

whyWrong.A: This reverses the effect of \( v < z \): a smaller angle subtracted from the same 136 gives a larger result, so \(x\) exceeds \(w\).
whyWrong.C: Equality would need \( v = z \), which the condition \( v < z \) rules out.
whyWrong.D: \( w = 87 \) alone already exceeds 90 when added to any positive \(x\); nothing here makes the two angles complementary.

note: Figure needed: vertical parallel lines a and b crossed by three transversals — c rising to the right, d and e falling to the right. v is at a on line d, y and z are at b on lines c and e, x is where c meets d (right of b), and w is where c meets e (left of a).
imageAlt: A line diagram: two parallel vertical lines labelled a and b crossed by three slanted lines labelled c, d and e, with five of the angles formed marked by letters.

stem: Right rectangular prism X is similar to right rectangular prism Y. The surface area of right rectangular prism X is 59 square centimeters \( \left(\text{cm}^2\right) \), and the surface area of right rectangular prism Y is 1,475 cm². The volume of right rectangular prism Y is 1,500 cubic centimeters \( \left(\text{cm}^3\right) \). What is the sum of the volumes, in cm³, of right rectangular prism X and right rectangular prism Y?
whyCorrect: For similar solids, areas scale as the square of the linear ratio and volumes as the cube. The surface areas are in the ratio \( \frac{1475}{59} = 25 \), so the linear ratio of Y to X is \( \sqrt{25} = 5 \) and the volume ratio is \( 5^3 = 125 \). So prism X has volume \( \frac{1500}{125} = 12 \) cm³, and the two volumes sum to \( 12+1500 = 1512 \) cm³.

stem: In the figure, \( \overline{LQ} \) intersects \( \overline{MP} \) at point \(R\) and \( \overline{LM} \) is parallel to \( \overline{PQ} \). The lengths of \( \overline{MR} \) and \( \overline{RP} \) are 8 and 14 units, respectively. The area of \( \triangle LMR \) is 36 square units. What is the area of \( \triangle PQR \), in square units?
whyCorrect: The parallel sides make the alternate interior angles equal, and the angles at \(R\) are vertical, so \( \triangle LMR \sim \triangle QPR \) with \(MR\) corresponding to \(RP\). The linear ratio from \(LMR\) to \(PQR\) is \( \frac{14}{8} = \frac{7}{4} \), and areas scale by the square of that: \( \left(\frac{7}{4}\right)^2 = \frac{49}{16} \). So the area is \( 36 \times \frac{49}{16} = \frac{441}{4} \).

whyWrong.A: \( \frac{576}{49} \) is \( 36 \times \frac{16}{49} \) — the ratio applied upside down, shrinking the larger triangle.
whyWrong.B: \( \frac{144}{7} \) is \( 36 \times \frac{4}{7} \), using the linear ratio (also inverted) instead of its square.
whyWrong.C: 63 is \( 36 \times \frac{7}{4} \), scaling the area by the linear ratio rather than by its square.

note: Figure needed: segments LQ and MP crossing at R, with triangle LMR above-left and triangle PQR below-right, LM parallel to PQ.
imageAlt: Two straight segments crossing at a labelled interior point, forming two triangles that point in opposite directions; all five points are labelled.

stem: A right square pyramid has a total surface area of 28,160 square inches, and the combined surface area of the four lateral faces of this pyramid is 16,060 square inches. What is the height, in inches, of this pyramid?
whyCorrect: Subtract to get the base: \( 28{,}160-16{,}060 = 12{,}100 \) square inches, so the base edge is \( \sqrt{12{,}100} = 110 \). Each lateral face is a triangle with base 110 and height equal to the slant height \(l\), so \( 4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}(110)l = 16{,}060 \) gives \( l = 73 \). The slant height, the pyramid's height, and half the base edge form a right triangle: \( h = \sqrt{73^2-55^2} = \sqrt{2{,}304} = 48 \).

whyWrong.B: 55 is half the base edge, one leg of that right triangle, not the height.
whyWrong.C: 73 is the slant height — the distance up the middle of a triangular face, not the vertical height.
whyWrong.D: 110 is the base edge itself.

stem: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of the acute angles is \( (7x-610)^\circ \). The sum of the measures of one of the acute angles and three of the obtuse angles is \( (-14x+w)^\circ \). What is the value of \(w\)?
whyCorrect: With two parallel lines and a transversal, all four acute angles are equal and each obtuse angle is the supplement of an acute one. Writing the acute measure as \( a = 7x-610 \), the required sum is \( a+3(180-a) = 540-2a \). Substituting, \( 540-2(7x-610) = 540-14x+1220 = -14x+1760 \), so matching the given form gives \( w = 1760 \).

stem: In the figure, \( AC = CD \). The measure of angle \(EBC\) is 29°, and the measure of angle \(ACD\) is 108°. What is the value of \(x\)?
whyCorrect: Triangle \(ACD\) is isosceles with \( AC = CD \), so its base angles are equal: \( \frac{180-108}{2} = 36^\circ \) each, which makes angle \(CDA\) — and therefore angle \(BDE\), since \(C\) lies on \( \overline{DB} \) — equal to 36°. Now look at triangle \(DBE\): the angle at \(D\) is 36° and the angle at \(B\) is 29° (angle \(EBC\) is the same as angle \(EBD\)). The angle \(x^\circ\) is exterior to that triangle at \(E\), so it equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: \( 36+29 = 65 \).
note: Figure needed: D, E, A collinear left to right; C above between D and B; segment DB through C; segment CA; segment BE meeting DA at E; x is the angle at E between EB and EA.
imageAlt: A plane diagram with a horizontal base line carrying three labelled points, a slanted line from the left-hand end rising to a labelled point above, and two further segments drawn across the interior; one angle is marked with a letter.

stem: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of the acute angles is (9x − 490)°. The sum of the measures of one of the acute angles and three of the obtuse angles is (−18x + w)°. What is the value of w?
whyCorrect: When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, every acute angle is congruent to every other acute angle and every obtuse angle is supplementary to them. So each obtuse angle measures 180 − (9x − 490). One acute plus three obtuse is (9x − 490) + 3[180 − (9x − 490)] = 540 − 2(9x − 490) = 540 − 18x + 980 = 1520 − 18x. Matching that to −18x + w gives w = 1520. Notice you never need x itself — the −18x on both sides is the signal that the x-terms are meant to cancel.

stem: The perimeter of an isosceles right triangle is \(52+52\sqrt{2}\) inches. What is the length, in inches, of the hypotenuse of this triangle?
whyCorrect: An isosceles right triangle with leg \(a\) has hypotenuse \(a\sqrt{2}\), so its perimeter is \(2a+a\sqrt{2}=a(2+\sqrt{2})\). Set that equal to \(52+52\sqrt{2}=52(1+\sqrt{2})\) and solve: \(a=\frac{52(1+\sqrt{2})}{2+\sqrt{2}}\). Multiply top and bottom by \(2-\sqrt{2}\); the denominator becomes 2 and the numerator becomes \(52\sqrt{2}\), so \(a=26\sqrt{2}\). The hypotenuse is \(a\sqrt{2}=26\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}=52\). The trap is that the perimeter is written to look like it splits as leg + leg + hypotenuse; it does not.

whyWrong.A: This is half of 52, which would be the answer if you read the perimeter's first term, 52, as the sum of the two legs. The two parts of \(52+52\sqrt{2}\) are not the legs and the hypotenuse.
whyWrong.B: This is the leg length \(a\), the value you get partway through. The question asks for the hypotenuse, which is \(a\sqrt{2}\).
whyWrong.D: This treats the \(52\sqrt{2}\) term of the perimeter as the hypotenuse directly. If it were, the two legs would sum to 52, making each leg 26 and the hypotenuse \(26\sqrt{2}\), which contradicts the assumption.

stem: A property owner wants to find the length \(x\), in feet, across a pond as represented in the figure. PR intersects ST at point Q, and angle PTQ is congruent to angle RSQ. The lengths represented by PQ, TQ, QS, and RS were determined to be 4,200 feet, 8,400 feet, 1,400 feet, and 1,600 feet, respectively. What is the value of \(x\)?
whyCorrect: Angles PQT and RQS are vertical angles, so they are congruent, and you are told angle PTQ is congruent to angle RSQ. That makes triangle PTQ similar to triangle RSQ, with P matching R, T matching S, and Q matching Q. The scale factor comes from the pair of corresponding sides you know completely: TQ : SQ = 8,400 : 1,400 = 6. The distance across the pond is PT, which corresponds to RS, so \(x = 6 \times 1{,}600 = 9{,}600\) feet.
note: Figure needed: two segments PR and ST crossing at Q. T is below P on the left (PT spans the pond, labelled x, drawn as a lens/oval shape); S is upper right and R is lower right, so PR runs from upper left down to lower right and ST runs from lower left up to upper right, crossing at Q.
imageAlt: Two straight paths crossing at a labelled point: one runs from P at the upper left down to R at the lower right, the other from T at the lower left up to S at the upper right. A narrow oval marks the pond around segment PT, and the segment SR is drawn on the right.

stem: A right square pyramid has a surface area of 75,264 square inches, which includes a base area of 36,864 square inches. What is the slant height, in inches, of this pyramid?
whyCorrect: The base is a square of area 36,864, so its side is \(\sqrt{36{,}864}=192\) inches. Subtract the base from the total to get the lateral area: 75,264 − 36,864 = 38,400 square inches. That lateral area is four congruent triangles, each with base 192 and height equal to the slant height \(\ell\), so \(4\cdot\frac{1}{2}(192)\ell = 384\ell = 38{,}400\). Therefore \(\ell = 100\) inches.

stem: \[x^{2}-16x+y^{2}-10y-55=0\]In the xy-plane, the graph of the given equation is a circle. If this circle is inscribed in a square, what is the perimeter of the square?
whyCorrect: Complete the square: \(x^{2}-16x\) needs +64 and \(y^{2}-10y\) needs +25, giving \((x-8)^{2}+(y-5)^{2}=55+64+25=144\). The radius is 12, so the diameter is 24. An inscribed circle touches all four sides of the square, so the square's side is that diameter, 24, and the perimeter is 4(24) = 96.

whyWrong.A: This is the side of the square (the diameter), not its perimeter.
whyWrong.B: This is 4 times the radius. The side of the square is the diameter 24, not the radius 12.
whyWrong.D: This is 4(55), using the constant term of the equation as though it were a length. That 55 has to be moved across and combined with the 64 and 25 from completing the square before you have \(r^{2}\).

stem: \[2x^{2}+2y^{2}+tx+ty-78=0\]The given equation, where t is a positive constant, defines a circle in the xy-plane. The radius of this circle is \(\sqrt{41}\). What is the value of t?
whyCorrect: Divide through by 2 first so the squared terms have coefficient 1: \(x^{2}+y^{2}+\frac{t}{2}x+\frac{t}{2}y-39=0\). Completing the square on each variable adds \(\left(\frac{t}{4}\right)^{2}\) twice, giving \(\left(x+\frac{t}{4}\right)^{2}+\left(y+\frac{t}{4}\right)^{2}=39+\frac{t^{2}}{8}\). Set that equal to \(r^{2}=41\): \(\frac{t^{2}}{8}=2\), so \(t^{2}=16\) and, since t is positive, t = 4. Skipping the division by 2 is the usual mistake - completing the square only works once the leading coefficients are 1.

stem: Two isosceles triangles are shown above. If 180 − z = 3y and y = 50, what is the value of x?
whyCorrect: The angles of the right-hand triangle sum to 180, and its two tick-marked sides are congruent, so its two base angles are equal and together they measure \(180-z\). You are handed that quantity directly: \(180-z=3y=3(50)=150\), so each base angle is 75. The angle marked x is not that base angle - it sits on the other side of the slanted segment, between the segment and the upward continuation of the vertical line, so it is the base angle's supplement: \(x=180-75=105\). You never need z or the left-hand triangle at all.
note: Figure needed, and the answer turns on one detail of it. Two vertical lines bound the figure. Four segments meet at a single point between them: two run left to the left-hand vertical line (marked with single ticks, forming the left isosceles triangle with apex angle y inside), two run right to the right-hand vertical line (marked with double ticks, forming the right isosceles triangle with apex angle z inside). The label x sits ABOVE the upper right-hand segment and to the LEFT of the right vertical line, i.e. in the wedge between that segment and the part of the vertical line running upward past the vertex - so x is the EXTERIOR angle there, 105, not the interior base angle, 75. If the printed key is 75, the disagreement is over exactly this label placement. Also note the four segments bend at the shared point (the upper-left segment does not continue as the lower-right one), so y and z are not vertical angles and there is no contradiction with y = 50.
imageAlt: Two vertical lines with four segments meeting at a single point between them: two run left to the left-hand line and carry one tick mark each, two run right to the right-hand line and carry two tick marks each. Three angles are labelled with variables.

stem: The solid in the figure is the shaded part of a cone with a height of 10 cm obtained by cutting its top parallel to the base, 10 cm from its tip. The volume of the solid is
whyCorrect: The shaded solid is a frustum: the whole cone (radius 3, height 20) with the small top cone (radius 1.5, height 10) removed. Work with the difference rather than memorising a frustum formula: \(\frac{1}{3}\pi(3)^{2}(20)-\frac{1}{3}\pi(1.5)^{2}(10)=60\pi-7.5\pi=52.5\pi\). That evaluates to about 164.93 cubic centimeters. The check that the setup is right is that the small cone is similar to the big one - half the radius and half the height.

whyWrong.A: \(60\pi\) is the volume of the entire cone, before the top is cut off. You still have to remove the small cone.
whyWrong.B: \(7.5\pi\) is the volume of the small cone that was cut away, not the piece that remains.
whyWrong.D: This is not produced by any correct route; it is close enough to the answer to look plausible. If you got it, check that you used the full cone's height of 20, not 10, and subtracted the small cone rather than averaging the two radii.

note: Figure needed: a cone standing point-up, total height 20 marked on the right, the top 10 cm marked on the left, a horizontal cut 10 cm from the tip where the radius is 1.5, and a base radius of 3. The frustum below the cut is shaded. The radii 1.5 and 3 appear only in the figure, so the question is unanswerable without it.
imageAlt: A cone standing point upward, cut by a horizontal plane parallel to the base; the piece below the cut is shaded. The height of the whole cone, the height of the removed tip, and the radius of both circles are marked with dimension lines.

stem: In the xy-plane, a circle has center C with coordinates (p, 8), where p is a constant. Points G and H lie on the circle. Point G has coordinates \((p+3\sqrt{5},\, 14)\), and point H has coordinates (q, 8), where q is a constant greater than p. What is the area, in square units, of triangle CGH?
whyCorrect: Find the radius from G: it sits \(3\sqrt{5}\) to the right of the center and 6 above it, so \(r=\sqrt{(3\sqrt{5})^{2}+6^{2}}=\sqrt{45+36}=\sqrt{81}=9\). The radical disappears, which is the whole point of the numbers chosen. H has the same y-coordinate as the center, so it is 9 units horizontally from C, and since q > p it is at \((p+9,\,8)\). Take CH as the base: it is horizontal with length 9, and G is 14 − 8 = 6 units above that line, so the area is \(\frac{1}{2}(9)(6)=27\).

whyWrong.A: This carries a stray \(\sqrt{5}\) from G's coordinate into the answer. Once you square \(3\sqrt{5}\) to get 45 and add 36, the radius is the whole number 9 and no radical survives.
whyWrong.C: \(5\sqrt{27}=15\sqrt{3}\approx 25.98\), which is close enough to 27 to look right but is not it. It comes from swapping the 5 and the 27 inside the radical rather than computing the base and height.
whyWrong.D: This attaches a \(\sqrt{6}\) to the correct value 27, taking the height 6 from under a radical it was never under. The height is exactly 6 units, the difference of the y-coordinates.

stem: In the xy-plane, the line y = 3x − 14 is tangent to a circle with center (h, 1). Which of the following is a possible value for h if the center lies to the right of the tangent line?
whyCorrect: The radius is never given, so tangency alone puts no restriction on h - any center can be tangent to the line for the right radius. The only condition that bites is the position. Find where the line reaches the height of the center: set y = 1, so 1 = 3h − 14 gives x = 5. At the height y = 1 the line sits at x = 5, so the center (h, 1) is to the right of the line exactly when h > 5. Only 7 qualifies.

whyWrong.A: 2 is less than 5, so this center sits to the left of the line.
whyWrong.B: 3 is less than 5, so this center also sits to the left of the line.
whyWrong.C: At h = 5 the point (5, 1) lies exactly on the line y = 3x − 14, not to the right of it, and a center on the tangent line is impossible anyway.

stem: In a circle, chord RS is parallel to diameter PQ. If the length of RS is \(\frac{3}{4}\) of the length of PQ and the distance between the chord and the diameter is \(2\sqrt{7}\), what is the radius of the circle?
whyCorrect: Write everything in terms of the radius r. The diameter is 2r, so \(RS=\frac{3}{4}(2r)=\frac{3r}{2}\) and half the chord is \(\frac{3r}{4}\). Drop the perpendicular from the center to the chord: it has length \(2\sqrt{7}\) and, with half the chord, forms a right triangle whose hypotenuse is a radius. So \(r^{2}=\left(\frac{3r}{4}\right)^{2}+(2\sqrt{7})^{2}=\frac{9r^{2}}{16}+28\). Then \(\frac{7r^{2}}{16}=28\), \(r^{2}=64\), r = 8. The trap is using \(\frac{3}{4}\) of the radius, or forgetting to halve the chord.

whyWrong.A: 6 is half of the chord RS once you know r = 8 (RS = 12), an intermediate value rather than the radius.
whyWrong.B: This scales the given distance \(2\sqrt{7}\) by \(\frac{3}{2}\). The chord ratio does not act on the distance; the distance and half the chord are the two legs of a right triangle, so they combine by the Pythagorean theorem, not by multiplication.
whyWrong.D: This doubles the given distance, treating \(2\sqrt{7}\) as half the radius. The perpendicular distance is a leg of the right triangle, not a piece of the radius.

stem: The ratio of the internal angles of triangle A is 1:2:3. Triangle B is an equilateral triangle with a side of 12 cm. If the area of triangle A and B are equal and the perimeter of triangle A is \(m\sqrt{2}+n\sqrt{6}\), what is the value of \(m+n\)?
whyCorrect: Angles in the ratio 1:2:3 summing to 180 are 30, 60 and 90, so triangle A is a 30-60-90 triangle with sides \(k\), \(k\sqrt{3}\), \(2k\) and area \(\frac{1}{2}(k)(k\sqrt{3})=\frac{k^{2}\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Triangle B has area \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(12)^{2}=36\sqrt{3}\). Setting them equal gives \(k^{2}=72\), so \(k=6\sqrt{2}\). The perimeter is \(k(1+\sqrt{3}+2)=6\sqrt{2}(3+\sqrt{3})=18\sqrt{2}+6\sqrt{6}\), so m = 18, n = 6 and \(m+n=24\).

whyWrong.A: 6 is n on its own. The question asks for \(m+n\), and m = 18.
whyWrong.B: 12 is the side of the equilateral triangle. You get it as k if you apply the equilateral area formula \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}k^{2}\) to triangle A, but triangle A is a right triangle, so its area is \(\frac{1}{2}\) times the two legs.
whyWrong.C: 18 is m on its own. Add n = 6.

stem: The figure above shows a semicircle with the lengths of the adjacent arcs a, a + 1, a + 2, a + 3, and a + 4. If the value of x is 42, what is the value of a?
whyCorrect: Central angles are proportional to the arcs they cut off, and the five arcs make up a semicircle, so their central angles total 180 degrees. The five arcs sum to \(a+(a+1)+(a+2)+(a+3)+(a+4)=5a+10\), and \(x^{\circ}\) is the central angle belonging to the arc of length \(a+4\). So \(\frac{a+4}{5a+10}=\frac{42}{180}\). Cross-multiplying, \(180a+720=210a+420\), giving \(30a=300\) and a = 10. Check: the arcs are 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, totalling 60, and \(\frac{14}{60}(180)=42\).

whyWrong.A: With a = 7 the arcs total 45 and the last arc is 11, giving a central angle of \(\frac{11}{45}(180)=44\), not 42.
whyWrong.B: With a = 8 the arcs total 50 and the last arc is 12, giving \(\frac{12}{50}(180)=43.2\).
whyWrong.C: With a = 9 the arcs total 55 and the last arc is 13, giving \(\frac{13}{55}(180)\approx 42.5\) - close, which is why it is offered, but not exact.

note: Figure needed: a semicircle with centre O on the flat side, divided into five arcs by four radii. Going from the left end of the diameter to the right end the arcs are labelled a, a + 1, a + 2, a + 3, a + 4. The central angle of the last arc (a + 4), nearest the right end of the diameter, is labelled x degrees. Without the figure there is nothing telling the student which arc x belongs to.
imageAlt: A semicircle with its centre marked on the flat side, divided into five adjacent arcs by four radii; each arc carries an algebraic length label and one central angle is labelled in degrees.

stem: Right rectangular prism X is similar to right rectangular prism Y. The surface area of right rectangular prism X is 59 cm<sup>2</sup>, and the surface area of right rectangular prism Y is 1,475 cm<sup>2</sup>. The volume of right rectangular prism Y is 1,500 cm<sup>3</sup>. What is the sum of the volumes, in cm<sup>3</sup>, of right rectangular prism X and right rectangular prism Y?
whyCorrect: For similar solids, areas scale as the square of the linear ratio and volumes as the cube. The surface areas give \(\frac{1475}{59}=25\), so the linear ratio of Y to X is \(\sqrt{25}=5\). Volumes therefore scale by \(5^{3}=125\), so \(V_{X}=\frac{1500}{125}=12\). The sum is 12 + 1,500 = 1,512. The mistake to avoid is dividing the volume by 25 instead of 125.

stem: A circle is inscribed in an equilateral triangle as shown above. Point L is the center of the circle. Points A, B, and C all lie on the circle and the sides of the triangle. The perimeter of the triangle is \(90\sqrt{3}\). The length of arc AC is equal to \(k\pi\). What is the value of k?
whyCorrect: Each side of the equilateral triangle is \(\frac{90\sqrt{3}}{3}=30\sqrt{3}\), and the inradius of an equilateral triangle is \(\frac{s}{2\sqrt{3}}=\frac{30\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{3}}=15\). For the arc you need the central angle ALC. A and C are the points where the circle touches the two sides meeting at vertex Q, and a radius drawn to a point of tangency is perpendicular to the side, so quadrilateral QALC has two right angles and its angle at Q is 60 degrees; the remaining angle ALC is 360 − 90 − 90 − 60 = 120 degrees. The arc is therefore \(\frac{120}{360}\cdot 2\pi(15)=10\pi\), so k = 10.
note: Figure needed: an equilateral triangle PQR with P at the top, Q at the lower left and R at the lower right, and its inscribed circle centred at L. A is the point of tangency on side PQ, B the point of tangency on side PR, and C the point of tangency on side QR. Arc AC is the minor arc, the one on the Q side that does not contain B.
imageAlt: An equilateral triangle P Q R with a circle inscribed in it; the centre of the circle is marked L and the three points where the circle touches the sides are marked A, B and C.

stem: \[5x^{2}-40px+5y^{2}+70py=325p^{2}\]In the xy-plane, the graph of the given equation is a circle, where p is a constant. The center of the circle is (-8, 14). If a square is inscribed in the circle, what is the area of the square?
whyCorrect: Divide by 5 first: \(x^{2}-8px+y^{2}+14py=65p^{2}\). Completing the square gives \((x-4p)^{2}+(y+7p)^{2}=65p^{2}+16p^{2}+49p^{2}=130p^{2}\), so the center is \((4p,\,-7p)\). Matching to (-8, 14) gives p = -2 from either coordinate, so \(r^{2}=130(-2)^{2}=520\). For a square inscribed in a circle the diagonal is the diameter, \(2r\), so the side is \(\frac{2r}{\sqrt{2}}=r\sqrt{2}\) and the area is \(2r^{2}=2(520)=1040\). You never need r itself, only \(r^{2}\).

stem: In triangle DEF, angle F is a right angle, point Q lies on DE, point J lies on EF, and QJ is parallel to DF. If the length of EF is 45 units, the length of FJ is 24 units, and the area of triangle DEF is 630 square units, what is the perimeter of triangle QEJ, in units?
whyCorrect: The right angle is at F, so the legs are DF and EF: \(\frac{1}{2}(DF)(45)=630\) gives DF = 28, and the hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{28^{2}+45^{2}}=\sqrt{2809}=53\), so triangle DEF has perimeter 28 + 45 + 53 = 126. Since QJ is parallel to DF, triangle QEJ is similar to triangle DEF, and the matching sides along EF give the ratio. J is 24 from F, so EJ = 45 − 24 = 21 and the ratio is \(\frac{21}{45}=\frac{7}{15}\). Perimeters scale by the same ratio: \(\frac{7}{15}(126)=\frac{294}{5}\).

whyWrong.B: This is half of 126, which is what you get by treating J as the midpoint of EF. FJ = 24 and EJ = 21 are close but not equal, and the ratio is \(\frac{21}{45}\), not \(\frac{1}{2}\).
whyWrong.C: This scales the perimeter 126 by \(\frac{7}{10}\) instead of \(\frac{7}{15}\) - the similarity ratio read off the wrong pair of corresponding sides. The side of the small triangle along EF is EJ = 21, and it corresponds to the whole of EF = 45.
whyWrong.D: 126 is the perimeter of the large triangle DEF. Triangle QEJ is the small one cut off near vertex E.

stem: What is the area, in square units, of the triangle formed by connecting the three points shown?
whyCorrect: None of the three sides is horizontal or vertical, so there is no easy base and height - use the shoelace formula on the coordinates instead: \(\frac{1}{2}\left|x_{1}(y_{2}-y_{3})+x_{2}(y_{3}-y_{1})+x_{3}(y_{1}-y_{2})\right|\). With the points in the order shown that is \(\frac{1}{2}\left|(-3)(3-(-3))+5(-3-4)+4(4-3)\right|=\frac{1}{2}\left|-18-35+4\right|=\frac{49}{2}=24.5\). If you would rather avoid the formula, box the triangle in the 8-by-7 rectangle that just contains it (area 56) and subtract the three right triangles in the corners, which come to 31.5.
note: Figure needed: an xy-grid with x from -4 to 6 and y from -4 to 10, with three plotted points at (-3, 4), (5, 3) and (4, -3). The coordinates appear only in the figure.
imageAlt: Three plotted points on a square grid in the xy-plane; the x-axis runs from -5 to 7 and the y-axis from -5 to 10.

stem: The area of triangle ABC above is at least 48 but no more than 60. If y is an integer, what is one possible value of x?
whyCorrect: The base AC is 5 + 7 = 12 and the height is y, so the area is \(\frac{1}{2}(12)y=6y\). Requiring \(48 \le 6y \le 60\) gives \(8 \le y \le 10\), so the integer y can be 8, 9 or 10. The segment marked x is perpendicular to AC at a point 5 units from A, so the small triangle it forms with vertex A is similar to triangle ABC: \(\frac{x}{y}=\frac{5}{12}\), giving \(x=\frac{5y}{12}\). Taking y = 9 gives \(x=\frac{45}{12}=3.75\). The other allowed values are \(\frac{10}{3}\) (from y = 8) and \(\frac{25}{6}\) (from y = 10).
note: Figure needed: right triangle ABC with the right angle at C, A at the lower left, C at the lower right and B directly above C. Along AC, a vertical segment labelled x rises from a point on AC to meet AB, meeting AC at a right angle; the part of AC from A to its foot is labelled 5 and the part from the foot to C is labelled 7. The side BC is labelled y. Only y = 9 gives a terminating decimal, so 3.75 is recorded; 10/3 and 25/6 are equally valid.
imageAlt: A right triangle A B C with the right angle at C, A at the lower left and B directly above C. A vertical segment rises from a point on side AC to meet AB at a right angle; the two parts of AC and the segment itself carry labels, as does side BC.

stem: A circle has center A, and points B and C lie on the circle. Line segments BD and CD are tangent to the circle at points B and C, respectively. The measure of angle BDC is 120°. The length of line segment CD is 12 inches. What is the area of the region that is both inside quadrilateral ABDC and outside the circle, in square inches? (Round your answer to the nearest hundredth of a square inch)
whyCorrect: A radius meets a tangent at a right angle, so angles ABD and ACD are both 90°. The four angles of quadrilateral ABDC sum to 360, so angle BAC = 360 − 90 − 90 − 120 = 60°. Segment AD splits the figure into two congruent right triangles, each with a 30° angle at A, so \(\tan 30^{\circ}=\frac{12}{r}\) and \(r=12\sqrt{3}\). The quadrilateral's area is \(2\cdot\frac{1}{2}(r)(12)=12r=144\sqrt{3}\). The part of the circle inside it is the sector with central angle 60°: \(\frac{60}{360}\pi(12\sqrt{3})^{2}=72\pi\). Subtracting, \(144\sqrt{3}-72\pi\approx 249.415-226.195=23.22\) square inches.

stem: In the figure above, O is the center of the circle and AC is tangent to the circle at D. If triangle ABC is equilateral, what is the ratio \(\frac{FE}{AC}\)?
whyCorrect: Put D at the origin with AC along the x-axis, so \(A=(-\tfrac{s}{2},0)\), \(C=(\tfrac{s}{2},0)\) and \(B=(0,\tfrac{s\sqrt{3}}{2})\) for side s. The circle is tangent to AC at D, so its center is straight above D and its radius r satisfies 2r = height of the triangle, giving \(r=\frac{s\sqrt{3}}{4}\). Substituting the line AB into \(x^{2}+y^{2}-2ry=0\) gives \(4t^{2}-5t+1=0\) for the parameter t, whose roots are t = 1 (the point B) and \(t=\frac{1}{4}\) (the point F). So F is a quarter of the way from A to B, at \(x=-\frac{3s}{8}\), and by symmetry E is at \(x=\frac{3s}{8}\). Then \(FE=\frac{3s}{4}\) and \(\frac{FE}{AC}=\frac{3}{4}\).
note: Figure needed: equilateral triangle ABC with base AC horizontal at the bottom and apex B at the top, and a circle passing through B and tangent to AC at D, the midpoint of AC. O is the circle's centre, on segment BD. The circle cuts AB at F and BC at E, and the horizontal chord FE is drawn; the angle between FO and FE at F is marked 30 degrees. Points D, E and F exist only in the figure.
imageAlt: An equilateral triangle A B C with a circle through the apex B that touches the base at D; the circle's centre O lies on the segment from B to D. The circle crosses the two slanted sides at F and E, and the chord FE and the segment from F to O are drawn, with one angle at F marked in degrees.

stem: Two identical rectangular prisms each have a height of 90 centimeters (cm). The base of each prism is a square, and the surface area of each prism is K cm<sup>2</sup>. If the prisms are glued together along a square base, the resulting prism has a surface area of \(\frac{92}{47}K\) cm<sup>2</sup>. What is the side length, in cm, of each square base?
whyCorrect: With base side s, one prism has \(K=2s^{2}+4(90s)=2s^{2}+360s\). Gluing them base to base makes a single prism \(s\times s\times 180\), whose surface area is \(2s^{2}+720s\) - the two square faces that got glued are now interior and disappear, which is why the answer is less than 2K. Setting \(2s^{2}+720s=\frac{92}{47}(2s^{2}+360s)\) and clearing the fraction gives \(94s^{2}+33{,}840s=184s^{2}+33{,}120s\), so \(90s^{2}=720s\) and s = 8.

whyWrong.A: s = 4 makes the ratio \(\frac{4+360}{4+180}=\frac{91}{46}\), not \(\frac{92}{47}\). The two differ by little, so check the ratio rather than eyeballing it.
whyWrong.C: s = 9 makes the ratio \(\frac{369}{189}=\frac{41}{21}\).
whyWrong.D: s = 16 makes the ratio \(\frac{376}{196}=\frac{94}{49}\), which looks deceptively like \(\frac{92}{47}\) but is not equal to it.

stem: In the figure above, the area of triangle ABC is equal to \(2x^{2}\). What is the cosine of angle BCP?
whyCorrect: BP is the height of triangle ABC onto base AC, and both BP and AP equal x. So \(\frac{1}{2}(AC)(x)=2x^{2}\) gives AC = 4x, and therefore PC = 4x − x = 3x. Now work inside right triangle BPC, right-angled at P: the legs are BP = x and PC = 3x, so \(BC=\sqrt{x^{2}+9x^{2}}=x\sqrt{10}\). Cosine of the angle at C is adjacent over hypotenuse, \(\frac{3x}{x\sqrt{10}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\).

whyWrong.A: This is \(\frac{BP}{BC}\), the side opposite the angle over the hypotenuse - that is the sine of angle BCP, not the cosine.
whyWrong.C: This is \(\frac{BP}{PC}\), opposite over adjacent, which is the tangent.
whyWrong.D: This is \(\frac{PC}{BP}\), the reciprocal of the tangent. A cosine can never exceed 1, so this can be ruled out on sight.

note: Figure needed: triangle ABC with A at the lower left, C at the lower right and B above, between them but nearer A. The altitude BP is drawn from B perpendicular to AC, meeting it at P; the segment AP is labelled x and the segment BP is labelled x. Both x labels appear only in the figure.
imageAlt: A triangle A B C with base AC horizontal and apex B above a point P near A; the altitude from B meets AC at a right angle at P. The part of the base from A to P and the altitude itself are both labelled.

stem:

Cylinder ARH
Cylinder B4R3H + 24
Cylinders A and B are similar. The volume of cylinder A is \(1176\pi\) cm3. If the surface areas of cylinder B and A are \(n\pi\) cm2 and \(k\pi\) cm2, respectively, what is the value of \(n-k\)?
whyCorrect: Similar cylinders scale every length by the same factor, and the radii show that factor is 4. So the heights must scale by 4 too: \(3H+24=4H\), giving H = 24. Then \(\pi R^{2}(24)=1176\pi\) gives \(R^{2}=49\) and R = 7. Cylinder A's surface area is \(2\pi(49)+2\pi(7)(24)=98\pi+336\pi=434\pi\), so k = 434. Areas scale by \(4^{2}=16\), so \(n=16(434)=6{,}944\) and \(n-k=6{,}944-434=6{,}510\).

stem: In the diagram, OB = OA, AB = BC, the measure of angle FAO is 30°, DE is parallel to AC, and AB = 58. What is the length of BE?
whyCorrect: Put F at the origin with A = (-a, 0), C = (a, 0), B = (0, b) and O = (0, t) on BF. Angle FAO = 30° gives \(t=\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}\), and OA = OB gives \(a^{2}+t^{2}=(b-t)^{2}\), i.e. \(t=\frac{b^{2}-a^{2}}{2b}\). Setting those equal reduces to \(\tan 2\varphi=-\sqrt{3}\) for the base angle \(\varphi\) at A, so \(\varphi = 60^{\circ}\) and the triangle is in fact equilateral with every side 58. Then \(a = 29\), \(b=29\sqrt{3}\) and \(t=\frac{29}{\sqrt{3}}\), which is one third of the way up from AC to B. Since DE is parallel to AC, E sits two thirds of the way down BC from B, so \(BE=\frac{2}{3}(58)=\frac{116}{3}\).

whyWrong.B: 29 is half of 58, the answer if you assume O is the midpoint of BF and so E the midpoint of BC. O is one third of the way up, not halfway.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{87}{2}=\frac{3}{4}(58)\), which comes from placing DE a quarter of the way down from B rather than two thirds.
whyWrong.D: 58 is the whole of BC. E is an interior point of that side, so BE must be shorter.

note: Figure needed: triangle ABC with B at the top, A at the lower left and C at the lower right. A vertical segment BF runs from B to F on AC. O lies on BF, and the horizontal segment DE through O meets AB at D and BC at E. Segment AO is also drawn from A to O. All of D, E, F and O exist only in the figure.
imageAlt: A triangle A B C with apex B at the top; a vertical segment runs from B to a point F on AC, a horizontal segment DE crosses it at O with D on AB and E on BC, and a segment is drawn from A to O.

stem: The perimeter of an isosceles right triangle is \(48+48\sqrt{2}\) inches. What is the length, in inches, of the hypotenuse of this triangle?
whyCorrect: With leg \(a\) the hypotenuse is \(a\sqrt{2}\), so the perimeter is \(a(2+\sqrt{2})\). Set \(a(2+\sqrt{2})=48(1+\sqrt{2})\) and rationalise by multiplying top and bottom by \(2-\sqrt{2}\): the denominator becomes 2 and the numerator \(48\sqrt{2}\), so \(a=24\sqrt{2}\). The hypotenuse is then \(24\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}=48\). The perimeter is written to look as though it splits into legs and hypotenuse; it does not.

whyWrong.A: This is half of 48, which assumes the perimeter's first term is the sum of the two legs.
whyWrong.B: This is the leg length, the value you reach partway through. The hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{2}\) times it.
whyWrong.D: This reads the \(48\sqrt{2}\) term of the perimeter as the hypotenuse. If it were, the legs would sum to 48 and the hypotenuse would come out to \(24\sqrt{2}\), contradicting that reading.

note: Same item as Geometry #32 on page 52 with 52 replaced by 48 throughout.

stem: A real estate company offers a series of three webinars. 1,250 people attended the first webinar. 68% of the people who attended the first webinar attended the second webinar, and 32% of the people who attended the first and second webinars attended the third webinar. How many people attended all three webinars?
whyCorrect: Each percentage is taken of the group named just before it, not of the original 1,250. First to second: 0.68(1,250) = 850 people attended both the first and second. The 32% is then applied to that group of 850, not to 1,250: 0.32(850) = 272. The trap is multiplying 1,250 by 32% (which gives 400) or by 68% + 32% = 100%.

stem: Data set A consists of 18 different values that have a minimum of 12, a maximum of 80, a mean of 46 and a standard deviation of 17. The values 12 and 80 are removed from the set to create data set B, which consists of 16 different values. Which of the following statements is true?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The mean of data set B is greater than 46.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The mean of data set B is less than 46.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The standard deviation of data set B is greater than 17.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The standard deviation of data set B is less than 17.

whyCorrect: Check the mean first. The two removed values average \(\frac{12+80}{2}=46\), exactly the mean of A, so removing them leaves the mean untouched: the total was 18(46) = 828, and 828 − 92 = 736, with 736 ÷ 16 = 46. That kills both mean options. For the spread, 12 and 80 are each 34 away from the mean, further than any other value in the set can be, so deleting them removes the two largest deviations while the mean stays put - the spread must shrink. Numerically, \(\sum d^{2}=18(17^{2})=5{,}202\), minus \(2(34^{2})=2{,}312\), leaves 2,890 over 16 values, a standard deviation of about 13.4.

whyWrong.A: The mean does not move at all. Removing values changes the mean only when their average differs from the set's mean, and here 12 and 80 average to exactly 46.
whyWrong.B: Same reason as A - the mean stays at 46, so it is neither greater nor less.
whyWrong.C: Standard deviation measures spread about the mean. Taking away the minimum and the maximum, the two points furthest from the mean, always reduces the spread when the mean is unchanged.

stem: For the positive quantities h, j, and k, 94% of h is equivalent to 47% of j, and j is equivalent to 30% of k. What percentage of k is h? (Disregard the % sign when entering your answer. For example, if your answer is 39%, enter 39).
whyCorrect: Write each statement as an equation. \(0.94h=0.47j\), and since 0.94 is exactly twice 0.47, this says \(j=2h\). The second statement is \(j=0.30k\). Substituting, \(2h=0.30k\), so \(h=0.15k\) - h is 15% of k. Notice the first relation makes j the larger quantity, which is the step people reverse.

stem: A set of five consecutive even integers is ordered from least to greatest. The sum of the first and fourth even integers is 5,860% more than the quotient of the fifth even integer and 30. The first even integer is p% less than the fifth even integer, where p is a constant. What is the value of p?
whyCorrect: Call the integers \(n, n+2, n+4, n+6, n+8\). The first and fourth sum to \(2n+6\), and the quotient of the fifth and 30 is \(\frac{n+8}{30}\). "5,860% more than" means 59.6 times as much, not 58.6 times: \(2n+6=59.6\cdot\frac{n+8}{30}\). Multiplying by 30 gives \(60n+180=59.6n+476.8\), so \(0.4n=296.8\) and n = 742, making the fifth integer 750. Check: 742 + 748 = 1,490 and \(59.6\times 25=1{,}490\). Finally, \(p=\frac{750-742}{750}\times 100=\frac{800}{750}=\frac{16}{15}\), about 1.07.
note: The answer is 16/15, roughly 1.0667 - an unusually small and untidy value for a grid-in, though it is exactly what the stated numbers give.

The table shows the distribution of all stars within 12 light-years of Earth by total energy output per second, or luminosity.

Which of the following could be the median luminosity of all the stars within 12 light-years of Earth?
whyCorrect: You cannot read the median off a distribution without counting, so add the frequencies: 1 + 3 + 6 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 31 stars. With 31 values the median is the 16th when they are ordered, so count up from the dimmest end: the 9 stars below 0.001 take positions 1 to 9, and the 7 stars in 0.001 to 0.01 take positions 10 to 16. The 16th star therefore lies in the 0.001 to 0.01 band, and the only choice inside that band is 0.0063.

whyWrong.A: 0.18 falls in the 0.1 to 1 band, which holds positions 22 to 27 - far above the middle.
whyWrong.B: 0.052 falls in the 0.01 to 0.1 band, positions 17 to 21. Close to the middle, but the 16th value has not reached that band yet.
whyWrong.D: 0.0003 falls in the below-0.001 band, positions 1 to 9. That is the bottom third of the list, not the middle.

note: The book prints this as a horizontal bar graph with the count written inside each bar; converted to an equivalent table, so the values are exact.

The table summarizes two data sets, X and Y. Each data set consists of 25 whole numbers. Each row gives the frequency of whole numbers greater than or equal to the first bound and less than the second.

What is the largest possible difference between the median of data set Y and the mean of data set X?
whyCorrect: To make the difference as large as possible, push Y's median as high as it can go and X's mean as low as it can go. Y has 25 values so its median is the 13th; counting up, 4 values sit in 80-84 and 6 in 85-89, so positions 11 through 16 fall in the 90-94 interval and the 13th value can be at most 94. For X's mean, put every value at the bottom of its interval: nine 70s, six 75s, six 80s and four 85s sum to 630 + 450 + 480 + 340 = 1,900, a mean of \(\frac{1900}{25}=76\). The largest possible difference is 94 − 76 = 18.
