stem: Data set A consists of 20 different values that have a minimum of 22, a maximum of 86, a mean of 54, and a standard deviation of 15. The values 22 and 86 are removed from the set to create data set B, which consists of 18 different values. Which of the following statements is true?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The mean of data set B is greater than 54.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The mean of data set B is less than 54.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The standard deviation of data set B is greater than 15.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The standard deviation of data set B is less than 15.

whyCorrect: Check the mean first: the two removed values average \(\frac{22+86}{2}=54\), which is exactly the mean of A, so removing them leaves the mean at 54. (Total 20(54) = 1,080, minus 108, is 972, and 972 ÷ 18 = 54.) That rules out both mean statements. For the spread, 22 and 86 are each 32 from the mean - further than any other value can be - so deleting them removes the two largest deviations while the mean stays put, and the standard deviation must fall.

whyWrong.A: The mean does not move. Removing values shifts the mean only when their average differs from the set's mean, and here it does not.
whyWrong.B: Same reason as A - the mean stays exactly 54.
whyWrong.C: Standard deviation measures spread about the mean. Deleting the minimum and the maximum, the two points furthest from an unchanged mean, always reduces it.

note: Parsed upstream as free response, but the book prints four lettered choices; recorded here as multiple choice. Same item structure as Problem Solving #14 on page 77 with different numbers.

stem: A survey was conducted in Arlington to estimate the percent of adult residents who support the addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in their town. Based on the survey, it is estimated that 51% of all adult residents of Arlington support the addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in their town, with an associated margin of error of 7%. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about all adult residents of Arlington?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in the town is supported by more than 58% of all adult residents of Arlington.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Arlington who support the addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in their town are between 44% and 58%.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Arlington who support the addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in their town are either less than 44% or more than 58%.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in the town is supported by exactly 44% of all adult residents of Arlington.

whyCorrect: A margin of error turns a single estimate into an interval of plausible values for the whole population: the estimate plus or minus the margin. Here that is 51% − 7% to 51% + 7%, or 44% to 58%. The correct conclusion states that interval and calls the values inside it plausible - it does not claim a single exact figure or rule out the estimate.

whyWrong.A: 58% is the top of the interval, not a floor. The survey supports values as low as 44%, so it cannot say support exceeds 58%.
whyWrong.C: This has the interval inside out. The plausible values are the ones inside 44% to 58%, not outside it.
whyWrong.D: A margin of error exists precisely because the exact population percentage is unknown. Naming one exact value, and the endpoint of the interval at that, contradicts the whole idea.

stem: To determine if age and gender are related to pet ownership at his school, Mark selected a random sample of 50 male 14- to 15-year-old students from the school and a random sample of 60 female 17- to 18-year-old students from the school. For each student, he recorded the student's age, gender, and whether the student owned a pet. Which of the following provides the best explanation for why Mark cannot draw a valid conclusion from this study?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The sample sizes are too small.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The two samples are not of equal size.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Mark will be unable to tell whether a difference in pet ownership is related to age because the two age groups are too close in age.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Mark will be unable to tell whether a difference in pet ownership is related to gender because of the difference in age. Similarly, he will be unable to tell whether a difference in pet ownership is related to age.

whyCorrect: Every male in the study is 14-15 and every female is 17-18, so gender and age change together across the two groups. When two variables move in lockstep like this they are confounded: any difference in pet ownership could be caused by either one, and no analysis of these data can separate them.

whyWrong.A: 50 and 60 are perfectly workable sample sizes; the study fails no matter how many students are added, because the design itself ties gender to age.
whyWrong.B: Comparison groups do not have to be the same size. Unequal sizes affect precision slightly, not the validity of the conclusion.
whyWrong.C: 14-15 and 17-18 are distinct age bands, not "too close." And the problem is not the size of the age gap — it is that the age gap coincides exactly with the gender split.

stem: A development company is advertising that the mean area of the apartments in a new complex is 1,450 square feet. The complex consists of 10 buildings with a total of 1,000 apartments. A sample of 50 apartments will be selected from the complex to test the company's statement about the mean apartment area. Which of the following is an unbiased sampling method?

choices.label: B
choices.content: Select the first 50 apartments that are occupied.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Select at random 5 top-floor apartments from each of the buildings.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Select at random 50 apartments from all the apartments in the 10 buildings.

whyCorrect: A sample is unbiased when every apartment in the complex has the same chance of being chosen. Only D draws at random from all 1,000 apartments; every other method restricts the pool first, so whole categories of apartment can never appear.

whyWrong.A: Build order is not random — the first-built apartments may be a particular size or in particular buildings, and later ones can never be selected.
whyWrong.B: Occupancy is chosen by tenants, and cheaper or smaller units tend to fill first. That preference, not chance, decides the sample.
whyWrong.C: Top-floor apartments are systematically different (often penthouses or larger units), and no other floor can be selected at all. Randomizing within a biased pool does not remove the bias.

stem: For which of the following sets of 9 data points is the median less than the mean?
whyCorrect: Median below mean means the data are pulled to the right by a few high values, so look for the plot with its bulk on the left and a tail stretching right. Set A has four dots at 1, two at 2 and one each at 3, 4 and 5: the fifth value in order is 2, while the mean is \(\frac{4(1)+2(2)+3+4+5}{9}=\frac{20}{9}\approx 2.22\). Median 2 is less than mean 2.22. In set B the median is 4 against a mean of about 3.44, in set C the plot is symmetric so median and mean are both 3, and in set D the median is 4 against a mean of about 3.78 - all three have the median at or above the mean.

whyWrong.B: Set B is left-skewed (1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5): median 4, mean \(\frac{31}{9}\approx 3.44\), so the median is greater than the mean.
whyWrong.C: Set C (1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5) is symmetric about 3, so the median equals the mean rather than falling below it.
whyWrong.D: Set D (1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5) is left-skewed: median 4, mean \(\frac{34}{9}\approx 3.78\).

It is a reprint of Problem Solving #63 on page 87, where the plots do appear. Dot counts from that printing, each set totalling 9 points on a number line labelled 1 to 5 - A: 4, 2, 1, 1, 1; B: 1, 1, 2, 3, 2; C: 1, 2, 3, 2, 1; D: 1, 1, 1, 2, 4. The answer recorded is derived from those. stem:
Two data sets each containing 20 integers are summarized in the table. Each row gives the frequency of integers greater than or equal to the first bound and less than the second.
IntegerFrequency in Data Set AFrequency in Data Set B
30 to less than 4008
40 to less than 5044
50 to less than 6085
60 to less than 7083
The mean of Data Set A is equal to a. The mean of Data Set B is equal to b. What is the smallest possible value of \(\frac{b}{a}\)?
whyCorrect: A fraction is smallest when its numerator is as small as possible and its denominator as large as possible, so make b minimal and a maximal. For b, put every integer at the bottom of its interval: 8(30) + 4(40) + 5(50) + 3(60) = 830, so \(b_{\min}=\frac{830}{20}=41.5\). For a, push every integer to the top of its interval - and because the intervals exclude their upper bound and the values are integers, the largest allowed are 49, 59 and 69, not 50, 60 and 70. That gives 4(49) + 8(59) + 8(69) = 1,220, so \(a_{\max}=\frac{1220}{20}=61\). The smallest ratio is \(\frac{41.5}{61}=\frac{83}{122}\approx 0.680\).
note: The book prints two histograms with bin width 10 over 30 to 70; bar heights sit on gridlines, so the equivalent frequency table is exact. Two things about the printed stem: its description of the intervals is garbled (it says the first interval is 40 to 50 and the second is 30 to 40, running backwards), and the exact answer 83/122 = 0.6803... is not a tidy grid-in value; on a real test it would be entered as .680. Worth a human check.

stem: Scientists examined water samples from different water springs. For these samples, the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in a closed system (limited carbon dioxide supply) had a minimum of 0.014 atmosphere (atm) and a maximum of 0.180 atm. The partial pressure of carbon dioxide in an open system (unlimited carbon dioxide supply) had a minimum of 0.00049 atm and a maximum of 0.05900 atm. Which statement best compares the range of the partial pressure of carbon dioxide for closed systems and open systems?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The range for closed systems is less than the range for open systems.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The range for closed systems is greater than the range for open systems.

choices.label: D
choices.content: There is not enough information to compare the ranges.

whyCorrect: The range of a data set is maximum minus minimum, and both a maximum and a minimum are given for each system, so you have everything you need. Closed: 0.180 − 0.014 = 0.166 atm. Open: 0.05900 − 0.00049 = 0.05851 atm. 0.166 is bigger than 0.0585, so the closed-system range is greater.

whyWrong.A: This reverses the comparison. The open-system numbers have more decimal places, which makes them look more precise, but 0.05851 is still much smaller than 0.166.
whyWrong.C: The two differences are not equal — 0.166 against 0.05851, almost three times apart.
whyWrong.D: A range needs only the maximum and the minimum, and both are stated for both systems. You never need the individual data values.

stem:
The list gives the mass, in grams, of 5 ruffed lemurs:

3,910; 3,910; 3,130; 3,950; 3,150

What is the mean mass, in grams, of these 5 ruffed lemurs?
whyCorrect: Mean is the total divided by how many values there are. Add the five masses: 3,910 + 3,910 + 3,130 + 3,950 + 3,150 = 18,050. Divide by 5 to get 3,610 grams. Repeating a value (3,910 appears twice) does not mean you count it once — every listed value goes into both the sum and the count.

whyCorrect: Write the data out: 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 7, 8. With 9 values the median is the 5th, which is 3. The mean is 33 ÷ 9 ≈ 3.67. The two high values 7 and 8 sit far to the right of the bunched-up values, and the mean is pulled toward them while the median is not, so the mean ends up larger.

whyWrong.A: They would be equal only for a symmetric data set. This one has a long tail on the right and nothing balancing it on the left.

The temperature reading from the probe not recorded in the table was 73.27 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). Which statement correctly compares the mean temperature reading of the 49 probes recorded in the table to the mean temperature reading of all 50 probes?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The mean temperature reading of the 49 probes is greater than the mean temperature reading of all 50 probes.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The mean temperature reading of the 49 probes is less than the mean temperature reading of all 50 probes.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.content: There is not enough information to compare the means.

whyCorrect: You do not have to compute either mean. Every one of the 49 recorded readings lies between 79.97 and 80.03, so their mean is somewhere in that band, close to 80. The missing 50th reading, 73.27, is far below that band. Adding a value below the current mean always drags the mean down, so the 50-probe mean is smaller — equivalently, the 49-probe mean is greater.

whyWrong.B: This is the direction you get if you think adding one more probe raises the average. A new value moves the mean toward itself, and 73.27 is below, not above.
whyWrong.C: The mean only stays put when the added value equals the existing mean. 73.27 is nearly 7 degrees below it.
whyWrong.D: You have the full list of 49 readings and the value of the 50th, which is all the mean of each group requires.

stem: Ari examined a set of 86 plants. The lightest plant has a mass of 2.8 kilograms (kg) and the heaviest plant has a mass of 6.2 kg. Chihiro examined the same set of 86 plants and also an additional plant with a mass of 11.7 kg. Which of the following must be true about the set of plants that Ari examined and the set of plants that Chihiro examined?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The standard deviation of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Ari examined is greater than the standard deviation of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Chihiro examined.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The range of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Ari examined is greater than the range of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Chihiro examined.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The median of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Ari examined is less than the median of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Chihiro examined.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The mean of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Ari examined is less than the mean of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Chihiro examined.

whyCorrect: Every one of Ari's 86 masses is at most 6.2 kg, so Ari's mean is at most 6.2. Chihiro's set is Ari's set plus a single 11.7 kg plant, and adding a value that sits above the current mean always pulls the mean up. That argument works no matter what the 86 individual masses are, which is what "must be true" demands.

whyWrong.A: Backwards. The extra 11.7 kg plant sits far outside the 2.8–6.2 kg spread of the rest, so it increases the spread; Chihiro's standard deviation is the larger one.
whyWrong.B: Also backwards. Ari's range is 6.2 − 2.8 = 3.4 kg; Chihiro's is 11.7 − 2.8 = 8.9 kg.
whyWrong.C: The median can only move up or stay put, and "must be true" rules this out because it can stay put. Ari's median is the average of the 43rd and 44th masses; Chihiro's is the 44th. If those two masses are equal — entirely possible — the two medians are the same, so "less than" is not guaranteed.

II. 28

whyCorrect: Compare B with A term by term: 9, 12, 13, 16, 22 are exactly 8, 11, 12, 15, 21 each increased by 1. So if \(h = 28\), data set B is data set A shifted up by 1, and shifting every value by the same amount leaves the standard deviation unchanged — equal, not greater, so II fails. Making \(h\) larger than 28 stretches B's spread further, so III fails too. Only \(h = 23\) pulls the last value in toward the rest, making B's spread smaller than A's.

whyWrong.B: \(h = 28\) makes B a copy of A shifted up 1 unit. A shift moves the mean but not the spread, so the two standard deviations are equal and A's is not greater.
whyWrong.C: \(h = 29\) puts the top value even further from B's mean than 27 is from A's, so B's standard deviation comes out larger than A's, the opposite of what is required.
whyWrong.D: Both of these values make B at least as spread out as A, so neither satisfies the condition.

stem: An environmental scientist is investigating the volatility of 175 organic compounds by finding the boiling point of each compound. The mean boiling point of all 175 compounds is 167 degrees Celsius. The scientist classifies each of these compounds as either semivolatile or volatile. Of the 175 compounds, 50 compounds were classified as semivolatile, and these 50 compounds have a mean boiling point of 327 degrees Celsius. The remaining 125 compounds were classified as volatile. What is the mean boiling point, in degrees Celsius, of the 125 compounds classified as volatile compounds?
whyCorrect: Means do not combine by averaging — work with totals. The 175 compounds have a combined boiling point total of 175 × 167 = 29,225. The 50 semivolatile ones account for 50 × 327 = 16,350. So the 125 volatile compounds total 29,225 − 16,350 = 12,875, and their mean is 12,875 ÷ 125 = 103 degrees Celsius.

Data set \(F\) consists of 55 integers, where the value of each integer is between 150 and 260. Data set \(G\) consists of the same 55 integers in \(F\) as well as the integer 10. Which of the following must be less for data set \(G\) than for data set \(F\)?

I. The mean
II. The median
whyCorrect: The mean must fall, because 10 is below every value in \(F\) and so certainly below \(F\)'s mean; adding a value below the mean always pulls it down. The median need not fall. \(F\) has 55 values, so its median is the 28th; \(G\) has 56, so its median is the average of \(G\)'s 28th and 29th, which are \(F\)'s 27th and 28th. If \(F\)'s 27th and 28th values happen to be equal — nothing forbids it, since the integers may repeat — that average equals \(F\)'s median, so it is not less. "Must be less" fails for II.

whyWrong.B: The median is the one that can stay the same. The mean is the one that is forced down.
whyWrong.C: I is right but II is not guaranteed — repeated values around the middle position let the median stay exactly where it was.
whyWrong.D: The mean genuinely must decrease: 10 is far below every one of the 55 values, so it cannot leave the average unchanged or raise it.

whyCorrect: Add all five masses and divide by 5. The total is 3,810 + 3,810 + 3,030 + 3,850 + 3,050 = 17,550, and 17,550 ÷ 5 = 3,510 grams. A quick shortcut: every value is 3,000 plus something, so average the leftovers 810, 810, 30, 850, 50 — that is 2,550 ÷ 5 = 510 — and add 3,000.

stem: A survey of the daily commuting times, in minutes, of seven different Chicago-based employees at a certain company yielded a data set consisting of the values 31, 13, 44, 32, 53, 22, and 44. If the means of the two data sets are equal, what is the value of \(x\)?
whyCorrect: Both data sets have 7 values, so equal means is the same as equal totals — you never have to divide. The Chicago total is 31 + 13 + 44 + 32 + 53 + 22 + 44 = 239. The six known San Francisco values total 46 + 31 + 19 + 33 + 48 + 38 = 215. So \(x = 239 - 215 = 24\).

A total of 90 students were selected at random from all students in grades 6, 7, and 8 in a large school district in the US. The selected students were asked to report their level of school spirit as either low, medium, or high. The table summarizes the distribution of the selected students by grade.
Grade678
Number of students302634
If the results of the study suggest a relationship between the self-reported level of school spirit and the amount of time spent on extracurricular activities by students in grades 6, 7, and 8, which of the following aspects of the study will prevent the results from being generalized to all students in grades 6, 7, and 8 in the US?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The selected students are not all from the same school.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The number of selected students is too small.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The number of selected students from each grade is different.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The students were not selected at random from all students in grades 6, 7, and 8.

whyCorrect: A result generalizes only to the population the sample was randomly drawn from. Here the random draw was made inside one large school district, so the population it represents is that district — not every 6th, 7th and 8th grader in the US. Students outside the district had no chance of being selected, and no sample size fixes that.

whyWrong.A: Drawing from several schools makes a sample broader, not narrower. It is a strength, not the flaw.
whyWrong.B: 90 is a workable sample size, and in any case sample size affects the margin of error, not which population the result applies to.
whyWrong.C: The grade counts are close to even, and unequal group sizes within a random sample are normal; they do not block generalization.

stem: A machine fills bags with approximately 10 ounces of cranberries. To test the accuracy of the filling process, 148 bags of cranberries were selected at random and weighed. Based on the sample, it is estimated that the average weight of all bags of cranberries filled by the machine in an 8-hour period is 9.89 ounces, with an associated margin of error of 0.14 ounce. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this estimate?

choices.label: A
choices.content: Plausible values for the average weight of all bags of cranberries filled by the machine are between 9.75 ounces and 10.03 ounces.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Plausible values for the average weight of all bags of cranberries filled by the machine are less than 9.75 ounces or greater than 10.03 ounces.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The average weight of all bags of cranberries filled by the machine is greater than 9.99 ounces.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The average weight of all bags of cranberries filled by the machine is less than 9.99 ounces.

whyCorrect: A margin of error marks off an interval on either side of the estimate, and the values inside that interval are the plausible ones. Here that is 9.89 − 0.14 = 9.75 up to 9.89 + 0.14 = 10.03 ounces.

whyWrong.B: This has the interval inside out. Values further than 0.14 from the estimate are the implausible ones.
whyWrong.C: 9.99 is 9.89 + 0.10, which is not either endpoint, and a margin of error never lets you claim the true average lies on one side of a single number.
whyWrong.D: Same problem: the estimate supports a two-sided interval, not a one-sided claim, and 9.99 is not an endpoint of it.

stem: A town manager selected 2 random samples of residents in the town to estimate the percentage of all residents that planned to vote in favor of a new business in the downtown area. Based on the first sample, he estimated that 75% of the residents in town planned to vote in favor, with an associated margin of error of 8.3%. Based on the second sample, he estimated that 83% of the residents in the town planned to vote in favor, with an associated margin of error of 6.7%. Assuming the margins of error were calculated the same way, which of the following best explains why the first sample obtained a larger margin of error than the second sample?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The first sample contained fewer residents than the second sample.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The first sample contained more residents than the second sample.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The first sample contained a lower percentage of residents that planned to vote in favor of a new business in the downtown area.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The first sample contained a higher percentage of residents that planned to vote in favor of a new business in the downtown area.

whyCorrect: Margin of error shrinks as the sample gets bigger — more people surveyed means a more precise estimate. The first sample's margin of error is the larger one (8.3% against 6.7%), so the first sample must have been the smaller one.

whyWrong.B: This has the relationship backwards. A larger sample produces a smaller margin of error, not a larger one.
whyWrong.C: The estimated percentage itself is not what drives the size of the margin of error here; the question says the margins were calculated the same way, leaving sample size as the explanation.
whyWrong.D: Same issue, and it is also false as stated — the first sample's percentage was 75%, lower than the second sample's 83%.

stem: A district board in a certain state is proposing a change to the time school starts to all high schools in the district. A sample of 353 high school students were selected from all high school students in the district. The selected students were asked if they approved of the proposed change, and 300 students responded that they did not approve. Which of the following is the largest population that the results of the survey can be generalized?

choices.label: A
choices.content: All high school students in the district

choices.label: C
choices.content: The 300 students that responded that they did not approve of the proposed change

choices.label: D
choices.content: All high school students in the state

whyCorrect: The results generalize to the group the sample was drawn from, and no further. The 353 students were selected from all high school students in the district, so that district-wide group is the largest population the survey speaks for.

whyWrong.B: The whole point of sampling is to say something about a group larger than the sample itself, so this is not the largest population.
whyWrong.C: This is a subset of the sample, smaller still, and it is defined by the answer given — not a population you would generalize to at all.
whyWrong.D: Students in other districts had no chance of being selected, so the survey says nothing about the state as a whole.

stem: A company that produces only one type of item wants to estimate the percent of the items produced in a typical week that are defective. A random sample of 400 of the items produced in a certain week were tested. Based on the sample, it is estimated that 8.5% of all items produced by the company in this week were defective, with an associated margin of error of 2.73%. Based on the estimate and associated margin of error, which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about all items produced by the company during this week?

choices.label: B
choices.content: It is plausible that between 5.77% and 11.23% of the items are defective.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It is plausible that more than 11.23% of the items are defective.

whyCorrect: The estimate plus and minus the margin of error gives the interval of plausible values: 8.5 − 2.73 = 5.77% and 8.5 + 2.73 = 11.23%. The conclusion has to be stated as a plausible range, because a sample can only narrow the possibilities, never pin down the true percent.

whyWrong.A: 2.73% is the margin of error, the width on either side of the estimate — not a defect rate.
whyWrong.C: 8.5% is the sample's estimate. Reporting it as the exact figure for all items throws away the margin of error, which exists precisely because the sample may miss.
whyWrong.D: 11.23% is the top of the plausible range, so values above it are the implausible ones.

stem: To estimate the proportion of a population that has a certain characteristic, a random sample was selected from the population. Based on the sample, it is estimated that the proportion of the population that has the characteristic is 0.2, with an associated margin of error of 0.08. Based on this estimate and margin of error, which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about the proportion of the population that has the characteristic?

choices.label: A
choices.content: It is plausible that the proportion is between 0.12 and 0.28.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It is plausible that the proportion is less than 0.12.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It is plausible that the proportion is greater than 0.28.

whyCorrect: Subtract and add the margin of error to the estimate: 0.2 − 0.08 = 0.12 and 0.2 + 0.08 = 0.28. Everything inside that interval is plausible; everything outside it is not supported by the sample.

whyWrong.B: 0.12 is the bottom end of the plausible interval, so proportions below it are the ones the estimate argues against.
whyWrong.C: 0.2 is a sample estimate, not a measurement of the whole population. If it were exact there would be no reason to report a margin of error.
whyWrong.D: 0.28 is the top end of the interval, so values above it fall outside the plausible range.

stem: The manager of a gym selected a sample of 139 members at random to estimate the percentage of the gym's members that would continue to pay for a membership if the price increased. From the survey, the manager estimates that 82% of the gym's members would continue to pay for membership if the price increased, with an associated margin of error of 6.39%. If the survey is repeated with a random sample of 278 members and the results are calculated in the same way, which of the following will be the most likely effect of using the larger random sample compared to the smaller random sample?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The margin of error will be lower

choices.label: B
choices.content: The margin of error will be higher

choices.label: C
choices.content: The estimate of the percentage of the gym's members that would continue to pay for a membership if the price increased will be lower

choices.label: D
choices.content: The estimate of the percentage of the gym's members that would continue to pay for a membership if the price increased will be higher

whyCorrect: Surveying more people gives a more precise estimate, and precision is exactly what the margin of error measures. Doubling the sample from 139 to 278 therefore shrinks the margin of error. Note the direction: bigger sample, smaller margin.

whyWrong.B: This is the relationship inverted. Small samples are the unreliable ones, so they carry the larger margins of error.
whyWrong.C: A larger sample changes how precise the estimate is, not which way it points. There is no reason for the percentage itself to fall.
whyWrong.D: Same reason — the estimate could come out slightly higher or slightly lower, so neither direction is "most likely". Only the margin of error has a predictable direction.

stem: A machine fills bags with approximately 29 ounces of walnuts. To test the accuracy of the filling process, 169 bags of walnuts were selected at random and weighed. Based on the sample, it is estimated that the average weight of all bags of walnuts filled by the machine in an 8-hour period is 28.88 ounces, with an associated margin of error of 0.13 ounce. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this estimate?

choices.label: A
choices.content: Plausible values for the average weight of all bags of walnuts filled by the machine are between 28.75 ounces and 29.01 ounces.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Plausible values for the average weight of all bags of walnuts filled by the machine are less than 28.75 ounces or greater than 29.01 ounces.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The average weight of all bags of walnuts filled by the machine is less than 28.99 ounces.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The average weight of all bags of walnuts filled by the machine is greater than 28.99 ounces.

whyCorrect: Take the estimate and step the margin of error off in both directions: 28.88 − 0.13 = 28.75 and 28.88 + 0.13 = 29.01. Those two numbers bracket the plausible values for the true average.

whyWrong.B: This names the values outside the interval, which are the ones the estimate argues against.
whyWrong.C: 28.99 is not an endpoint of anything here, and a margin of error supports a two-sided interval rather than a one-sided claim.
whyWrong.D: Same problem in the other direction, and 28.99 does not come from 28.88 and 0.13 at all.

note: Same template as ma2 Research organizing #2 (cranberries, 9.89 ± 0.14); do not place both in one test.

stem: A researcher is designing a study to investigate the average number of hours a student at a high school spends reading per day. The researcher will report the average number of hours a student at the high school spends reading with an associated margin of error. The researcher is considering using a random sample of either 105 or 210 students from the high school. Which of the following could be the most likely effect of using the larger random sample compared to the smaller random sample?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The reported margin of error would be lower.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The reported margin of error would be higher.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The reported average number of hours would be lower.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The reported average number of hours would be higher.

whyCorrect: A bigger sample estimates the population more precisely, and margin of error is the measure of that imprecision, so going from 105 students to 210 lowers it. Nothing about sample size predicts which way the average itself will come out.

whyWrong.B: Backwards — the smaller sample is the one with the larger margin of error.
whyWrong.C: The average could land above or below the smaller sample's figure. Sample size controls precision, not direction.
whyWrong.D: Same reason: no direction of change in the average is more likely than the other.

note: Same template as ma2 Research organizing #7 (gym members, 139 vs 278); do not place both in one test.

stem: A survey was conducted in Franklin to estimate the number of adult residents who supported the addition of a parking garage in their town. Based on the survey, it is estimated that 77% of all adult residents of Franklin support the addition of a parking garage in their town, with an associated margin of error of 5%. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about all adult residents of Franklin?

choices.label: A
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Franklin who support the addition of a parking garage in their town are between 72% and 82%

choices.label: B
choices.content: The addition of a parking garage in the town is supported by exactly 72% of all adult residents of Franklin

choices.label: C
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Franklin who support the addition of a parking garage in their town are either less than 72% or more than 82%

choices.label: D
choices.content: The addition of a parking garage in the town is supported by more than 82% of all adult residents of Franklin

whyCorrect: Subtract and add the margin of error: 77 − 5 = 72 and 77 + 5 = 82. The survey supports the claim that the true percentage lies somewhere in that band, and says nothing more precise than that.

whyWrong.B: 72% is the low end of the interval, not a value the survey singles out, and a sample never establishes an exact population percentage.
whyWrong.C: This names everything outside the interval — the values the survey argues against, not for.
whyWrong.D: 82% is the top of the interval, so support above it is what the estimate rules out as unlikely.

stem: A research manager selected 2 random samples of ovens of a certain type to estimate the average amount of time this type of oven takes to preheat to 325 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The research manager recorded the amount of time, in minutes, each oven takes to preheat to 325°F. Based on the first sample, the research manager estimated that this type of oven takes an average of 15.2 minutes to preheat to 325°F, with an associated margin of error of 1 minute. Based on the second sample, the research manager estimated that this type of oven takes an average of 15.4 minutes to preheat to 325°F, with an associated margin of error of 2.2 minutes. Assuming the margins of error were calculated the same way, which of the following best explains why the first sample obtained a smaller margin of error than the second sample?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The first sample contained more ovens than the second sample.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The first sample contained fewer ovens than the second sample.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The first sample took more time on average to preheat to 325°F than the second sample.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The first sample took less time on average to preheat to 325°F than the second sample.

whyCorrect: With the margins of error calculated the same way, the one that comes out smaller belongs to the larger sample — more data means a more precise estimate. The first sample's margin is 1 minute against the second's 2.2 minutes, so the first sample must have had more ovens in it.

whyWrong.B: This inverts the rule. Fewer ovens would have produced the larger margin of error.
whyWrong.C: The size of the estimated average does not set the margin of error, and it is false here anyway — the first sample's average, 15.2, is the smaller of the two.
whyWrong.D: It is true that 15.2 is less than 15.4, but that difference is not what makes a margin of error small. Only the sample size explains it.

note: Same template as ma2 Research organizing #3 (town manager, 8.3% vs 6.7%); do not place both in one test.

stem: A survey was conducted in Madison to estimate the percent of adult residents who support the addition of streetlights at every corner in their town. Based on the survey, it is estimated that 40% of all adult residents of Madison support the addition of streetlights at every corner in their town, with an associated margin of error of 6%. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about all adult residents of Madison?

choices.label: A
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Madison who support the addition of streetlights at every corner in their town are between 34% and 46%.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The addition of streetlights at every corner in the town is supported by exactly 34% of all adult residents of Madison.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Madison who support the addition of streetlights at every corner in their town are either less than 34% or more than 46%.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The addition of streetlights at every corner in the town is supported by more than 46% of all adult residents of Madison.

whyCorrect: Step the margin of error off either side of the estimate: 40 − 6 = 34 and 40 + 6 = 46. Those two percentages bound the plausible values for the true level of support.

whyWrong.B: 34% is simply the lower endpoint. An interval estimate never asserts an exact population value.
whyWrong.C: These are the values outside the interval, which the survey makes less plausible, not more.
whyWrong.D: 46% is the upper endpoint, so figures above it lie outside what the survey supports.

note: Same template as ma2 Research organizing #10 (Franklin, 77% ± 5%); do not place both in one test.

stem: A group of 40 employees selected at random from all the employees at a company were surveyed about the number of books they read last year. From the data collected, it was estimated that the mean number of books employees at the company read last year is 6.8, with an associated margin of error of 1.1. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.content: It is plausible that the actual mean number of books employees at the company read last year is less than 5.7.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It is plausible that the actual mean number of books employees at the company read last year is between 5.7 and 7.9.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It is plausible that every employee at the company read between 6.8 and 10.1 books last year.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It is plausible that the actual mean number of books employees at the company read last year is greater than 7.9.

whyCorrect: The interval runs from 6.8 − 1.1 = 5.7 to 6.8 + 1.1 = 7.9, and it is a statement about the mean for all employees. Watch that last part: the margin of error bounds the average, not the individual readers.

whyWrong.A: 5.7 is the bottom of the plausible interval, so means below it are the ones the estimate makes unlikely.
whyWrong.C: Two errors at once: the interval describes the company-wide mean, not what each employee did, and 6.8 to 10.1 is not the interval the numbers give.
whyWrong.D: 7.9 is the top of the interval, so means above it fall outside the plausible range.

stem: In the figure, \(RT = TU\), the measure of angle \(VST\) is 23° and the measure of angle \(RVS\) is 44°. What is the value of \(x\)?
whyCorrect: Work in triangle \(USV\) first. Because \(T\) lies on segment \(US\), angle \(VST\) and angle \(VSU\) are the same angle, so the angle at \(S\) is 23°. Because \(U\), \(V\), \(R\) are collinear, angle \(UVS\) = 180° − 44° = 136°. That leaves angle \(SUV\) = 180 − 136 − 23 = 21°. Now use \(RT = TU\): triangle \(RTU\) is isosceles, so its base angles at \(U\) and \(R\) are both 21°, and \(x = 180 - 21 - 21 = 138\).
note: Needs the figure. Reading of the page image: U, V, R lie on one horizontal line in that order; S is above and right of R; segment US passes through T; segment TR runs from T down to R and crosses segment VS; x° marks the angle at T between ray TU and ray TR, inside triangle RTU. Labelled "Figure not drawn to scale" is not printed for this item.
imageAlt: Line drawing with U, V and R on one horizontal line and S above to the right; segment U S passes through T, segment T R and segment S V are drawn and cross, and the angle at T below T is labelled x degrees.

stem: A polygon has exactly 73 sides. If the measure of each of the 73 interior angles of this polygon is \((180p)^\circ\), what is the value of \(p\)?
whyCorrect: The interior angles of an \(n\)-sided polygon add to \((n-2)180^\circ\), so here they total \(71 \times 180\) degrees. All 73 angles are equal, so each one is \(\frac{71 \times 180}{73}\) degrees. Setting that equal to \(180p\) makes the 180 cancel: \(p = \frac{71}{73}\). Notice you never need to work out the angle in degrees.
note: Answer is the fraction 71/73 (about 0.9726); it is not an integer.

stem: Quadrilaterals \(PQRS\) and \(WXYZ\) are similar, where \(P\), \(Q\), and \(R\) correspond to \(W\), \(X\), and \(Y\), respectively. The measure of \(\angle S\) is 105°, \(PS = 25\), and \(WZ = 5\). What is the measure of \(\angle Z\)?
whyCorrect: Similar figures have equal corresponding angles; only the side lengths scale. Three correspondences are given, so the fourth vertices must match too: \(S\) corresponds to \(Z\). Therefore \(\angle Z = \angle S = 105^\circ\). The lengths 25 and 5 are there to tempt you into scaling the angle, which similarity never does.

whyWrong.A: 5 is the length \(WZ\), not an angle measure.
whyWrong.B: 21° is 105 ÷ 5, applying the side ratio to the angle. Angles are unchanged by a dilation, so they are never divided by the scale factor.
whyWrong.C: 75° is the supplement of 105°. Corresponding angles in similar figures are equal, not supplementary.

stem: Two lines intersect at exactly one point, forming two acute angles and two obtuse angles. The measure of one of these angles is \((9x - 190)^\circ\). Which of the following could NOT be the sum of the measures of any two of these angles?
whyCorrect: Call the given angle \(a = 9x - 190\). Two intersecting lines make only two distinct measures: \(a\) twice (vertical angles) and \(180 - a\) twice. So there are exactly three possible sums of two angles: \(2a = 18x - 380\), \(a + (180 - a) = 180\), and \(2(180 - a) = 360 - (18x - 380) = -18x + 740\). Choice A, \(-18x + 380\), matches none of these. The trap is that it looks like \(2a\) with the sign flipped, but flipping the sign of \(2a\) is not one of the sums.

whyWrong.B: This is the sum of the two angles that each measure \(180 - a\): \(360 - (18x - 380) = -18x + 740\).
whyWrong.C: This is \(2a\), the sum of the pair of vertical angles equal to the given one.
whyWrong.D: This is an angle plus its neighbour on a straight line, which always totals 180°.

stem: Quadrilaterals \(PQRS\) and \(WXYZ\) are similar, where \(P\), \(Q\), and \(R\) correspond to \(W\), \(X\), and \(Y\), respectively. The measure of \(\angle S\) is 135°, \(PS = 45\), and \(WZ = 9\). What is the measure of \(\angle Z\)?
whyCorrect: Similarity scales lengths but leaves angles alone. Three of the four correspondences are stated, so the remaining vertices pair up as well: \(S\) with \(Z\). Hence \(\angle Z = \angle S = 135^\circ\), and the side lengths 45 and 9 are irrelevant to the angle.

whyWrong.A: 5 is the scale factor between the two sides, 45 ÷ 9 — a ratio of lengths, not a number of degrees.
whyWrong.B: 27° is 135 ÷ 5, dividing the angle by the scale factor. Dilating a figure never changes an angle.
whyWrong.C: 45 is the length \(PS\) reused as an angle measure.

note: Same template as ma2 Lines&Angles #5 (105°, PS = 25, WZ = 5); do not place both in one test. The book prints "THe" for "The"; corrected.

stem: A polygon has exactly 83 sides. If the measure of each of the 83 interior angles of this polygon is \((180p)^\circ\), what is the value of \(p\)?
whyCorrect: The interior angles of an \(n\)-gon sum to \((n-2)180^\circ\), so all 83 angles together make \(81 \times 180\) degrees. Each equal angle is \(\frac{81 \times 180}{83}\), and setting that equal to \(180p\) cancels the 180, leaving \(p = \frac{81}{83}\).
note: Answer is the fraction 81/83 (about 0.9759); it is not an integer. Same template as ma2 Lines&Angles #3 (73 sides); do not place both in one test. The book prints "the measures of each of the 83 interior angles ... what value of p"; wording tidied.

stem: Quadrilateral \(P'Q'R'S'\) is similar to quadrilateral \(PQRS\), where \(P\), \(Q\), \(R\), and \(S\) correspond to \(P'\), \(Q'\), \(R'\), and \(S'\), respectively. The measure of angle \(P\) is 45°, the measure of angle \(Q\) is 70°, and the measure of angle \(R\) is 90°. The length of each side of \(P'Q'R'S'\) is 3 times the length of each corresponding side of \(PQRS\). What is the measure of angle \(P'\)?
whyCorrect: Enlarging a figure by a scale factor stretches every length but leaves every angle exactly as it was. \(P'\) corresponds to \(P\), so the measure of angle \(P'\) is the same 45°. The measures of angles \(Q\) and \(R\) and the scale factor 3 are all there to distract.

whyWrong.A: 15° is 45 ÷ 3, applying the scale factor to the angle. Similarity never scales angles.
whyWrong.C: 60° does not come from any correct step; it would need the angles to change, which similarity forbids.
whyWrong.D: 135° is 45 × 3, multiplying the angle by the scale factor — the same mistake as A in the opposite direction.

note: Third item in this book with the same similar-quadrilateral setup (see also Lines&Angles #5 and #9); do not place more than one in a test.

stem: In triangle \(PQR\), \(\overline{QR}\) is extended to point \(S\). The measure of \(\angle PQR\) is 142°, and the measure of \(\angle PRS\) is 166°. What is the measure of \(\angle QPR\)?
whyCorrect: Because \(\overline{QR}\) is extended to \(S\), the points \(Q\), \(R\), \(S\) lie on one line, so \(\angle PRQ\) and \(\angle PRS\) are supplementary: \(\angle PRQ = 180 - 166 = 14^\circ\). Now the three angles of triangle \(PQR\) add to 180°, so \(\angle QPR = 180 - 142 - 14 = 24^\circ\).

whyWrong.A: 14° is \(\angle PRQ\), the angle you find on the way, not the angle at \(P\).
whyWrong.B: 19° does not come from any correct step here.
whyWrong.D: 38° is 180 − 142, treating \(\angle PQR\) as if it had a supplement inside the triangle. Only the angle at \(R\) has a supplement in this figure, because only \(\overline{QR}\) is extended.

stem: In triangle PQR, the measure of angle P is \((3x + 5)^\circ\), the measure of angle Q is \((2x + 9)^\circ\), and the measure of angle R is \((4y + 5)^\circ\). If side QR is extended through point R to point S and the measure of angle PRS is \((x + y)^\circ\), what is the value of \(x + y\)?
whyCorrect: Angle PRS is the exterior angle at R, so it equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: \(x + y = (3x+5) + (2x+9) = 5x + 14\). It is also supplementary to angle R, so \((x+y) + (4y+5) = 180\). The first equation gives \(y = 4x + 14\); substituting into \(x + 5y = 175\) gives \(21x = 105\), so \(x = 5\) and \(y = 34\), and \(x + y = 39\). (Check: the angles are 20°, 19° and 141°, which sum to 180°.)

stem: In \(\triangle JKL\), the measures of both \(\angle J\) and \(\angle K\) are equal, and the measure of \(\angle L\) is 134°. What is the measure of \(\angle J\)?
whyCorrect: The three angles total 180°, so \(\angle J\) and \(\angle K\) together make 180 − 134 = 46°. They are equal, so each is 46 ÷ 2 = 23°.

whyWrong.B: 46° is the combined measure of both remaining angles. You still have to halve it.
whyWrong.C: 67° is 134 ÷ 2, halving the wrong angle.
whyWrong.D: 90° would make the triangle's angles total more than 180° on its own with \(\angle L\) already at 134°.

stem: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of these eight angles is \( (7x - 250)^{\circ} \) . The sum of the measures of four of the eight angles is \( k^{\circ} \) . Which of the following could NOT be equivalent to k, for all values of x?
whyCorrect: A transversal across two parallel lines makes only two distinct measures: four copies of an acute angle a and four of its supplement 180 - a. Take a = 7x - 250, so the obtuse measure is 430 - 7x. Any four of the eight angles sum to one of five values: 4a = 28x - 1,000; 3a + one obtuse = 14x - 320; two and two = 360; one acute and three obtuse = 1,040 - 14x; four obtuse = 1,720 - 28x. (Starting from the obtuse angle instead produces the same five.) Choices B, C and D are on that list; \( -14x + 1{,}540 \) is not — the matching entry is \( -14x + 1{,}040 \) .

whyWrong.B: 14x - 320 is the sum of three acute angles and one obtuse: 3(7x - 250) + (430 - 7x).
whyWrong.C: -28x + 1,720 is the sum of all four obtuse angles: 4(430 - 7x).
whyWrong.D: 360 is the sum of two acute and two obtuse angles, since each acute-obtuse pair adds to 180. It is a valid sum for every x.

stem: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of the acute angles is \((7x - 619)^\circ\). The sum of the measure of one of the acute and three of the obtuse angles is \((-14x + w)^\circ\). What is the value of \(w\)?
whyCorrect: Every obtuse angle here is the supplement of every acute one, so if the acute angle is \(a = 7x - 619\), each obtuse angle is \(180 - a\). One acute plus three obtuse is \(a + 3(180 - a) = 540 - 2a\). Substituting: \(540 - 2(7x - 619) = 540 - 14x + 1{,}238 = -14x + 1{,}778\). Matching this against \(-14x + w\) gives \(w = 1{,}778\).

stem:
In the figure shown, point T lies on segment SW, and segment TU is parallel to segment VW. The measure of angle V is 26°, and the measure of angle STU is 74°. What is the value of \( p - r \) ?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Treat SW as a transversal of the parallel segments TU and VW: angle STU and the angle at W open the same way on the same side, so they are corresponding angles and r = 74. Then look at trapezoid TUVW: UV is a transversal of the same two parallel segments, so the angles at U and V are same-side interior angles and add to 180, giving p = 180 - 26 = 154. Therefore p - r = 154 - 74 = 80.
note: Measured reading of the figure: S is at the top, W at the lower left with T on segment SW between them, U is to the right of T and V at the lower right, forming trapezoid TUVW with TU parallel to WV. The angle marked p is the interior angle at U, and r is the interior angle at W.
imageAlt: Line drawing of trapezoid T U V W with S on the extension of side W T above T; the angle at U is labelled p degrees and the angle at W is labelled r degrees.

stem: Triangles \(ABC\) and \(DEF\) are congruent, where \(A\) corresponds to \(D\), and \(B\) and \(E\) are right angles. The measure of angle \(A\) is 62°. What is the value of angle \(F\)?
whyCorrect: Track the correspondence: \(A\) matches \(D\) and \(B\) matches \(E\), so the remaining vertices match too — \(C\) with \(F\). Angle \(C\) is what is left in triangle \(ABC\) after the right angle and the 62° angle: \(180 - 90 - 62 = 28^\circ\). Congruence makes angle \(F\) equal to that, 28°.

whyWrong.B: 62° is angle \(D\), the partner of angle \(A\), not of angle \(F\).
whyWrong.C: 90° is angle \(E\), the right angle, which corresponds to \(B\).
whyWrong.D: 118° is 180 − 62, a supplement rather than the third angle of a right triangle.

stem: In triangle RST, the measure of angle R is 18 degrees and the measure of angle T is 72 degrees. Point L lies on \( \overline{RS} \) , point K lies on \( \overline{ST} \) , and \( \overline{LK} \) is parallel to \( \overline{RT} \) . What is the measure, in degrees, of angle SKL? (Disregard the degree symbol when entering your answer.)
whyCorrect: You do not need angle S at all. \( \overline{ST} \) crosses the two parallel segments \( \overline{LK} \) and \( \overline{RT} \) , so angle SKL at K and angle STR at T are corresponding angles and are equal. Angle STR is angle T, which is 72°. (The 18° at R is there to tempt you into solving for angle S = 90° first, which is not needed.)
note: Same template as Hard Book Geometry #5, with the angles given as numbers rather than expressions. Do not place both in one test.

stem: In the figure shown, point \(D\) lies on \(\overline{AB}\), point \(E\) lies on \(\overline{CB}\), and line segments \(AC\) and \(DE\) are parallel. The measure of angle \(ACB\) is 58°, and \(AB = 1.5DB\). What is the measure, in degrees, of angle \(DEB\)? (Disregard the degree symbol when entering your answer.)
whyCorrect: \(\overline{CB}\) crosses the two parallel segments \(\overline{DE}\) and \(\overline{AC}\), so angle \(DEB\) and angle \(ACB\) are corresponding angles and therefore equal: 58°. The ratio \(AB = 1.5DB\) fixes how much smaller the inner triangle is, but a scale factor never changes an angle, so it plays no part in the answer.
note: The book shows this only as a figure; the sentence placing D on AB and E on CB has been written into the stem so the question stands without the picture.

stem: A triangle has a base length of 82 centimeters and a height of 164 centimeters. What is the area, in square centimeters, of the triangle?
whyCorrect: Area of a triangle is \(\frac{1}{2}bh\). Here that is \(\frac{1}{2}(82)(164) = 41 \times 164 = 6{,}724\) square centimeters.

whyWrong.A: 246 is 82 + 164, adding the two lengths instead of multiplying them.
whyWrong.B: 3,362 is \(\frac{1}{2}\) of 82 times \(\frac{1}{2}\) of 164 — the one-half applied twice.
whyWrong.D: 13,448 is \(82 \times 164\), the area of a rectangle with those dimensions. A triangle is half of it.

stem: Triangles \(ABC\) and \(DEF\) are congruent, where \(A\) corresponds to \(D\), and \(B\) and \(E\) are right angles. The measure of angle \(A\) is 27°. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle \(F\)?
whyCorrect: Angle \(F\) is not the partner of angle \(A\). With \(A\) matching \(D\) and \(B\) matching \(E\), the leftover vertices \(C\) and \(F\) match each other. Find angle \(C\) first: \(180 - 90 - 27 = 63^\circ\). Congruent triangles have equal corresponding angles, so angle \(F\) is also 63°.
note: Same template as ma2 Triangles #1 (62°) and #12 (71°); do not place more than one in a test.

stem:
In triangle ABC and triangle DEF, sides \( \overline{AB} \) and \( \overline{DE} \) each have a side length of 10 inches, and angles A and D each have an angle measure of 40°. Which of the following additional pieces of information is (are) sufficient to prove whether triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF?

I. The measures of angles B and C are equal.
II. The lengths of sides \( \overline{AC} \) and \( \overline{DF} \) are equal.
III. The lengths of sides \( \overline{BC} \) and \( \overline{EF} \) are equal.

choices.label: A
choices.content: I is sufficient, but II and III are not.

choices.label: B
choices.content: II is sufficient, but I and III are not.

choices.label: C
choices.content: III is sufficient, but I and II are not.

choices.label: D
choices.content: II is sufficient and III is sufficient, but I is not.

whyCorrect: Statement II adds the side on the other arm of the 40° angle, so you have side-angle-side with the angle between the two known sides — that fixes the triangle completely, and SAS proves congruence. Statement I only describes triangle ABC and says nothing at all about DEF. Statement III gives side-side-angle, with the equal angle not between the equal sides, which is the ambiguous case: two different triangles can share those measurements.

whyWrong.A: I compares two angles inside the same triangle. It constrains the shape of ABC but tells you nothing about DEF, so it cannot decide congruence.
whyWrong.C: III is SSA. Because BC lies opposite the known 40° angle rather than beside it, two non-congruent triangles can satisfy every stated measurement.
whyWrong.D: II works, but adding III to it is the SSA trap. Only the included-angle version, SAS, is a congruence criterion.

stem: Triangles \(ABC\) and \(DEF\) are similar. Each side length of triangle \(ABC\) is 2 times the corresponding side length of triangle \(DEF\). The area of triangle \(ABC\) is 300 square centimeters. What is the area, in square centimeters, of triangle \(DEF\)?
whyCorrect: Areas scale by the square of the length ratio, not the ratio itself. Lengths in \(ABC\) are 2 times those in \(DEF\), so the area of \(ABC\) is \(2^2 = 4\) times the area of \(DEF\). Therefore \(DEF\) has area \(300 \div 4 = 75\) square centimeters. Dividing by 2 instead gives 150, which is the usual mistake here.

stem:
Triangles \(ABC\) and \(DEF\) are similar, where \(A\) corresponds to \(D\), and \(B\) corresponds to \(E\). The measure of angle \(A\) is 26°, and \(AB = 4\). Which of the following statements must be true?

I. The measure of angle \(D\) is 26°
II. \(DE = 4\)
whyCorrect: Similar means same shape, not same size. Corresponding angles are always equal, so angle \(D\) must be 26° and I holds. Corresponding sides are only proportional, so \(DE\) could be 4 but could equally be 2 or 40 — nothing fixes the scale factor, so II is not forced.

whyWrong.B: II is the statement that is not guaranteed. Similarity permits any scale factor.
whyWrong.C: This would require the triangles to be congruent, which similarity alone does not give.
whyWrong.D: I is guaranteed: equal corresponding angles is exactly what similarity means.

note: The book labels both roman numerals "I."; the second is II and has been renumbered.

stem: A triangle inequality theorem states that the sum of any two sides of a triangle must be greater than the length of the third side. If a triangle has side lengths of 8 and 13, which of the following inequalities represents the possible length, \(x\), of the third side of the triangle?
whyCorrect: Apply the inequality all three ways, not just once. \(8 + 13 > x\) gives \(x < 21\); \(8 + x > 13\) gives \(x > 5\); \(13 + x > 8\) is automatic for a positive length. Both real constraints must hold at the same time, so \(5 < x < 21\). The shortcut worth remembering: the third side lies strictly between the difference and the sum of the other two.

whyWrong.A: This is only the upper bound. It allows \(x = 2\), and a triangle with sides 2, 8, 13 cannot close because 2 + 8 < 13.
whyWrong.B: Backwards — 21 is the largest \(x\) can approach, not the smallest.
whyWrong.D: This is the set of lengths that make a triangle impossible, the exact opposite of what is asked.

stem: The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is 876 centimeters. The three vertices of the triangle lie on a circle. The radius of the circle is \( w\sqrt{3} \) centimeters. What is the value of w?
whyCorrect: The side is \( \frac{876}{3} = 292 \) . For an equilateral triangle the circumradius is \( R = \frac{s}{\sqrt{3}} \) (from \( R = \frac{s}{2\sin 60^{\circ}} \) ), so \( R = \frac{292}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{292\sqrt{3}}{3} \) . Matching that against \( w\sqrt{3} \) gives \( w = \frac{292}{3} \) . Do not confuse this with the inradius \( \frac{s}{2\sqrt{3}} \) , which is half as large.
note: Exact value 292/3, about 97.33. Enter as the fraction 292/3.

stem: In \(\triangle FGH\), the measure of \(\angle F\) and \(\angle G\) are each 39°. What is the measure of \(\angle H\)?
whyCorrect: The two equal angles account for \(39 + 39 = 78\) degrees. The three angles of a triangle total 180°, so \(\angle H = 180 - 78 = 102^\circ\).

whyWrong.A: 78° is the combined measure of \(\angle F\) and \(\angle G\), not what remains for \(\angle H\).
whyWrong.C: 129° is 90 + 39, which would only apply if one of the angles were a right angle.
whyWrong.D: 141° is 180 − 39, subtracting only one of the two 39° angles.

stem: In the figure shown, \(A\), \(C\) and \(E\) lie on one line in that order, \(B\) lies on \(\overline{AD}\), and \(\overline{BC}\) and \(\overline{DE}\) are both perpendicular to \(\overline{AE}\). If \(AB = \sqrt{89}\) units, \(AC = 8\) units, and \(CE = 24\) units, what is the area, in square units, of triangle \(ADE\)?
whyCorrect: First get \(BC\) from the small right triangle \(ABC\): \(BC = \sqrt{89 - 64} = \sqrt{25} = 5\). Triangles \(ABC\) and \(ADE\) share the angle at \(A\) and both have a right angle, so they are similar, and \(AE = 8 + 24 = 32\) is 4 times \(AC = 8\). That makes \(DE = 4 \times 5 = 20\). Finally the area of \(ADE\) is \(\frac{1}{2}(32)(20) = 320\).
note: The book gives the arrangement only in the figure; the sentence placing A, C, E on a line with B on AD and the two perpendiculars has been written into the stem so the question stands without the picture.

stem: In triangle \(ABC\), angle \(B\) is a right angle. The length of side \(AB\) is \(10\sqrt{39}\) and the length of side \(BC\) is \(24\sqrt{39}\). What is the length of side \(AC\)?
whyCorrect: \(AC\) is the hypotenuse, so \(AC^2 = (10\sqrt{39})^2 + (24\sqrt{39})^2 = 100(39) + 576(39) = 676(39)\). Since \(676 = 26^2\), \(AC = 26\sqrt{39}\). The common factor \(\sqrt{39}\) rides along untouched, so really you are just using the 10-24-26 right triangle.

whyWrong.A: \(14\sqrt{39}\) is the difference \(24 - 10\) times \(\sqrt{39}\). Subtracting legs is not the Pythagorean theorem.
whyWrong.C: \(34\sqrt{39}\) is the sum \(10 + 24\) times \(\sqrt{39}\), which would make the triangle degenerate — the hypotenuse is always shorter than the two legs combined.
whyWrong.D: This drops the leg \(AB\) entirely and mixes up the coefficient with the radicand.

stem: In triangle \(ABC\) and triangle \(DEF\), \(AB\) and \(DE\) are each equal to 5 centimeters, and angles \(A\) and \(D\) each have measure 35°. Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle \(ABC\) is congruent to triangle \(DEF\)?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The lengths of sides \(BC\) and \(EF\) are equal.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The lengths of sides \(AC\) and \(DF\) are equal.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The measures of angles \(B\) and \(C\) are equal.

choices.label: D
choices.content: No additional information is necessary to prove that the two triangles are congruent.

whyCorrect: Angle \(A\) lies between sides \(AB\) and \(AC\), and angle \(D\) lies between \(DE\) and \(DF\). Adding \(AC = DF\) therefore completes side-angle-side, with the known angle sandwiched between the two known sides, and SAS guarantees congruence.

whyWrong.A: \(BC\) is opposite angle \(A\), not next to it, so this gives side-side-angle. That arrangement is ambiguous — two genuinely different triangles can share it.
whyWrong.C: This compares two angles inside triangle \(ABC\) to each other and says nothing about triangle \(DEF\), so it cannot connect the two.
whyWrong.D: One side and one angle leave the triangle wide open; the third piece of information is genuinely needed.

note: Same template as ma2 Triangles #15 and #63; do not place more than one in a test.

stem: In the figure, \(LQ\) intersects \(MP\) at point \(R\), and \(\overline{LM}\) is parallel to \(\overline{PQ}\). The lengths of \(MR\), \(LR\), and \(RP\) are 9, 10, and 19, respectively. What is the length of \(LQ\)?
whyCorrect: The vertical angles at \(R\) are equal, and \(\overline{LM} \parallel \overline{PQ}\) makes the alternate interior angles equal, so \(\triangle LRM \sim \triangle QRP\) with \(L \to Q\), \(M \to P\). That gives \(\frac{LR}{QR} = \frac{MR}{PR} = \frac{9}{19}\), so \(QR = 10 \cdot \frac{19}{9} = \frac{190}{9}\). The question asks for the whole segment: \(LQ = LR + RQ = 10 + \frac{190}{9} = \frac{280}{9}\).

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{280}{19}\) uses the ratio upside down, dividing by 19 where the similar triangles call for 9.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{190}{9}\) is \(RQ\) alone. You still have to add \(LR = 10\) to reach \(Q\) from \(L\).
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{271}{9}\) is \(\frac{190}{9}\) plus 9, adding \(MR\) instead of \(LR\).

stem: In the figure shown, the measure of angle \(X\) is 52°. The length of \(\overline{XY}\) is 24 units and the length of \(\overline{XZ}\) is 17 units. What is the area, in square units, of triangle \(XYZ\)?
whyCorrect: \(XY\) and \(XZ\) are the two sides meeting at the 52° angle, so use \(\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C\): \(\frac{1}{2}(24)(17)\sin 52^\circ = 204\sin 52^\circ\). Equivalently, the height from \(Z\) down to \(\overline{XY}\) is \(17\sin 52^\circ\), and \(\frac{1}{2}(24)(17\sin 52^\circ)\) is the same thing.

whyWrong.A: 204 is \(\frac{1}{2}(24)(17)\), which would be the area only if the angle at \(X\) were 90°. Since it is 52°, the height is shorter than 17.
whyWrong.B: 408 is the full product \(24 \times 17\) — no halving and no sine.
whyWrong.D: 408 sin 52° leaves out the factor of \(\frac{1}{2}\); it is the area of the parallelogram on those two sides.

stem: A property owner wants to find the length \(x\), in feet, across a pond. \(PR\) intersects \(ST\) at point \(Q\), triangle \(PTQ\) is similar to triangle \(RSQ\), and \(x\) is the length of \(\overline{PT}\). The lengths represented by \(PQ\), \(TQ\), \(QS\), and \(RS\) were determined to be 4,200 feet, 8,400 feet, 1,400 feet, and 1,600 feet, respectively. What is the value of \(x\)?
whyCorrect: In \(\triangle PTQ \sim \triangle RSQ\) the vertices pair up as \(P \to R\), \(T \to S\), \(Q \to Q\), so \(\overline{PT}\) corresponds to \(\overline{RS}\) and \(\overline{TQ}\) corresponds to \(\overline{SQ}\). Find the scale factor from the pair you know completely: \(\frac{TQ}{SQ} = \frac{8{,}400}{1{,}400} = 6\). Then \(PT = 6 \times RS = 6 \times 1{,}600 = 9{,}600\) feet. \(PQ\) is not needed.
note: The book labels x only on the figure; the stem now states that x is the length of PT so the question stands without the picture.

stem: In triangle \(ABC\), angle \(B\) is a right angle, the measure of angle \(C\) is 30°, and \(BC = 36\sqrt{3}\). What is the value of \(\cos A\)?
whyCorrect: The three angles must total 180°, so angle \(A = 180 - 90 - 30 = 60^\circ\), and \(\cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\). The side length \(36\sqrt{3}\) is not needed — a cosine depends only on the angle, not on how big the triangle is.
note: Answer 1/2 (equivalently 0.5). The given side length is not used.

stem: In triangle \(ABC\), the measure of angle \(A\) is 52° and \(AC = 35\). In triangle \(PQR\), the measure of angle \(P\) is 52° and \(PR = 105\). Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle \(ABC\) is similar to triangle \(PQR\)?

choices.label: C
choices.content: The measures of angle \(B\) and angle \(R\) are 34° and 94°, respectively.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The measures of angle \(B\) and angle \(Q\) are 52° and 34°, respectively.

whyCorrect: Two pairs of equal angles are enough for similarity. If angle \(B = 34^\circ\) then angle \(C = 180 - 52 - 34 = 94^\circ\); if angle \(R = 94^\circ\) then angle \(Q = 180 - 52 - 94 = 34^\circ\). Both triangles then have angles 52°, 34°, 94°, matching as \(A \leftrightarrow P\), \(B \leftrightarrow Q\), \(C \leftrightarrow R\).

whyWrong.A: For side-angle-side similarity the two sides around the 52° angle must be in the same ratio. \(AC : PR\) is 35 : 105 = 1 : 3, but \(AB : PQ\) would be 30 : 30 = 1 : 1, so this actually rules similarity out.
whyWrong.B: \(AB\) corresponds to \(PQ\) and \(QR\) corresponds to \(BC\). Knowing one side from each triangle that are not partners tells you nothing about the ratio.
whyWrong.D: This gives triangle \(ABC\) angles 52°, 52°, 76° and triangle \(PQR\) angles 52°, 34°, 94°. Those sets do not match, so it disproves similarity rather than proving it.

note: Same template as ma2 Triangles #56 (58°, 30 and 120); do not place both in one test.

stem: In triangle \(ABC\), the measure of angle \(A\) is 58° and \(AC = 30\). In triangle \(PQR\), the measure of angle \(P\) is 58° and \(PR = 120\). Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle \(ABC\) is similar to triangle \(PQR\)?

choices.label: C
choices.content: The measures of angle \(B\) and angle \(R\) are 34° and 88°, respectively

choices.label: D
choices.content: The measures of angle \(B\) and angle \(Q\) are 58° and 34°, respectively

whyCorrect: Angle-angle is enough for similarity. With angle \(B = 34^\circ\), angle \(C = 180 - 58 - 34 = 88^\circ\); with angle \(R = 88^\circ\), angle \(Q = 180 - 58 - 88 = 34^\circ\). Both triangles then have angles 58°, 34°, 88° matched as \(A \leftrightarrow P\), \(B \leftrightarrow Q\), \(C \leftrightarrow R\).

whyWrong.A: Side-angle-side similarity needs both sides around the 58° angle in the same ratio. \(AC : PR\) is 30 : 120 = 1 : 4, while \(AB : PQ\) here is 35 : 35 = 1 : 1, so this contradicts similarity.
whyWrong.B: \(AB\) pairs with \(PQ\) and \(QR\) pairs with \(BC\). One side from each triangle that are not partners fixes no ratio.
whyWrong.D: This makes triangle \(ABC\) 58°, 58°, 64° and triangle \(PQR\) 58°, 34°, 88° — different shapes, so it disproves similarity.

note: Same template as ma2 Triangles #51 (52°, 35 and 105); do not place both in one test.

stem: In triangle \(FGH\), the measure of angle \(F\) is 63°. Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle \(FGH\) is a right triangle?

choices.label: D
choices.content: The sum of the measures of angles \(F\), \(G\), and \(H\) is 180°.

whyCorrect: If angle \(H\) is 27°, the remaining angle is \(180 - 63 - 27 = 90^\circ\), so angle \(G\) is a right angle and the triangle is right. Notice 63 and 27 are complementary, which is the hint that the third angle takes the whole 90°.

whyWrong.A: A single side length tells you nothing about the angles — the triangle can be stretched at that side length into any shape.
whyWrong.B: Same problem. One length with no other length or angle to compare it against fixes nothing.
whyWrong.D: That sum is 180° in every triangle, so this statement adds no information at all.

stem: In triangle \(DEF\), the measure of angle \(D\) is 47° and the measure of angle \(E\) is 97°. In triangle \(RST\), the measure of angle \(R\) is 47° and the measure of angle \(S\) is 97°. Which of the following additional pieces of information is needed to determine whether triangle \(DEF\) is similar to triangle \(RST\)?

choices.label: C
choices.content: The measure of angle \(F\) and the measure of angle \(T\)

whyCorrect: Two pairs of equal angles already guarantee similarity — that is the angle-angle criterion. The third angle is forced anyway: both are \(180 - 47 - 97 = 36^\circ\). So nothing further is required.

whyWrong.A: Angle \(F\) is determined by the two angles you already have; measuring it adds nothing new.
whyWrong.B: Same for angle \(T\) — it must be 36° whatever you do.
whyWrong.C: Both are already determined, so knowing both is still no new information.

stem: In right triangle \(ABC\), angle \(B\) is a right angle, the measure of angle \(C\) is 30°, and \(CA = 124\). What is the value of \(\tan A\)?
whyCorrect: The angles total 180°, so angle \(A = 180 - 90 - 30 = 60^\circ\), and \(\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.732\). The length 124 never enters — a tangent depends only on the angle. If you prefer to see it through the sides: the leg opposite \(A\) is \(124\sin 60^\circ = 62\sqrt{3}\) and the leg adjacent is \(124\sin 30^\circ = 62\), and their ratio is \(\sqrt{3}\).
note: Exact answer \(\sqrt{3}\); as a grid-in enter 1.732 (or 1.73). Not a whole number.

stem: In the figure shown, triangle \(CAE\) is similar to triangle \(CBD\). The measure of angle \(CBD\) is 57°, and \(AE = 21(BD)\). What is the measure of angle \(CAE\)?
whyCorrect: Read the similarity statement in order: \(C \to C\), \(A \to B\), \(E \to D\). So angle \(CAE\) corresponds to angle \(CBD\), and corresponding angles in similar triangles are equal — 57°. The relation \(AE = 21(BD)\) is the scale factor, which stretches lengths and leaves angles alone.

whyWrong.A: Multiplying the angle by the scale factor gives 1,197°, which is not even a possible angle in a triangle.
whyWrong.B: Adding the scale factor to the angle mixes two different kinds of quantity; a ratio of lengths cannot be added to a number of degrees.
whyWrong.D: 21 is the scale factor, not an angle.

stem: A right triangle has a leg of length 14 and a hypotenuse of length 27. The angle formed by that leg and the hypotenuse has measure \(x\). What is the value of \(\cos x\)?
whyCorrect: Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse. The leg of length 14 forms the angle together with the hypotenuse, so it is the adjacent side, and the hypotenuse is 27. That gives \(\cos x = \frac{14}{27}\), about 0.519. You never need the third side.
note: The book shows only a labelled figure (right angle at the foot of the leg marked 14, hypotenuse marked 27, x at the top vertex); the stem has been written out so the question stands without the picture. Answer 14/27 (about 0.5185), not an integer.

stem: \[2\cos(90 - a)^\circ \cdot \cos b^\circ + \sin(a + y)^\circ \cdot \sin(90 - b)^\circ\]In the given expression, \(a\) and \(b\) are constants such that \(\sin a^\circ = 0.5\), \(\cos b^\circ = 0.99\), and \(0 < b < 90\). What is the value of the given expression when \(y = 0\)?
whyCorrect: Use the cofunction identities rather than trying to find \(a\) and \(b\) themselves. \(\cos(90 - a)^\circ = \sin a^\circ = 0.5\) and \(\sin(90 - b)^\circ = \cos b^\circ = 0.99\). With \(y = 0\), \(\sin(a + y)^\circ = \sin a^\circ = 0.5\). The expression becomes \(2(0.5)(0.99) + (0.5)(0.99) = 0.99 + 0.495 = 1.485\).
note: Answer 1.485 exactly; it fits a grid-in without rounding.

stem: In right triangle \(ABC\), angle \(C\) is a right angle, \(AC = 12\) and \(AB = 24\). What is the value of \(\sin A\)?
whyCorrect: The quickest route is through the angle. \(AC\) is adjacent to \(A\) and \(AB\) is the hypotenuse, so \(\cos A = \frac{12}{24} = \frac{1}{2}\), which makes \(A = 60^\circ\) and \(\sin A = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866\). The long way works too: \(BC = \sqrt{24^2 - 12^2} = 12\sqrt{3}\), and \(\sin A = \frac{12\sqrt{3}}{24} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
note: The book gives the triangle only as a figure (right angle at C, AC = 12, AB = 24); written into the stem. Exact answer \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\); as a grid-in enter .866 or 0.866.

stem: In right triangle \(RST\), angle \(S\) is a right angle, \(TR = 53\) and \(RS = \sqrt{105}\). What is the value of \(\sin R\)?
whyCorrect: \(\sin R\) is the side opposite \(R\) over the hypotenuse, that is \(\frac{TS}{TR}\), so you need \(TS\) first. By the Pythagorean theorem \(TS = \sqrt{53^2 - (\sqrt{105})^2} = \sqrt{2809 - 105} = \sqrt{2704} = 52\). Therefore \(\sin R = \frac{52}{53}\), about 0.981. Note the radical disappears the moment you square it.
note: The book gives the triangle only as a figure (right angle at S, hypotenuse TR = 53, RS = \(\sqrt{105}\)); written into the stem. Answer 52/53 (about 0.9811), not an integer.

stem: In right triangle \(QRS\), angle \(R\) is a right angle and \(RS = 47\). Which expression represents the length of \(\overline{QS}\)?
whyCorrect: With the right angle at \(R\), the hypotenuse is \(\overline{QS}\) and the side \(\overline{RS}\) is opposite angle \(Q\). So \(\sin Q = \frac{RS}{QS} = \frac{47}{QS}\), and rearranging gives \(QS = \frac{47}{\sin Q}\). A sanity check: the hypotenuse is the longest side, and dividing by \(\sin Q\) (a number below 1) makes the result larger than 47, as it must be.

whyWrong.A: \(47\cos Q\) is smaller than 47, so it cannot be the hypotenuse. It also uses the wrong ratio — 47 is opposite \(Q\), not adjacent to it.
whyWrong.B: \(47\sin Q\) is the result of multiplying instead of dividing; it is smaller than 47 and so cannot be the hypotenuse.
whyWrong.C: This treats 47 as the side adjacent to \(Q\). The side adjacent to \(Q\) is \(\overline{QR}\), not \(\overline{RS}\).

note: The book gives the triangle as a figure with the right angle at R and RS = 47, plus the condition QR < RS, which is not needed; written into the stem.

stem: In triangle \(XYZ\), angle \(Y\) is a right angle, the measure of angle \(Z\) is 39°, and the length of \(\overline{YZ}\) is 22 units. If the area, in square units, of triangle \(XYZ\) can be represented by the expression \(k\tan 39^\circ\), where \(k\) is a constant, what is the value of \(k\)?
whyCorrect: The right angle is at \(Y\), so the two legs \(\overline{XY}\) and \(\overline{YZ}\) serve as base and height. From angle \(Z\), \(\tan 39^\circ = \frac{XY}{YZ} = \frac{XY}{22}\), so \(XY = 22\tan 39^\circ\). The area is \(\frac{1}{2}(22)(22\tan 39^\circ) = 242\tan 39^\circ\), so \(k = 242\). Do not evaluate the tangent — it stays in the expression.

stem: What is the diameter of the circle in the \(xy\)-plane with equation \((x - 5)^2 + (y - 4)^2 = 64\)?
whyCorrect: In the form \((x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2\), the number on the right is the radius squared. Here \(r^2 = 64\), so \(r = 8\), and the diameter is \(2r = 16\). Answering 64 or 8 means stopping one step early.

stem: \[(x + 3)^2 + (y - 4)^2 = 25\]In the \(xy\)-plane, the graph of the given equation is a circle. Which point lies on this circle?
whyCorrect: A point is on the circle when substituting it makes the left side equal 25. With \(x = \sqrt{11} - 3\), the term \(x + 3\) collapses to \(\sqrt{11}\); with \(y = \sqrt{14} + 4\), the term \(y - 4\) collapses to \(\sqrt{14}\). So the left side is \(11 + 14 = 25\). The radicals are chosen so the shifts cancel — look for that instead of computing.

whyWrong.A: \((-3, 4)\) is the centre, where the left side evaluates to 0, not 25. The centre is never on its own circle.
whyWrong.B: Substituting gives \(6^2 + (-8)^2 = 100\), which is the circle of radius 10, not 5.
whyWrong.C: The signs are flipped, so nothing cancels: you get \((\sqrt{11}+6)^2 + (\sqrt{14}-8)^2\), which is about 133, not 25.

stem: Circle \(A\) has equation \((x - 3)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 16\). In the \(xy\)-plane, circle \(B\) is obtained by translating circle \(A\) to the right 2 units. Which equation represents circle \(B\)?
